Destined to chart the course of Freemasonry in California during
the Centennial Observance of the Grand Lodge the Most Worshipful
Ullaworth Meyer, 84th Grand Master of Masons in California, has
completed a climactic episode in his career.
He was born in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, on February 27, 1905,
the son of Leonard H. and Ida A. Meyer.
Upon completion of elementary and high school education Brother
Meyer enrolled in Pomona College, there receiving his A.B. Degree,
and continued the pursuit of education at the University of California
and at the University of Southern California, receiving his LL.B. Degree
at the latter.
These early years of manhood foreshadowed recognition of outatanding ability, most noteworthy that of being selected one of the
national winners of the Inter-Collegiate Oratorical Contest in 1926 and
being President of the U.S.C. Student Body, 1929-30. His interest in
and service to these institutions has been constant as evidenced by
service as President of the University Dinner Club, 1943-1945, President of Pomona College Alumni Association, 1945-46, and as a member
of the Board of Trustees of California College in China Foundation
since 1946.
On June 18, 1930, he was united in marriage to Miss Hazel E.
Reeves, whose graciousness is well known. This union has been blessed
by two children, Sondra Jean and Grant Edward.
Pursuing the legal profession as a means of livelihood Brother Meyer
served as Deputy City Attorney, City of Los Angeles, 1930-1945,
became "Municipal Judge in 1945 and in 1949 was elevated to the
Superior Court Bench which office he now holds' by virtue of election
in 1950.
His Masonic career commenced in Claremont Lodge No. 436 where
he was Raised on March 25, 1927. Later, becoming a charter member
of Liberal Arts Lodge No. 677, he served as Master of that Lodge in
1934. Activity in affairs of Grand Lodge followed by appointment to

the Board ol Directors oE the U.C.L.A. Clubhouse in 1935, he being
Vice-Chairman from 1937 to 1948 and Chairman from 1948 to date.
From 1940 to 1942 he was a member of the Co~mittee on Credentials,
from 1940 to 1946 a member of the Committee on Lodge Research and
member of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes, 1946-1949.
Further honor and recognition were bestowed in his appointment as
Grand Orator in 1939 and in 1942, as Inspector of the 85th Masonic
District which duty he fulfilled until 1946. During this period, in 1944,
the Order of DeMolay elected Brother Meyer to the Honorary Legion
of Honor. After election as Junior Grand Warden in 1946 he was
progressively chosen Senior Grand Warden in 1947, Deputy Grand
Master in 1948 and Grand Master in 1949, to serve during the 1950
Centennial Observance year.
His outstanding career in Scottish Rite Freemasonry strikes a
parallel with that of Blue Lodge Freemasonry and the Grand Lodge.
Becoming a 32° member of Los Angeles Consistory, A. & A. S. R., in
1937, his contributions to Masonry were early recognized by election,
in 1939, by the Supreme Council of the Thirty~third Degree to the rank
of Knight Commander of the Court of Honor and, by similar procedure
of that august body, being coroneted a 33° Mason in 1943. From 1942
to 1946 he served as Master of Kadosh and presently is Venerable
Master of the Los Angeles Consistory. having held that distinction since
1945.
Among various civic activities has been his participation in the
direction of the Midnight Mission in Los Angeles as a member of the
Board of Directors from 1943 to date and as President in 1944.
Two outstanding events during the Grand Master's year were the
dedication of the restored Columbia Masonic Temple and the laying
of the corner stone of the Crippled Childrens Hospital. in Los Angeles,
being constructed by Al Malaikah Temple. A.A.O.N.M.S .• of which
Brother Meyer is a member.
Throughout this epochal year in the history of California Freemasonry the Fraternty has been fortunate in having as its Grand Master
one whose untiring devotion and proven capability assured leadership
and accomplishment of which we may be justly proud.
Each task falling upon the Grand Master, and numerous and demanding they have been, has received no less attention and effort than
essential for proper fulAllment. Yet, each seemed transformed to a
pleasure through his competent and respectful manner.
Difficult will be the challenge to those who follow if they would
emulate or surpass his affability and sincerity which have been so
enjoyed throughout the jurisdiction, particularly by the lay-members of
the Fraternity.
Finis coronat opus.

2,638 officers and representatives from 586 Lodges and nine Lodges
under dispensation, together with 2,286 Master Masons, were reported
as present, and the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge was opened in ample
form, following which the Flag of our Country was received, held at
the altar while the assembled Brethren sang the "Star Spangled
Banner," and was placed in the East.

In the devotional service this morning, I wish to take as a theme an
rlptlon on the capitol building at Sacramento "Give me men to
111.i"h my mountains" and as a text from the Holy Word, that Magna
l huta declaration of man's true greatness found in the 8th Psalm:
1
When I consider Thy heavens, the moon and the stars which Thou
h1 i ordained, what is man that Thou are mindful of him, or the son of
ffi 1U1 that Thou visitest him. For Thou hast made him but a little lower
thnn God. Thou crownest him with glory and honor. Thou has made
him to have dominion over the works of Thy hands. Thou hast put all
things under his feet." And as a keynote, that bugle call by Paul to the
1rly Christian Church: "Quit you like men. Be strong."

1111

Very many years ago, my family, knowing my love of mountain
t1tll1, gave me a pair of high hiking boots. I wore them for decades.
!'hey grew shabby and were often resoled. What a saga these boots
ould have told, for they had taken my tired feet over so many of the
t11U1 in all sections of our California mountains. I think I can say, I
know the mountains of our State. How I have enjoyed them. What
marvelous mountains they are! To name them is to flash pictures of
trandeur before one's eyes, pictures of titanic peaks, awesome glaciers,
nyons of depth, gem#like little lakes, fragrant mountain meadows,
d11hlng mountain streams. Small wonder that they stirred John Muir
fl ' rapturous expressions of wonder and joy.
What a source of wealth they have been to California. First the
gold found in them, gold that focused the eyes of the world on California.
Uut more wealth has come from the fertile valleys of California than was
ver panned or dug from her gulches. But it has been the silt from these
mountains that has made these valleys verdant and productive. But for
the mountains, California would be a desert. It has been the mountain#
d streams and great irrigation systems that have transformed arid
w11te#land into garden spots of production and beauty. In these same
mountains has been developed the hydro#electrical power that lights
our homes and provides the motive power that has made possible the
111mendous development in manufacturing. These mountains are a
perennial ·source of delight to artists and all lovers of beauty. They
J'll'OV!de a vacation land without a peer. They are tonic zones for health
ind zestful living. The sight of them exalts all beholders with a vision
>f Immensity and grandeur. I am grateful that they have been on my
horizon nearly all my life.

. PROCEEDINGS OF THE

As we of today think of these mountains, we realize our debt to
them and rejoice that they are a part of our commonwealth.
But a century ago, the impact they made was totally different. As
those dust-stained pioneers came West, how appalled they must have
been by those frowning ramparts of granite, giant barriers. There they
stretched the entire length of California, threatening in height, terrible in
the tangle of peaks and canyons. They seemed to defy and mock any
who would undertake to cross them.
What daring, what terrific toil. what dauntless courage it required to
make that perilous trip in those covered wagons. What labor, what
vision it has required to master them. We salute those brave men and
women who pioneered the way. Modestly we admit that California is a
great state. But her greatness is due to the fact that her sons and daughters have by faith, courage, energy and patience more than matched
these mountains that in the beginning were mountains of difficulty.
These mountains that were so ominous and threatening to our
pioneer forebears are a fitting symbol of the world today. For we of this
generation are confronted with mountains of danger more terrible than
the Siskiyou or the Sierras were to the pioneers.
It is pertinent to think for a moment, and very sketchily, of some
of the staggering problems that confront us. The greatest achievement
of the ages has been the growing realization of the worth, the dignity,
the greatness of the individual. But a score of movements characteristic
of this modern age conspire to reduce man to pigmy size. The great
Palomar lenses have pushed back the physical boundaries to almost
unbelievable distance. In the vastness of such a universe what is man?
He is less than a speck. The villages, the towns of yesterday have grown
into great sprawling cities that tend to obscure and dwarf the individual
citizen almost to a zero. Giant corporations, great labor unions all tend
to impersonalize human relations. A man is a cog merely in the economic
system. He is only number so and so on the assembly line: he is a serial
number in the army of defense.
Fairly successfully man has developed behavior patterns, social
attitudes, moral standards to enable him to live with a reasonable degree
of peace, good order, decency and happiness in a horse and buggy age,
the age in which I grew to manhood. But by a series of marvelous inventions, the ends of the earth have been brought together. It took us eight
days to come by train in 1888 to California. Now one can travel around
the world in that time. In my early ministry I envied the old-time preachers with the orotund voices that could be heard great distances. But two
years ago I gave the Easter Sunrise message in the Hollywood Bowl.
Our children in Connecticut heard it and made a wire recording, and a
woman in West China heard it over short-wave radio. This illustrates

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

11

the fact that all of a sudden we are called on to develop a technique of
living happily with strange peoples, folks utterly alien in customs, ideas,
language, standards of subsistence, methods of industry.
That was a magic night when the Curies went into a little laboratory
in Paris, and lo, a blue light was burning. Radium had been seccessfully
extracted from pltch-blende. It was a rainy afternoon in a laboratory
under the playing field of Chicago University. A little group of physicists had gathered. One threw a switch, and lo, flssion was a reality.
What terrible power is linked up in these and like discoveries-power
to reduce our vaunted civilization to cave life and jungle obscurity. Possible terrible destruction looms in atomic and hydrogen weapons.
• In the political world we are faced also by dangers more threatening
than any mountain pass. I think it is safe to say liberty and freedom
have never encountered as deadly, diabolical a foe as now menaces them
In world-seeking Communism. The struggle is not to be side-stepped by
scented diplomacy nor appeased by visionaries. The clash of ideas and
principles is inevitable. Freedom and Communism cannot exist in peace
in the same world. How long, how costly in men and treasure the
struggle will be only God knows. Neither can one gauge accurately the
effect of such a struggle on our American way of life.
But as serious as is the threat of Communism without, is the threat
of corroding. disintegrating forces within our republic.
America was born of faith, daring and sacrifice. It was that spirit
that has made her great and prosperous. But today, the whole economy
of America is menaced by the philosophy of the Easy Road, by a willingness to barter our dear-bought liberties for security not realizing that
there is no security in material things, that the only security is an inner
security based on character. Dangerous indeed is the willingness of
multitudes of people to listen and believe in the schemes of half-baked
politicians and venal promoters, that utopias can be produced by legislation. The drift in many fields toward totalitarianism is very ominous:
the nationalization of industry, information, education is a movement
fraught with grave consequences. Socialism however one garbs it is a
halfway house on the road to Communism.
Vast numbers of people have lost the will to do. They want government to support them. Others have lost a sense of responsibility and so
they are saying "Let George do it."
Then like storm clouds over the peaks, are the dark clouds of fear
and doubt, producing a sense of frustration and futility, a feeling of
hopelessness.
Let us say it-frankly, we are living in a most dangerous sort of
world. Confronting us as we look forward are terrifying mountains of
difficulties. But let us not be dismayed. Let us say with the poet Hovey,
"In the face of a dark today here's to a brave tomorrow." Life never has

12

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

been easy. There is no really safe road. An hour of change is always
loaded with peril. But the truth is-a dangerous hour may be the bridge
to 'a great hour. It was so in the Elizabethan Age, it was so with the
landing of the Pilgrim Fathers, it was so when the Declaration of
Independence was signed.
What we need today is men to match these mountains of danger with
their daring, conquer them by wise heroic action, and turn them-as did
the pioneers of a century ago--illto highways to opportunity. · Such men
will be they who put the common good ahead of private advantage, men
of independent mien, possessed of the good sense to cooperate. Men
who couple dreams with deeds. Men of conscience, men with noble
convictions. Men dedicated to fhe right. Men who do not quit when
the going is tough. They will be men with a spiritual faith in God-that
He is, that He is able and that He will not fail. Men with faith in the
universe that it is "no blot nor blunder." Men with faith in themselves,
men with faith in their fellow men.
Such men can master mountains, transform deserts and drive successfully the horses of the sun. These are the men for the hour. Such
men Masons ought to be.
I say this is an hour for Masons. One recalls with pride the glorious
part Masons 'have played in the struggle for liberal institutions, for
truth and freedom in Europe, in America, and in California history.
Again this is an hour for Masons to be true to our historic tradition.
We are here to render service and give dynamic leadership in this time
of crisis. Not as a Grand Lodge nor yet as Lodges, but as individual
Masons, each true to his best light and true to his obligations to follow it.
I say that advisedly. We are picked men, we are not ordinary citi~
zens. We have been selected because of worth and attainments. We
are men who believe in human worth. We are men of character. We are
men who believe in and rely on God. The sorry mess the world is in
today is due primarily to a lack of energizing faith in God. Man seeking
to build by himself the Tower of Babel failed. Man cannot build a safe
society, a good world without God's help, without faith in God. We
have too largely left God out of the equation. We thought we were
clever and scientific and did not need Him. We have put our reliance
in treaties, in systems, in organizations, in tools and gadgets and test
tubes. But they have failed us! We need to "seek Him who made the
Seven Stars and Orion, who tumeth the night into day, who strength~
eneth the spoiled against the strong." We need to remember that before
Him, the eternal God, dynasties and dictators are as the small dust in
the :balance.
We, as Masons, are entitled to know and to possess the wisdom and

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

13

power that come from an alliance with God. In this hour, when many are
palsied with quaking fear, let us bring to our day the confidence that is
born of faith in an omnipotent God. Such a rebirth of faith can change
the climate and the whole aspect of our day.
It is true that we represent only a fraction of our citizenry. But all
progress has been achieved by the pioneering of valiant minorities. It is
remarkable what a few resolute men can do. Starr King, Unitarian
preacher in lawless San Francisco, stricken with tuberculosis, did more
than any other man or group of men to save California to the Union.
That we have the giant Sequoia groves to enjoy as a perpetual heritage
la due to the single-handed crusade John Muir fought for their preser~
vatlon. David Livingstone, sick, plodding the soggy trails of Equatorial
Africa, put fhat continent on the map of the world and on the conscience
of Christendom. This republic of ours exists today because of the wisdom, courage and faith of a small body of men in the colonies. Their
names are now blazoned in glory. It was the belated vote of a sick man,
Caesar Rodney, who rode eighty miles through wind and rain that
helped to carry Richard Henry Lee's Resolution that fateful day, the
2nd of July, 1776.
There are enough good Masons and true in California to master the
mountains of difficulty and danger that do now confront us. So let
us be the pioneers of a nobler Americanism and a wider freedom.
Let us not play the part of Hamlet nor that of Omar Khayyam.
Rather let us say with that young Oxford poet of World War I fame
Rupert Brooke: "Now God be thanked who has matched me with Hi~
hour."
This is a critical moment. Destiny hinges on the way men act today.
This is our hour. Let us quit ourselves like men, like true Masons. Let
us match our hour with conquering courage, sacrifice, wisdom and faith.
To the supreme task-a rebirth of freedom, honor, integrity, faith,
and righteousness let us dedicate ourselves as we face the second century
of Masonry in California.
At this Centennial Communication let us pledge each other and God
that we will preserve our free institutions and keep the Stars and Stripes
11tlll flying over a united, happy, glorious, progressive country-the home
of free men.
To this solemn pledge and endeavor may the Supreme Grand Master
add His divine benediction.
God of our fathers and our God: make us big enough, brave enough,
wise enough, good enough to match our day of destiny and make it the
bridgehead for a greater Tomorrow.

ELLSWORTH MEYER, Grand Master

I wish that I could tell you about the Grand Lodge of California: tell
you how it was formed in a little building at Fifth and J Streets, in
Sacramento, one hundred years ago. I wish that I could paint for you a
word picture of the frontier times and land in which it was born, the
days of 1849 and '50, the days of "Gold in California." I wish that I
could sketch for you its growth from three lodges with a membership
of about one hundred Master Masons to its present . size. But these
cannot be done in an hour.
Instead, it will be necessary to give you facts and figures of 1949 and
'50 and a few suggestions for the future. These recommendations, perhaps, should be of grand proportions to befit an occasion when we are
closing the first century of this Grand Lodge and opening its second,
but I would not judge them so.
Our communication is historic not only ·because of the anniversary
we are observing, .but because of the distinguished guests in attendance.
Never before has a communication been graced by the presence of thirtynine Grand Masters from every part of the Union and five foreign
countries. Never before have we been honored by the presence of a
comparable number of Deputy Grand Masters, Grand Secretaries and
Past Grand Masters from other jurisdictions. Their presence makes us
feel both humble and proud, humble as to our own accomplishments and
proud that they would evidence their interest in Masonry in California
by traveling so far to view it at first hand. If their pleasure is in proportion to our appreciation, we shall indeed be happy.
This afternoon we shall have the pleasure of receiving most of our
guests in a Masonic manner befitting to their positions and a few will
arrive later. I have set aside certain periods on our schedule and requested several of our guests to address the communication on topics of
their selection that you might have the benefit of Masonic thinking on
different subjects. I was confident that they would enjoy hearing some
of the songs of California and to that end requested the Grand Organist
to make certain innovations in the concert and processional which you
have already heard.
Today, the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California extends a
thousand miles from north to south and on the Atlantic Coast would be
from southern Massachusetts to Savannah, Georgia. From its most
easterly lodge to the most westerly is more than two thousand four
hundred miles. Upon its roster are 607 active lodges with a membership
approaching 197,000 Master Masons and within our boundaries reside
another hundred thousand who retain their membership elsewhere. As
has been said each year by the Grand Master, the number of lodges and
our mtmbership constitute new highs, but on this occasion let us not

CONSTITUTION OP NEW LoDGES

The first official duty after our last annual communication was to
constitute the four lodges which received charters and this was done
within the statutory sixty-day period. These lodges were: Bixby Knolls
No. 699, Long Beach, Los Angeles County: Ponderosa No. 700, Fresno,
Fresno County: Santa Ynez Valley No. 701, Los Olivos, Santa Barbara
County and Rosemead No. 702, Rosemead, Los Angeles County. At
each of these ceremonies a large majority of the Grand Lodge officers
attended and their presence and assistance was deeply appreciated.
There were unusual circumstances connected with the constitution
of Santa Ynez Valley Lodge No. 701 and I shall digress for a moment
to recount them. It should first be explained that under our law the
Master of a lodge under dispensation must be named in the charter and
be installed in order to become its first Past Master.
When we gathered at Los Olivos, a very tiny community, our hearts
were heavy because the Master who had served under dispensation had
contracted an eye infection which had required his removal to the
Veterans' Administration Hospital at Van Nuys in Los Angeles County.
I was told that the brethren despaired for his sight and were concerned
for his life.
A large segment of the constitution ceremony is the installation of
the officers and with no Master to install there is quite a gap. The other
parts of the ceremony were performed, but I too was thinking of the
absent brother. During the hundred-odd miles home and the following
days, I kept wondering what a judge could do, within our law, to effect
his installation. A peculiar inquiry from another lodge, a day or two
later, caused the realization that our rule as to public installations could
·be used with entire propriety. Accordingly, a letter was written to the
Senior Warden of Santa Ynez Valley Lodge asking him to open the
lodge on a regular meeting night, to call to refreshment at a designated
hour for the purpose of installing the Master and to remain at refreshment for two hours. Arrangements were also made with the superintendent of the Birmingham Veterans' Hospital and at the appointed
time I drove the thirty miles out to the hospital.
A large room had been made available and in the presence of some
thirty Masons from among the patients and staff, I installed the Master
of Santa Ynez Valley Lodge. After the formalities were completed, in
the course of informal remarks, I stated that it was probably the first
installation in the history of the Grand Lodge of California to which all
but four had come ht their pajamas. For about two hours they told
about Masonry in their different jurisdictions and I answered questions

about California Masonry. Another reward was paid ~)so, because
when I left the hospital the Master walked out with me, cured, discharged and a member of his lodge was there to return him home. I
recall that my warmed-up dinner tasted very good that night and also,
that the reference for the legality of this procedure is Section 786.

elsewhere, Inspectors had six, seven or eight lodges. There were some
Inspectors who found it impossible to devote the necessary time to their
duties.
Accordingly, with the commencement of the new term of office for
Inspectors on January first, several lodges were transferred to other
districts. new districts were created and those which were designated
by a number and letter, which always sounded as if they were annexes
to real districts, were given numbers of their own. The greater number
of changes was effected in the Los Angeles Metropolitan area. Fully
aware of the apprehension which is usually caused in our ranks by any
change, it seemed desirable that the changes should be made by a Grand
Master from the area in which the greater number would occur. It has
been gratifying that so many have privately expressed their pleasure
with the action taken.

PROCLAMATIONS

During the year three proclamations by the Grand Master were sent
to the lodges of the jurisdiction. In reverse order, they were designating
Masonic Homes Endowment Month, Public Schools Week, both of
which have been proclaimed in other years, and a proclamation requiring
the Master of each lodge to appoint a committee to interest sojourning
Masons, who permanently reside in California, in visiting and becoming
active in our lodges.
This latter is an activity which I believe should be continued for
awhile longer. California is unique in regard to the great influx of
families from all over the world and it is regrettably true that many
Masons who come here to make their homes but leave their membership
elsewhere, in time, drop off the Masonic tree. Many who have a sentimental tie to a lodge elsewhere do not know that they may retain that
memb~rs~ip. a~d be ac~ive here, if they come from one of the thirty-six
other JUr1sd1ctions which also permit dual membership. If we manage
to keep these brethren within the Masonic fold we shall have strengthened Freemasonry as a whole, for one who allows his dues to lapse and
is suspended is of no value to the other jurisdictions or California.
Copies of these proclamations will be found in the appendix to this
message.

VISITATIONS

It is stated quite frankly that the year as Grand Master was approached with considerable apprehension because of a personal practice,
never to take time from the bench to appear before any organization. It
did not seem possible to maintain that practice and yet do those things
which are expected of the incumbent of this office. It was clear that the
only way engagements could be met was to schedule all events within
one hundred miles of Los Angeles for nights during the week, so that
a return could be made to the family domicile the same night and to
schedule all events at a greater distance during weekends. I mention
these factors only that I may again express my appreciation to the many
who scheduled meetings in accordance with the plan and that those
situated at points which required travel of two days each way will understand why it was necessary to decline invitations.
The apprehension would have been increased had it been possible
to foresee the unusual number of official meetings, special communications of the Grand Lodge, to dedicate temples and lay cornerstones,
which would occur. In June, the Grand Secretary advised that there
had been more of these than in any one of the past fifteen years and
then went on to make the prophecy th.at reference would be made in
the future t'o "Corner Stone Meyer." I hope not, but a corner stone or
dedication is a rare and happy event in the life of a lodge and some
concessions of time and effort should be made. The concessions which
the officers, from the Grand Tiler to the Deputy Grand Master, made
are worthy of your hearty approbation.

These visitations and affairs entailed travel in excess of 31,000 miles,
most of which was direct air mileage.
It will be observed that the engagements dotted the state fairly well
from San Diego to Sacramento and included three in the Mother Lode
country. It was a matter of regret that it was not feasible to reach the
extreme northern quarter of the state on any occasion, but consolation
was derived from the fact that the Deputy Grand Master hails from
that portion of the state and probably would make up for this year.
The ninety ·appearances listed were possible by an almost exclusive
use of air lines, and the fortunate fact that Mrs. Meyer is an unexcelled
packer of suitcases. When starting back home, I frequently wished that
I had just one more suitcase~ When I was on the ground in the north,
Grand Tiler HQrwege or Grand Pursuivant Triggs usually handled the
wheel and Senior Grand Deacon Edwards drove me to three quarters
of all the affairs between Fresno and San Diego. Not satisfied with that
extensive travel, he usually drove to affairs in the north while I Hew.
His record of attendance is most unusual and praiseworthy.

Included in the list of appearances are several of which particular

meetings here in California. Located in Waco, it is a truly magnificent
building, a modern replica of King Solomon's Temple and it achieves
the spectacular through simplicity. Thirteen grand jurisdictions were

were established at that time. It was most pleasant to 'he with Brother
Albert De Lange, who was instaJled Grand Master, and the Past Grand
. Masters. We shaJI have the pleasure of hearing the Grand Master of

Next in point of time was attendance at the Conference of Grand
Masters of North America in Washington, D. C. and the other meetings
scheduled for the same period. Our Deputy Grand Master, Grand
Secretary and Past Grand Master Ogden also attended these sessions.
In order to insure keeping the Grand Master of California off the streets,
he was assigned the opening address on the agenda of the Conference

As is customary, a visit was made to the George Washington
National Masonic Memorial on Washington's birthday. The sessions
of the association are comparatively brief. but on this occasion were
foJlowed by the unveiling of the seventeen foot bronze statue of the first
President. The speaker for the occasion was the President of the United
States, previous to whom representatives of various Masonic bodies
·
extended brief greetings.
Later, the Deputy Grand Master and I visited Washington-Alexandda Lodge No. 22 of the Grand Lodge of Virginia and witnessed a
third degree conferred by Grand Master Flowers of Virginia, who also
honors us by his presence today. The work was beautifuJly done. This
was the seventh jurisdiction, the ritualistic work of which has been
personally observed. It is fascinating to study the many differences from
jurisdiction to jurisdiction and the common threads which run through

all, even though no two of the forty-nine jurisdictions in the United
States are identical in their ritual. In order that our guests may make
comparisons, we have asked one of our lodges to confer a third degree
on Thursday evening.
On April 19, 1950, the actual centennial day of the Grand Lodge,
the Columbia Broadcasting Company made available the facilities of
their network and the Grand Master delivered a fifteen minute address
on the topic "A Century of Masonry in California." The address was
broadcast in the afternoon and again in the evening. Many requests
from men and women were received for copies of this address and
printed copies were made available by the Scottish Rite Bodies in Los
Angeles. The time of the broadcasts did not coincide with normal lodge
hours and several brethren in different parts of the state made recordings
of the broadcast and have made these and the necessary equipment
available to lodges for use at meetings. One member of the Committee
on Grievances has presented the grievance that he has now heard the
address eight times. His grievance is well taken. A copy of the address
will be found in the appendix to this message.
In accordance with the appropriations made at the last annual communication, I requested the Deputy Grand Master and Grand Wardens
to visit our neighbors. Deputy Grand Master Paulsen attended the
annual communication of the Grand Lodge of Washington, Senior
Grand Warden Drapeau that of Oregon and Junior Grand Warden
Warren that of Nevada. These communications were held in June. I
requested a brother to attend the Grand Lodge of Arizona but unforeseen events prevented representation there this year.
Two pleasurable visits were those to Columbia, first to lay the corner
stone for and then to dedicate the completed Columbia temple which
you have restored in that community. The State of California is revitalizing Columbia as a state park and living memorial to the Gold Rush
Days. The temple has been built on the exact spot occupied by the
original and as nearly similar as research could make it. In laying the
corner stone, I used the trowel which had been used by old Columbia
Lodge No. 28 when it existed. At the dedication ceremony we were
favored by the attendance of six of our Past Grand Masters and a host
of Inspectors and others, some of whom had come from as far as San
Diego for the ceremony. We had a jolly and inspiring afternoon.
Request has been made of the special committee on the restoration
of Columbia temple to present recommendations to you, at this session,
for the maintenance and use of the temple by lodges which desire to
go there to confer degrees and later in this message I will recommend
the amendment of section 121 of the Ordinances to permit the use of
this lodge room as is now possible with respect to the lodge room at
our home at Decoto.
It has become a tradition for the Grand Master each year to officially

visit each of the club houses at the Berkeley and Los Angeles campuses
of the University of California. These visits were particularly pleasur- ·
able to me because graduate study had been taken on the first campus
and some years of membership on the board of the southern club house
had been experienced. Both buildings. although totally different. are
ornaments to their respective communities and do credit to Masonry.
The student groups of 600 active members at each are enthusiastic and,
to use a colloquialism, went all out to express their appreciation for the
facilities you have provided. ·
The remaining visit of which particular mention will be made was
to our eight lodges in the Hawaiian Islands. Each Grand Master who
has visited the Islands has attempted to describe the hospitality of our
brethren and the tropic beauty of this "Paradise of the Pacific." They
would probably be the first to concede that they failed. I freely admit
that I would too. One has to visit the Islands to appreciate the sheer
beauty of Oahu, Maui, Hawaii and Kauai, the four islands on which
we have lodges. Words cannot convey adequate pictures of the eternal
green of mile upon mile of sugar cane, the red earth of the pineapple
fields, or the green growth which goes up one side of the sharp mountains and without break down the other. How can you describe tall
coconut palms curving up and out to the sea? Or the blues of the sea
and sky broken by the white of billowing clouds and rolling surf? Who
could describe for you the beauty of the hulas as performed in the
Islands, not the Hollywood version? Or of the score of different flowers?
Who could hope to capture in words the golden head of a shower tree?
There is an aspect of the Islands which is dangerous and that is its
music. If you have never heard a native sing the original version of an
Hawaiian song you may be better off, for there is something about
Aloha Oe and Kopola which will seep down into you. When you have
heard for the second or third time the Hawiian wedding song, Ke Kali
Nei Au, you are doomed, for you can never again silence those slow,
easy full throated notes, and what is more. you don't want to.
We are happy indeed that each of the eight lodges is represented
by one or more officers at this communication and that both of our
Inspectors in the Islands are present today.

About the same time a notice was brought to my attention that ·
another lodge in this vicinity, was scheduling a "Forty-niner Night" at
which there was to be a drawing for three prizes, a television set, a set
of tires and a case of bonded whiskey. I sent a telegram to the Master
ordering him to abandon this drawing or any other system of distributing prizes.
·
A club, which is really a temple association, in the Los Angeles area
planned an evening of entertainment to raise funds to pay the cost of
refurnishing a temple. The plan was to sell tickets although the price
was printed on the tickets as " Donation $1.00." I advised it that the
proposed distribution of tickets would violate our laws.
Some of our brethren observing non-Masonic groups engaging in
these activities seem to feel that Masonic groups may do so. In the hope
that ' it may serve to clear away the misunderstanding I point out that
section 288 of our Ordinances prohibits any lottery in any Masonic
lodge or any organization in which the prerequisite to membership is
that one be a Mason. It vests in the Grand Master power to suspend
any Mason who participates in a lottery. It is the only instance in which
the Grand Master can suspend a brother from the rights and privileges
of Masonry, and he may do so without filing of charges or a trial in a
constituent lodge. Also, I call attention to the decision of Grand Master
Whitsell, reported in section 740, Ross Digest, that the giving of door
prizes at an entertainment is prohibited and to the decision of Grand
Master Smith, section 795; that a lodge or temple association may not
hold a public entertainment for the purpose of raising funds to pay the
debt on a temple.
Rumors that a group of Knight Templars were contemplating what
would have been a lottery reached' me and I brought the matter to the
attention of the Grand Commander of the Grand Commandery of
California. The rumored event did not take place.
In June, the mail brought tickets for a lottery set up for the Imperial
Council Sessions of the Shrine. The first prize was a luxurious automobile and the proposed prizes descended through some fifty thousand
dollars of merchandise to liquor and coffee. I sent for the DirectorGeneral of the sessions and had him read section 288 of our Ordinances.
That night a notice was sent through the mail to all recipients of tickets
advising them that the tickets previously sent would not be admission
tickets to the temple. would not entitle the holder to any chance on any
prize and would be used solely for the purpose of admission to the
balcony restaurant and a meal therein.
I mention this instance at some length because of the happy differences from those which Grand Master Gaylord had to report as to an
earlier Imperial Council Session and for the further purpose of bringing
home to any future promoter in a lodge or other organization the
existence and efficacy of section 288.

DISCIPLINE

A reading of the annual messages of our Grand Masters in other
years will disclose that each has had to take some disciplinary action.
This year there wasn't even a cloud in the sky for the first six months,
but April brought the first rain.
Contrary to our custom and the proclamation of the Grand Master,
one of our large lodges held a major entertainment on the regular
meeting night during Public Schools Week and a public schools meeting
two nights later. I suspended the Master from office for the next three
months.

The insignia or name of an organization may not be placed on

Two of our Inspectors presented facts relative to an entered apprentice and a fellow craft and questions as to their advan~ement. The
entered apprentice had been initiated some years ago, had not reported
for coaching, in subsequent years had become ill and, over a period of
time, had lost his sight to the extent that from the altar he could not
possibly observe the Master aproaching him. The fellow craft had suffered a heart condition which precluded the second section of the third
degree in even the mild form which alone is authorized. After careful
Inquiry as to details, it was held:
DEc1s10N No. 7.
An entered apprentice or fellowcraft who has become blind, or
whose physical condition has become such that deviations in the
ritual would be necessary. cannot be passed or raised.
One of our entered apprentices became a permanent resident in
another state and requested courtesy work. He was asked to apply to
his lodge for a demit. He did not apply, but wrote further letters and
the Grand Secretary of that jurisdiction made inquiries. Our Grand
Secretary replied explaining that we would not request courtesy work
because he was permanently residing outside California, but we would
be glad to grant a demit on his request so he could petition a lodge at
his new residence. No demit was requested, but he was elected in the
other :jurisdiction and received the other two degrees. He then demanded
a return of fees out here. Unfortunately under our law the granting of
a demit is a prerequisite to a refund. He refused to ask for it and then
made it impossible to grant.
DECISION No. 8.
No refund may be made to an entered .apprentice who was elected
and received further degrees in another jurisdiction without a demit
or relinquishment of jurisdiction by his California lodge.

During the year more than fifty requests were received for decisions
on points of law which already had been decided, approved and reported
in the Ross Digest. Such requests were answered by referring the officer
to the digest and perhaps adding a word of explanation or clarification.
No purpose would be served by repeating those matters now, but I do
report twelve interpretations which were made.
A section frequently interpreted for lodges is section 121, which lays
down requirements as to the place lodge meetings must be held and the
extent to which a dispensation may go. A number of dispositions may
be stated in the following three decisions:
DEc1s10N No. 1.
Under Section 121 of the Ordinances a lodge may hold a meeting
in any suitable building in the city, town or community named in
its dispensation or charter without a dispensation from the Grand
Master.
DECISION No. 2.
Section 121 of the Ordinances, as it now reads, does not empower
the Grand Master to grant a dispensation to confer degrees in the
open. It requires that all meetings of lodges shall be held in a
building.
DEc1s10N No. 3.
Section 121 of the Ordinances limits the power o.f the Grand Master
to grant a dispensation for a meeting in another city to meetings
for the conferring of degrees. He cannot grant such a dispensation
for purposes such as tendering a reception to the Grand Master.
In the absence of a requirement by the Grand Lodge, I could find
no sanction in the general power to make rules and regulations governing local boards of relief, for a Board of Control rule requiring the
approval of the Grand Master before a lodge could join an existing
board .of relief, hence:
DEc1s10N No. 4.
The permission of the Grand Master is not required before a lodge

DEc1s10N No. 5.

An applicant to Menorah Lodge answered "No" to the eighth question on the form of application for the degrees, "Have you ever presented a petition to any Masonic lodge? If so, when and to what lodge?
............. " You will recall that the next question on the form is "Have

DECISION No. 11,
An application for the degrees has been presented to a Masonic
lodge, within the meaning of question eight on the application form,
when the applicant has handed it to a member of the lodge to
which he is applying, even though it may be returned to him or
he may ask to withdraw it. The act to which the quest.ion refers
is not the act of the lodge in receiving it under section 224 of the
Ordinances.
In three instances in which lodges had caused. the incorporation of

DECISION No. 12,
A Master of a lodge, as such, cannot direct the acts of an incorporated temple association unless provision for such control is contained in the articles or by-laws of the corporation.
For your information, I call attention to the seldom known fact that
the Corporations Code of California authorizes external controls of a
non-profit corporation. Reasonable use of these permissive powers might
avoid the possibility of friction.

The personal appearances of the Grand Master were touched upon
earlier, not for the purpose of securing your accolade, but because of a
considered opinion that our present system is not necessary, wise or fair.
It may be said of many of the burdens of the office as Mark Twain
said of the weather, "Everybody talks about it, but nobody does anything about it."
You may estimate for yourselves the time and effort required of any
Grand Master in making personal appearances, but I consider this the
lighter part of the work. The more arduous portion is the never ending
paper work. Under our system whenever a lodge votes to change its
meeting night, its dues, its fees or even to add a holiday it had forgotten
to put in the blank space in the uniform code of by-laws, the ftle must
go to the Grand Master for his approval. The only thing he really passes
upon is whether the lodge gave notice of the proposed change as
required; nevertheless, he must open the letter, read one to three pages,
sign and date the two copies of the amendment. This takes a few
minutes at least and multiplied by the number which come in, the time
consumed is substantial.
Inter-jurisdiction requests for courtesy degrees by or for our lodges
run from one hundred to three hundred in a normal year and much
higher in wartime. These all go to the Grand Master with a file of not
less than three letters. The question upon which his conclusion rests in

each instance is. "Where is the applicant's permanent residence?"
Whenever an elective officer of any of our lodges dies or resigns
the lodge may adopt a resolution requesting permission to hold a special

·
·
Of the so,called decisions on law which the Grand Master makes
in a year the larger number consist of calling attention to the fact that
the matter has already been decided. In each instance checking the
digest, and dictating the reply is required.
About this time you are saying to yourselves, certainly all those
things may well be divided among the Deputy Grand Master and Grand
Wardens. and why is he spending so much time on them? Simply, this:
I propose a short amendment to the section defining the duties of the
Grand Master, to permit him to assign these things to the Deputy Grand
Master or Grand Wardens. IF HE DESIRES TO DO SO. but find
opposition to the idea despite the fact ·that while the Grand Master
and Deputy Grand Master are out of the state to attend the Washington
Conference. the Senior Grand Warden does all of them and while the
Grand Master is out of the state to visit Hawaii, the Deputy Grand
Master does all of them in each instance because of the express provision of Section 29. It seems nonsensical to me that these men have
greater wisdom or ability when the Grand Master is absent than when
he is in the state and I cannot bring myself to believe that installation
as Grand Master in and of itself invests anyone with greater wisdom
than he previously possessed.
The contentions which I have heard against writing into our law
this power have been: The Grand Master can do it if he wants to
without anything being said about the matter and that you wouldn't
stand for it because you want the Grand Master to decide everything.
I have given both arguments due consideration and cannot find merit
in them. From the experience of fifteen years spent advising the boards
and officers of Los Angeles and representing them in court frequently
as to what powers could or could not be delegated, I am persuaded that
the Grand Master may not at present delegate these matters, that is he
may not lawfully. This opinion is expressed categorically because it is
not desirable to engage in a long legal argument on the point: it should
be sufficient to say that even if it can be legally done now, the Ordinances will not be unduly extended by adding exactly 34 more words.

Aa to the second argument, I do not believe that you desire that the
Out offic~r of the Grand Lodge shall be burdened with all this routine
work while the second, third and fourth officers have no work to do
rixcept as trustees of the Masonic Homes.
Prom time t~ time, there may be Grand Masters who wish to pass
upon these routine matters and with that thought in mind. I have framed
the proposed amendment, not to strip these from the incumbent, but to
legally and therefore honestly, permit him to delegate them.

3 lst Observance of Public Schools Week
To the Masters, Wardens and
Brethren of California and Hawaii:
The public school is one of the foundation stones upon which the
American way of life has been built. Awareness of the fact and of
the problems faced by the educational systems of our nation led the
Masons of California to inaugurate Public Schools Week thirty years
ago. With the cooperation of other civic minded groups. it has become
an annual. major event in California.
Today the educational systems of many states face the greatest
challenge in their history. If the challenge is not as great in this state
and if the schools of California are in somewhat better condition than
those elsewhere, no small portion of the credit is due to this annual
observance and all who have participated. There must be no lessening
of interest or support.
·
There is a direct relationship between the equality of the schools
and the interest of the community in its school system. Betterments and
strength will be developed only where there is understanding of problems, active interest and cooperation.
·
I therefore proclaim and direct:
I . That Public Schools Week be obsefved by all our lodges commencing Monday, April 24, 1950.
2. That no meeting other than a Public Schools Observance be
held by any lodge of this jurisdiction, unless its stated meeting
falls during said week and that no degree work be done during
said week.
3. That this proclamation be read at each stated meeting prior to
April 2i, 1950.
Dated: San Francisco, California,
February 9, 1950.

LLOYD E. WILSON

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH
To the Masters ,Wardens and Brethren
of California and Hawaii:
Freemasonry touches life at each level. Our home at Covina influences the lives of children from the first grade of grammar school until
graduation from high school. Our club houses at the Berkeley and Los
Angeles campuses of the University of California benefit those of
college age. Our lodges inspire during the active adult years and our
home at Decato is, a shelter and blessing in the late afternoon years.
Each year during the month of May we are particularly aware of
the opportunity of building the endowment fund for the homes at
Covina and Decato. The annual opportunity of contributing to this
fund comes to each of us without coercion or high pressure salesmanship. It is truly a voluntary matter.
No gift is too large, none too small and all are appreciated. The

41

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

measure of each gift is the ability of the donor in the light of the great
need. The endowment fund has not yet reached the point that the
income from it is sufficient to support the homes, but by steady growth
that goal can be reached.
I therefore proclaim:
That during the month of May 1950 each of the constituent lodges
of this jurisdiction shall devote at least a portion of one meeting to
acquainting our membership with the purpose and condition of the
endowment fund of our Masonic homes.
With cordial greetings, I am,

gold-gold in California, and the greatest migration in history was
under way.
The stories of hunger, thirst, hardship, of heroism and cruelty during that migration are well known, but it is not so widely known that
despite the haste of departure and the feverish desire to reach the gold
ftelds, time was taken by Masons to obtain charters and dispensations
from twelve eastern Grand Lodges for the establishment of fifteen
Masonic Lodges in this fabulous EI Dorado.
From Connecticut to Florida, from the District of Columbia to
Missouri, issued proper authorization for the establishment of lodges
in California.
The Masons who were assembled in Sacramento one hundred
years ago today. belonged to lodges which had been established in
Sacramento, Benton City, Benicia, and San Francisco.
They were motivated not only by their affection for the fraternity,
but by the suffering occasioned by the epidemics which had swept
through the camps and towns, the poverty of those who had come
inadequately equipped, and wide-spread disregard for the hallmarks
of civilization.
They recognized the necessity of banding together the good men
and true of different cities who had knelt at Masonic altars, who were
disciples of brotherly love and temperance in thought and deed: men
who understood and practiced charity.
In that first Grand Lodge session were men from Sacramento who
established the first hospital in California, who nursed the victims of
the several cholera epidemics, buried the dead, and expended more than
$33,000 of personal funds for the relief of the needy and the afflicted.
In the fever for gold, other men might become calloused, turn from
the hungry, the widow, and the orphan, but to these men of Masonry,
our doctrine of the Fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man was
no lofty preachment. no sounding pretensions: it was a way of life.
The presiding officer of the two-day convention which preceded the
formation of the Grand Lodge was Charles Gilman, a San Francisco
lawyer of note, who had already served one year as Grand Master in
New Hampshire and six years as Grand Master in Maryland. He was
the logical choice to be the first Grand Master in California, but
intended to return east shortly and deferred in favor of Colonel Jonathan D . Stevenson, his law partner, whom President Polk had sent to
California in command of the first New York Volunteers on the outbreak of war in Mexico.
Colonel Stevenson had brought his troops around South America
in three ships in 1847, and. as with many other easterners, he came
to California and stayed.
Early California Masonry had within her ranks many other colorful
men: Sam Brannan, . who founded San Francisco's first newspaper.

A CENTURY OF MASONRY IN CALIFORNIA
By ELLSWORTH MEYER,
Grand Master of Masons in California

'

(As broadcast over the Columbia network on April 19, 1950)
This day is of particular significance to the Masons of California
and Hawaii. One hundred years ago on April 19, 1950, a group of
Master Masons who had gathered in Sacramento completed their preliminary work. and. at high twelve, opened the first communication of
the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons for the State of California.
It might be said they were a bit optimistic in the selection of a name,
for California was not admitted to the Union yet and did not become
.
a state until five months later.
The California in which they lived was a very different California
from that which you know. There were no railroads, no broad highways, no rapid means of communication, no bridges across rivers and
swift mountain streams.
The population was concentrated, but not at the location of our
modern, great cities. Instead, it was to be found in narrow canyons by
the American and Feather Rivers and on the banks of the Sacramento.
These California communities were known by such picturesque
names as: Coloma, Hangtown, Angels Camp, Grass Valley, Chilli
Gulch, and Rough & Ready.
Within the year. thousands of men had come to these communities
and other thousands were on their way across the Rockies, by way of
Panama, or around the Horn. Around the world had gone the cry of

42

43

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

was the first to broadcast the discovery of gold, preached the first
Protestant sermon in California, and was the subject of the state's
first jury trial. John · W. Geary. who came to California after service
in the Mexican War, became the first Postmaster and the first Mayor
of San Francisco, and later a Brigadier General. and then the Governor
of Kansas and the Governor of Pennsylvania, and Robert Semple who
presided over the Constitutional Convention, and, with Hastings, conditioned Californians for wide-spread public education.
To chronicle the names of prominent men who have sat in California
Masonic Lodges during the past century would be to call the roll of
most of those who have left their names as noble legacies to the state,
and of those who are recognized as leaders today.
I shall mention but a few of those whose names stand like mountain
peaks high above the past: Commodore Sloat; Kit Carson, the renowned
Indian scout; Mark Twain, who gave the world "The Jumping Frog
of Calaveras County"; Stephen J. Field, who served longer on the
Supreme Court of the United States than any other justice; Thomas
Starr King. one of the two Californians in the Hall of Fame in Washington, and who was serving our Grand Lodge as Grand Orator at
the time of his early death; Peter Lassen, named as an officer ill the
charter issued by the Grand Lodge of Missouri, and for whom Mount
Lassen and Lassen County were named; Don Benito Wilson, who
located Riverside, was Mayor of Los Angeles in 1851, and for whom
Mount Wilson was named; Lester A. Pelton, who made hydroelectric
power possible 'by inventing the Pelton water wheel; Leland Stanford,
railroad president, Governor, and United States Senator, who gave
Stanford University; and Luther Burbank, who unfolded so many of
nature's secrets. These are but a few of the great names in a century
of California Masonry. and I have purposely omitted the names of
those still living who are a credit to Masonry, California, and these
United States.
The Grand Lodge founded in that upper room at the corner of
Fifth and "J" Streets in Sacramento has, in the century of its progress.
spread to the Oregon and Mexican borders and crossed the Pacific to
Hawaii, where the first Masonic Lodge had been established by the
Grand Orient of France and over which two Hawaiian Kings had
presided as Masters. It has grown until its membership is the fifth
largest in the United States and the seventh largest in the world. If
we were to add to its members. the thousands of Masons who reside
in California, but maintain their membership at their former homes,
the number would probably not be surpassed by any other American
jurisdiction, but California Masonry is not interested in mere numbers.
Unlike many organizations, it can invite no man to take its degrees.
He must seek admission of his own free will. It does not sit back in
smug. self-satisfaction as it reviews its record on this Centennial Day.

It is proud of its history, but not boastful. As individuals, its members
are serving in every cause which is building a better state and a better
society, and they will continue to serve.
The Grand Lodge of California today touches life at each level.
Through its home for children at Covina, it cares for orphans and half
orphans from the first grade of grammar school through graduation
from high school. By means of its club houses at Berkeley and Los
Angeles campuses of the University of California, it is an influence
during the collegiate years. Its lodges inspire during the active, adult
years, and its Home for the Aged at Decoto. in Alameda County, is
a haven for 300 in the late afternoon of life.
Masonry is not a religion, but it is religious. It does not require
a particular church affiliation and only asks a candidate whether he
believes in a Supreme Being and some form of future existence.
It is not a political organization, but it does impress upon its
members that they have civic duties to perform through channels of
expression outside its lodges.
It is not a benefit society. It offers no form of insurance, but it
need yield to none in works of charity.
It has no fancy uniforms. and the only badge of a Mason is the
apron. which is never worn in public except for the funeral of a brother.
or the performan~ of some other strictly Masonic duty.
It does not seek the front page, but it does not shun the light of
inquiry.
It is a secret society as to its modes of recognition and pass words,
but there is no secrecy as to its organization, principles, or purposes.
It denies the claims of dictators, political or religfous, but it is loyal
to governments established by free peoples.
It recognizes familiar tones in the Declaration of Independence and
the Constitution, and it has seen many of the signatures on those two
documents on the rosters of its own lodges.
Masonry was a stabilizing influence in the rough and ready days
of '49. It is an anchorage in the present and for the days to come.
It has helped to build California, and it will not now lay down the
plumb, the square, or the trowel. For a century in California, and for
many centuries elsewhere, Masonry has united ·at its altars of reverence,
men of good will who have striven by every resource of their art to
make tangible, the power of brotherhood, the worth of virtue, and the
reality of the ideal.
Masons will continue to build the temple of humanity among the
nations and in the hearts of men.
The Deputy Grand Master referred the Message to the Committee
on Segregation. appointing the following mt!nbers to serve thereon:
Elmer Lotz, Don Campbell and Roy Kiele.

RESOLUTIONS
The Grand Secretary then read the following resolutions, all of
which were referred by the Grand Master to the Committees as noted:

PLURAL MEMBERSHIP
WHEREAS, many small, isolated lodges find it increasingly difficult to obtain brothers who are willing or capable to assume the duties
of office and,
.
WHEREAS, many brothers living away from their home lodges
are very active in local Masonic work and would make good officers but
are hesitant to demit from their mother lodge for sentimental reasons
and,
WHEREAS, Masonry, in California, is being deprived of the benefit
of much good officer material who could legally express their talents in
thirty-five other jurisdictions without relinquishing their home lodge
membership,
NOW, THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED. that Section 163 of
the Ordinances of the Grand Lodge be amended by substituting for the
word "No" the word "A" and by substituting after the word "Mason",
for the word "Shall" the word "May" so that the section shall read as
follows:
"A Mason may be a member of more than one lodge in this jurisdiction at the same time."
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED. that the Ordinances of the Grand
Lodge be amended by the addition in Article VII, of a section to be
known as Section 261-A and entitled "Apportionment of Relief to
Members with Dual Membership" to read as follows:
"Lodges must divide equally the relief granted one of their members
who holds dual membership in another lodge in this jurisdiction so far
as their circumstances permit and the Lodge within whose jurisdictfon
the distressed brother resides shall determine the extent of relief to be
granted."
Respectfully submitted,
K. G. SUBLETTE, Master, Fort Crook No. 575.
Referred to the Committees on Policy and General Purposes and on
Jurisprudence.

CHANGE OF NAME
This is to certify that at a stated meeting of this Lodge held on the
5th day of October, 1950, the following resolution was presented and
duly adopted :
WHEREAS, the mem·b ers of this Lodge desire to change its name
from Lankershim· Lodge No. 542, F. & A. M. to North Hollywood
Lodge No. 542, F. & A. M. and feel such action would be advantageous
to and for the best interests of this Lodge;
NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED: That Lankershim
Lodge No. 542, F. & A. M. apply to the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of
the State of California for permission to change its name to North Hollywood Lodge No. 542, F. & A. M. and that the Master and Secretary
be and they are hereby authorized to present an application to Grand
Lodge for such change of name.
That the foregoing resolution was duly adopted by the unanimous
vote of members present at said meeting; that it would be advantageous
and for the best interests of Lankershim Lodge to change its name tQ
North Hollywood Lodge No. 542, F. & A. M . for the following reasons:
1. The Lodge was named.after the town of Lankershim bi which
it was located, and the name of the town has been changed to North
Hollywood.
2. The Lodge is now generally known in the area as North Hollywood Lodge and changing would avoid confusion. ·
3. The corporation building the new Masonic Temple in which the
Lodge will be located is known as the North Hollywood Building Association, and the building will be known as North Hollywood Masonic
Temple.
4. Other organizations meeting in this building are known by the
name of North Hollywood.
Dated this fifth day of October, 1950.
Respectfully submitted,
LANKERSHIM LoDGE No. 542, F. & A. M,

PREREQUISITE PERIOD
WHEREAS:
It would be to the benefit of Masonry in general and to the Blue
Lodges of this Jurisdiction in particular that the period of indoctrination of the newly raised Brother in the la_ws, customs and fraternal
workings of our order should be raised to a period of twelve months,
rather than the six months period mentioned in Question 13 of the
Application for Degrees, before applying for membership in any body,
order or organization, the prerequisite of membership wherein is that ·
he be a Master Mason would greatly help the attendam::e on the meetings of our Blue Lodges and serve to increase the interest of the newly
raised Brother in the fundamental teachings of Masonry.
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED:
That the period of time mentioned in Question 13 of the Application
for Degrees-to-wit six months-be altered to twelve months and that
Question 13 hereafter read as follows-Question 13. Do you promise
that you will not, within twelve months after receiving the degree of
Master Mason, apply for or receive any degree or be initiated in any
body, order, or organization the prerequisite of membership wherein
·
is that a person be a Master Mason?
Respectfully submitted for your action at the coming session of
your Honorable Body, October 9-13, 1950.
ARCH BALCHIN

TO PUBLISH NAMES OF CANDIDATES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
WHEREAS the practice of printing the names of candidates in
bulletins is now used in many of the Grand Jurisdictions of the United
States and in all the Lodges in the Dominion of Canada and England,
and,
WHEREAS such practice by the Lodges in this Jurisdiction would
stimulate attendance and give all the members an opportunity to pass
on candidates, and
WHEREAS the present restrictions on such practice was adopted

some 53 years ago when cities and lodges were smaller and which restriction now tends to protect the undesirable candidate at the expense of
the Lodge, now
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 696 and 6CJ7 of
the ordinances be rescinded, and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Lodges in this Jurisdiction
may. if they so desire, print the names of candidates in bulletins, provided such bulletins are enclosed in an envelope and mailed only to

LIMITS OF INVESTMENT

I hereby offer the following resolution and move its adoption, to wit:
To amend the first sentence of Section 152 of our Ordinances relating to
investment of funds, to read as follows, to wit:
"A lodge may invest not exceeding 40% of its funds in such
securities as men of prudence, discretion and intelligence exercise in the management of their own affairs, not in regard to
speculation, but in regard to the permanent disposition of their
funds, considering the probable income, as well as the probable
safety of their capital. Within the limitations of the foregoing
standard a lodge is authorized to acquire every kind of property, real. personal or mixed; and every kind of investment,
specifically including but not by way of limitation, corporate
obligations of every kind, and stocks, preferred or common,
which men of prudence, discretion and intelligence. acquire for
their own account."

"also" immediately after the word "may" and before the word "invest",
so that the sentence hereafter shall read as follows:
"Provided that after first obtaining the consent of the Grand
Lodge Committee on Lodge financing, it may also invest its
funds as follows:"
To amend the last portion of said section 152 relative to the investment of life membership funds, by striking out:
"Securities other than those prescribed as legal for savings
banks by the laws of the State of California or by the laws of

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

One year ago the Grand Treasurer recommended that consideration
be given to (such) extension of qualified investments by adopting what
is designated the "Prudent Man Rule," which recommendation was
supported by a monograph of pertinent facts prepared ·by the Assistant
Grand Treasurer and annexed as an exhibit.
The recommendation and proposed legislation presented by the
Grand Treasurer affecting the Prudent Man Rule were referred to the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes and the Finance Committee, and the Endowment Board: the first named committee reported:
"Much of the time of these Committees during this Communication of Grand Lodge has been devoted to this proposal.
Numerous joint conferences have been held. The Homes Board
and individual members of Grand Lodge have requested and have
been granted extended hearings. AJJ phases of the Prudent Man
Rule have been explored and able dissertations have been given
with reference to investment. trust and financial policies. Your
Committee on Policy and General Purposes and the Committee
on Finance as weJJ as the Endowment Board favor, as a matter
of policy. the adoption of the Prudent Man Rule. We feel,
however, since its adoption would mean a departure from our
present practice as set forth in our laws. that more time should
be given to study of the matter before the proposed Resolution
is ftnaUy submitted for adoption or rejection by the Grand Lodge.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, therefore,
submits the foJJowing Resolution in which the Committee on
Finance joins:
"RESOLVED: That the incoming Grand Master be requested to appoint a Committee of five qualified members of Grand
Lodge to study and consider during the coming year the proposed adoption of the Prudent Man Rule as set forth herein in
Past Grand Master Keesling' s Resolution and to report to Grand
Lodge at its regular Communication in 1950."
This Resolution was adopted.
In the report of the Finance Committee the foJJowing appears:
"The recommendation of the Grand Treasurer with reference
to the adoption of the 'Prudent Man Rule' was referred to this
Committee as well as the Committee on Policy and General Purposes and the Endowment Board. This Committee concurs in
the report which was given by the Committee on Policy and
Genera) Purposes. We have no intention of prolonging discus-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

59

sion of the matter except to express, for the record, our approval
of the legislation which is proposed. and to suggest that a11 members of the Grand Lodge endeavor to familiarize themselves
with the principles under which the Prudent Man Rule operates
so that they may be prepared to express themselves at the next
Annual Communication. It is a very important question. We
trust that it will be given careful consideration."
I feel it is my duty to reaffirm my position as set forth in my report
as Grand Treasurer at the Grand Communication in 1949, and in that
respect refer to that report, particularly to that portion relating to the
Prudent Man Rule. The Grand Treasurer is charged with considerable
responsibility respecting investment, including without limitation as to
generality all funds owned or belonging to Grand Lodge, some of which
are controJJed by Trustees of the Masonic Homes and the Committee
on Investment of Endowment Funds.
Currently. the yield on total funds approximates 2y.f %. controlled
largely by limitations on investments by regulation. The minimum increase in yields on the investments which would fall within the Prudent
Man Rule may be fairly estimated at 2% . The result of an increase in
yield of 2% on $5,000,000.00 is simple mathematics. If that yield may
be obtained by an investment policy that has spread rapidly over the
United States, we are convinced that the course to pursue is manifest
and that there is a mandate of sound business practice. It is the opiniQn
of the Grand Treasurer that he should invite merited criticism if he did
not urge consideration of the Prudent Man Rule whereby the earnings
of Grand Lodge will be substantiaJJy increased without inf ury to principal.
Lodges are confronted with the same problem, only their problems
are more urgent. If the yields on investment moneys are insufficient for
expenses, the only recourse is to raise dues. This must be seriously
considered.

It has been suggested that consideration be given to investment in
mutual funds. This we believe to be inadvisable for Grand Lodge purposes. The cost of management exceeds what we need to pay for
unquestionably excellent investment counsel. It is obvious that there
should be such independent expert counsel. Investment in mutual funds
would not only offer a complicated problem to co-ordinate with other
Investments of Grand Lodge but would interfere with a desirable selective procedure. There may be some alarm with respect to removing
existing limitations on lodges from a fear of inexperienced and inexpert
control. However, this may be safeguarded.

61

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Some difficulties are presented by the limitation of investments
"legal for savings banks." The State of California long had a "legal
for savings bank" investment list. In itself, it was not a guarantee of
safety. In fact, many such "legal" bonds defaulted both in interest and
principal. This emphasizes one ever-present requirement, namely, that
prudent investigation is always necessary, list or no list. In other words,
the Prudent Man principle had to be applied to the legal for savings
banks bond list.

These data have been assembled and made available. for the Grand
Master, members of the Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes
Committees, the Endowment Board and Trustees of the Masonic
Homes.

60

Since October 1, 1949, there has been no legal for savings bank
investment list in California. The rule of prudence now applies. There
are certain percentage limits in various types and kinds of indebtedness,
both for savings and commercial banks in California, but the legal list
is no more. It is no longer possible for Grand Lodge or lodges to adapt
bond investment policy to legal list. While it would be feasible to fix
percentages of funds which must be invested in bonds or equivalent
securities, it is the considered judgment of the Grand Treasurer and the
Assistant Grand Treasurer that it would be more advisable by far to
operate under the principle of the Prudent Man Rule with independent
experienced investment counsel which may be had at a surprisingly
reasonable cost.
The Prudent Man Rule is not, as some may think, a "common
stock" rule. As stated in my report last year, it remains as originally
expressed in 1830 by Justice Putnam of Massachusetts: "In acquiring,
investing, reinvesting, exchanging, retaining, selling and managing property for the benefit of another, a fiduciary shall exercise the judgment
and care under the circumstances then prevailing, which men of prudence, discretion and intelligence exercise in the management of their
own affairs, not in regard to speculation but in regard to the permanent disposition of their funds, considering the probable income as well
as the probable safety of their capital."
The rule of Prudent Man investing would include bonds, preferred
stocks, common stocks, and any other investments which prudent .men
would acquire.
Supporting the foregoing and the recommendation contained in my
1949 report as Grand Treasurer, are additional data which have been
arduously assembled by the Assistant Grand Treasurer, and indicate
the many hours of study and compiling and manifest the earnest, devoted and efficient service which typifies our Assistant Grand Treasurer.

Respectfully submitted,
FRANCIS V. KEESLING

Grand Treasurer
