I. CONSTRUCTION
Under direction of the building committee of the Board, extensive
remodeling of the clubhouse took place during the summer months of
1949. This remodeling greatly increased the existing facilities of the
building, and provided the students with modern equipment and lighting.
The acceptance of student suggestions and sincere cooperation of
the building committee was greatly appreciated by the members of the
club.
Throughout this report mention will be made of the individual
improvements and how they were put to use by the students.
The thanks and appreciation of the students were sent to the Grand
Lodge at the beginning of the 1949 communication and the appreciation
has been continuous since that time as the club has put to use the
improved facilities.
II. NEW EQUIPMENT
The students in their efforts to provide added service to the membership purchased and had installed a public address system throughout
the building. The need for this equipment has been noticed and mentioned for several years. The use of this system has greatly increased
the efficiency of the council and members.
Various items of office equipment were found to be needed and were
obtained.
Snack bar equipment was purchased from student funds to provide
the membership with added lunch and coffee facilities.
It might be noted here, for general information, that student funds
collected through dues, are used by the students for social affairs and
for the purchase of needed student equipment and supplies. The funds
collected are consumed, for the most part, during the year in which they
were collected.

Ill. ORGANIZATION
The club is governed by the Executive Council, elected by the membership and composed of both upper and lower division students. This
council acts under the authority of the constitution and by-laws, recently
revised.
Each term the organizational systems by which the club is run are
changed or retained at the discretion of the president and the council
to meet the everchanging conditions.
This process of striving to improve the conditions under which the
club is maintained provides an excellent education in business management and student government, thus giving the student a practical background to supplement his studies on campus.

126

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA
PROCEEDINGS OP THE

In the year 1949-1950 several systems of organization were inaugurated under the direction of the president.
.
The council was allotted duty hours in the office, scheduled into
their free hours on campus. By this method we accomplished what we
believed was a two-fold purpose: that of relieving the detail of club
management formerly imposed upon the hostess, and secondly, pr.oviding the council members certain, a~ministrati".e experi~~ce. Whi.le ~n
duty it was the council member s :Job to receive all vi~itors, maintain
order and do all in his power to see that the club functioned smoothly
and that the members were furnished every service that could be offered.
Several other systems and procedures were inaugurated; their outcome will be decided in future years. In a report to the new president,
suggestions and comments on these and other ideas wil~ be retafn~d in
the club files along with reports and comments of the various committees
operating within the organization. These reports will be augmented by
each succeeding council for the benefit of future officers.
Needless to say the social activities mentioned later provide the
student with the needed relief from the academic pressure encountered
in college life.
IV. MEMBERSHIP
Membership for the year 1949-50:
Fall semester .................................................................. 405
Spring semester ............................................................ 380
New members are brought into the club under an orientation program
designed to aid them in meeting the active members and interest them
in the activities of the club. They are helpfully assisted in their adjustment to university life.
- This program, introduced several semesters ago, is improving each
term and should develop into a very essential part of the club life,

v. SNACK BAR
The lunch service, operated as a "Snack bar," went into full operation with the opening of the club in the fall. The increased facilities and
accessibility afforded by the new kitchen downstairs aided the students
in planning a well-rounded lunch consisting of one or more hot dishes,
salads, sandwiches, soup, coffee, tea, and milk. It was decided to employ
a part-time cook to prepare and serve the meals. She was paid $1 per
hour for four hours a day, five days a week. Workmens' Compensation
coverage was taken out in the name of the council.
The snack bar served coffee and doughnuts from 9:00 A.M. and
lunch from 11 :00 A.M. to 1:00 P.M.
. Minimum prices were charged and service was restricted to club
members. Daily use is estimated between 150 and 200 persons. Operation showed a slight profit over and above the equipment purchased.

127

VI. ACTIVITIES, RECREATIONAL AND SOCIAL
Recreational facilities include three ping pong tables, two pool tables
in men's lounge, and the newly equipped card room. Heavy daily use
of all these facilities was experienced throughout the year. The card
room provided a much-needed retreat for bridge players, where quiet
concentration is a prerequisite for an enjoyable game. The playing
equipment for these activities is maintained by student funds.
Intramural teams of baseball and football were organized and competed with other clubs on campus. Both teams this year came home with
few victories.
The proximity of the men's w~shroom to the men's lounge relieved
an awkward situation and cut down the unnecessary traffic by the study
rooms .The moving of the washroom to the basement provided much
needed study space on the mezzanine.
The social activities of the year were well-rounded and enthusiastically attended as evidenced by the following summary:
1. Open Houses
Each semester during registration and the first two weeks of instruction, the club holds open house with record dances on Saturday evenings.
Attendance at these affairs runs between 200 and 400 people. Cokes and
cookies are served and members are on duty to answer questions and
take memberships.
2. Grand Lodge Visit
During the annual Communication the club was host to many visiting
brethren.
3. Football Activities
During football seasons dances are held either on Friday or Saturday
nights. Attendance is usually quite large for these affairs. Dances usually
follow the rallies on campus. Games with U .S.C. and Stanford are
ordinarily cause for larger and more elaborate affairs.
When the U.C.L.A. game is held in Los Angeles many club members
travel south and enjoy the hospitality of the Masonic Club on that
campus. Approximately 75 members journeyed south for the 1949
U .C.L.A. game.
4, Christmas Activities
Prior to Christmas recess, the club holds its Christmas formal.
Always well attended, it brought forth over 400 people this year.
As part of its philanthropic activities, the club held a Christmas
party for 25 underprivileged children. Santa Claus arrived and distributed toys and games collected by the members. The night before
this party about 50 members got together and had a tree-trimming party.
5. Initiation
Near the end of each semester the club has its formal initiation
ceremony. accompanied by a banquet and dance. Turn-out for these

VII. DAILY USE
As mentioned before, the club experienced heavy daily use: the
lounge as a gathering place, the study rooms for quiet concentration,
the library for reference work, the ping pong and pool tables, the card
room for relaxation, and the snack bar for refreshments.
The club was opened on Sundays from I to 9 P .M. so that members
could make use of the facilities when other places on campus were closed.

VIII. PUBLICITY
It was found that many Masons whose sons and daughters were
attending Cal did not know the club existed or that their children were
eligible for membership. With this in mind efforts were made throughout
the year to publicize the club and its activities at every opportunity. The
president and vice president gave short talks to various groups and
distributed pamphlets which contained photographs of the club and
explained its functions.
·
Through the aid of E . H. Phillips, Chairman of the Masonic Spring
Breakfast, wide publicity of the club was given a t that affair.
Several lodge secretaries aided in this work by mentioning the club
·
in their bulletins.
Attractive paper hook matches were printed and distributed at various Masonic gatherings.
Within the club itself, the Masonic Murmurs, official organ of the
club, had a somewhat dubious existence. It is felt that this type of
publicity of club activities is worth while, but for the ·year 49-50 it
proved quite expensive and time-consuming.
Its function of informing the membership of coming affairs was taken
over by the faster means of communication of using postcards.

IX. CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGES
By vote of the general membership, executive council term of o.ffice,
with the exception of the upper and lower division representatives, was
extended to one year. It was felt that this would greatly facilitate the
management of the club throughout the school year.
.
The offices of Manager of the Snack Bar and Editor of the Murmurs
were added to the list of appointive officers.
Various by-laws were amended to clarify duties and procedure.

X. PHOTOGRAPHY ROOM
Interest in this activity ·is felt to be high. Although the dark room
experienced relatively little use during the year 49.:50, we feel that this
was due to the lack of spare time available to the students. Plans for
increased use of this equipment are being worked out.

MRS. EDNA H. MORTON, for her valuable aid and advice fully
deserves the credit for the successful term just completed. To her I

not only. for students attending the summer sessions and who use the
study hall and other facilities in the Clubhouse, but also, for the other
members. Groups meet in various parts of the county for potluck dinners,
swimming parties, weiner roasts, roller skating and various other informal parties.
As usual the biggest social event of the season was the Grand
Master's Reception. It had more than ordinary significance this year because the Grand Master has long been associated with the Club and is
well known to the students. The students planned it long and carefully.
Needless to say, the Grand Master rose to the occasion and his usual
inspiring message was particularly well received.
It is not all play and no work. One of the best patronized features
of the Clubhouse is the quiet and attractive study hall. Also many of the
Club activities consist of lectures and study groups. Twice each year
the officers and committees and other interested students meet in " retreats", break up into discussion groups under committee leadership and
plan the activities of the Club. Such retreats last for several days and
are well attended.
In keeping with their past tradition the students have not overlooked
the charitable side of club activities. A Thanksgiving dinner was served
for children from the All Nations Boys Club and Girls Club. Again,
during the Spring semester. dinner was served for some of the children
and their parents from the All Nations Hollenbeck Center.
The students, through the help of the Board, purchased a television
set. This together with the radio, record player, ping pong tables, card
tables, pool tables, chess and checkers, piano, lounge room and library
make the Clubhouse a recreational center at all times.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON DE MOLAY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The present year, as in past years, has seen the activities of your
Committee on De Molay devoted to spreading information among the
members of the Fraternity as to the meaning, aims and accomplishments
of the Order. This is a pleasant task for the reason that, having had
four years of close contact with many Chapters of De Mol~y'.· your
Committee is thoroughly sold on the value of De Molay trammg to
the coming generation and we are sure that if we can succ~ed in getting
the Brethren only half as enthusiastic as is your Committee over the
possibilities of producing good solid, right thinking citizens for the
future, ample support for our endeavors will be forthcoming.
It is just too bad that more of our Masonic Brethren do not visit a
Chapter of De Malay and experience the uplift in spirits and in faith
in the future of our Country conveyed by the serious manner in wh~c~
the degree work is carried on. If it see~s like too much tro~ble ~o v1s1t
a Chapter, let any member of the Committee know and he will brmg the
Chapter to you on one of your Lodge meeting nights, that is fair enough
is it not.
A number of years ago our hard working Past Grand Master.
Charlie Adams, conceived the idea of having a public schools week each
year sponsored by our fraternity, the idea took h~ld and h.as proven a
grand success year after year. Without detractmg one iota for the
value of such a program, for we realize that its scope is g~eat, may w_e
call your attention to the fact that the value of our Pubh~ Schools is
stressed in every first degree in every De Malay Chapter m the land.
The school book, referred to in the ritual. taking its place beside the
Holy Bible on the altar where kneels the initiate.
During the past year Brother Louis Goldstein, Deputy of the Grand
Council of De Molay, has gone to his reward and Brother Carl Olsen
has been selected to fill the vacancy. Brother Olsen had set up a very
fine and comprehensive program for the Order in ~o~t.hern Califor~ia
which include, among thirty other items, such activities as debatmg
teams, plant visits, perfecting degree work and assisting at Masonic
affairs such as public installations, etc. He has also set up rules by
which Advisors may be guided, such as attending to well being of the
Chapter, approval of programs, t'he proper handling of the finances of
the Chapter, etc.
His basic guide for the conduct of Chapters is a concise set of instructions and his presentation of De Malay will give you a picture of its
aims and purposes:
A-To exemplify those traits taught at home.
B-To instill a desire for clean citizenship.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the following report.
Pursuant to authorization of the Grand Lodge, your Committee
undertook, two years and nine months ago, to prepare the manuscript
of One Hundred Years of Freemasonry in California.
We are pleased to report that our task has been completed and the
manuscript is now in the hands of the printers. It will comprise a set
of four volumes, containing material collected by the Committee over
a period of more than twenty years.
The writing of this history was a tremendous task and it is as com~
plete and accurate as the facts at hand and the time alloted for its preparation would permit. If the Committee has inadvertently omitted the
stories of any deserving brethren, or has incorrectly recorded facts
regarding any of them, we now offer our humble apologies. We are
hardly naive enough to presume that no errors will be found in a work
covering some two thousand odd pages and dealing with thousands of

140

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

persons whose collective activities embrace a period of more than one
hundred years.
At times the progress of this work was seriously hindered by the
failure of many Lodges to send any material whatsoever to the Committee. Nevertheless, the Committee has diligently endeavored to reconstruct their stories. We have pieced together the meager data in the
Grand Lodge Proceedings and other limited sources, and thereby
gleaned items of interest about certain Lodges that otherwise would
have received scant notice.
It should be further noted that this failure of Lodges to furnish
data on themselves was most unfortunate. During the past three years
the Committee has mailed three circular letters to every Lodge in this
Grand Jurisdiction requesting historical material. and a fourth circular
letter to such Lodges as did not respond to the other three. We have
also sent out literally thousands of letters and post cards to them or their
individual members in quest of specific information-frequently in vain.
Therefore, if any of them feel that they have not received sufficient
attention, they have only themselves to blame, for the Committee has at
all times been exceedingly reluctant to omit anything of real interest.
But despite the difficulties encountered and the extra work necessitated in last minute research, we have thoroughly enjoyed oi.tr work
and we hope that the completed history meets with your approval.
We sincerely thank the Grand Master for his patience, forbearance, and courteous consideration during the past year. He has at all
times shown a deep interest in the completion of this work and, whenever called upon, has materially assisted the Committee.
We are satisfied that many of us have tried his patience "over
much," but as he well knows, it was only in furtherance of the accomplishment of a task imposed upon us by Grand Lodge and not of our
own choosing.
We are also grateful to the members of the Committee on Finance
for their understanding and thoughtful consideration which permitted
us to bring this work to a conclusion at this time.
In conclusion we feel that the Committee on Masonic History
should be contin~ed and, therefore, offer the following resolution and
move its adoption:
· That the Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic History be continued for the ensuing Masonic year and that the sum of $150.00 be
appropriated and set aside for its use.
Respectfully submitted,

Referred to Committee on Finance.

LEON 0. WHITSELL
CHARLES R. INGRAM
WILSON E. NEWLON
SAMUEL STEELMAN
BEN R. WALKER

GENERAL FISCAL OPERATION

. A sur:ey of the operating figures for the last 20 years as reported
m the various proceedings indicate the following:
1. The major source of income to the Homes is derived from the
$25.0~ tax on Initiates and from the per capita levy upon the
Constituent Lodges.
·
2. Eli~inating the per .capita ~or the Building Fund, the revenue
available for Homes operation has been insufficient except for
the fiscal years of 1937, 1943, 1944, 1945, 1946, and 1947.
Considering these facts, it is necessary to examine the trend in First
degrees conferred and also total membership statistics.

144

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

First Degrees Conferred: From a total of 3,760 First Degrees in
1916, the figure rose to 10,547 in 1920. A sharp drop to 8,200 was
experienced in 1921. The figure then leveled off for 6 years with minor
changes. A decline was again experienced in 1928 and a precipitous
drop was felt in 1933 when the total fell to an all time low of 1.810
for that year. The totals again started to rise until 1941 when we went
up to 3,200. During the war years the applications poured in and the
high peak was 14,920 in 1946. Again a sharp drop was experienced in
1947-8 and today we are conferring about 9,000 per year with a tendency
to level off.
· Total Membership: Total membership moved slowly from 122,000
in 1926 to a high of 142,000 in 1931. A moderate decline then developed
until the low figure of 125 ,000 in 1941. Since then, we have increased
each year until our high point of 196,800 as of July 31. 1950. With
applications dropping off, it is entirely possible that we may stay at
approximately this figure for the next few years.
Translating these figures into dollars, the net result would be:
Annual funds available from lnitiates.......................... $225,000.00
Annual funds available from $1.00 per capita ............ 194,000.00
(allowing for remissions)
PER CAPITA

For many years a per capita was levied at the rate of $.50 to cover
Building Fund expenditures. This constitution~} requirement was repealed at the Communication of 1946. An additional levy for operation
in varying amounts was levied until 1943 when that levy was abandoned.
At the Communication of 1948. a levy was again made at the rate of
$.5q and ip. 1949 it was increased to $1.00.
CONTRIBUTIONS-BUILDING FUND

On August 8, 1948, the Trustees adopted a resolution to the effect
that all bequests under wills be allocated to the Building Fund unless a
specific clause prohibited such disposition.
This resolution provides for the development of the Building Fund
and will make available _sums which can be used for repairs and for new
construction.
COST OF MAINTENANCE

The cost of operating our Homes has increased materially during the
last ten years due to economic conditions. It should be apparent to all
that there will be no appreciable decline in these expenses. On the
contrary, the eniargement of our faciilties will increase the capacity of
the Homes. This requires an increase in cost for personnel and for
subsistence for new guests. In addition, the proposed , pension set-up
will also increase the general operating expenses.

"When the amount thus collected and so held shall be more than
sufficient, in the judgment of the Trustees, to provide for the
maintenance of the Homes and for such improvements as are
then in prol:Jress or contemplated for the immediate future, the
surplus shall be by them allocated to the Endowment Fund."
Under this provision, funds have been allocated to the Endowment
Fund and during the last five years, $300,000.00 has been thus transferred.
This provision places a restraint upon the Trustees and prevents them
from holding funds collected during good years for use during declines
when it would be unwise to further increase per capita taxes. In fact,
if the Homes had been permitted to .h old the last $300,000.00 in reserve,
there would be no occasion to restore the per capita levy against the
Lodges for some time to come. It is the recommendation of the Committee that necessary steps be taken to amend the Constitution to
eliminate this clause.
If this is carried out, then the Trustees should continue the levy of
$1.00 per capita placing it in the General Fund for operations with no
part thereof being allocated to building. They should also reserve the
right to transfer to building reserves such sums as my seem appropriate
if in their judgment a substantial surplus appears in the General Fund.
If these two measures are carried into effect, the Budget for the fiscal
year ending July 31. 1952 would appear as follows:

This would provide for a balanced budget provided the item of
income from endowments equaled 1950 and if our forecast of new
candidates is realized. The per capita and cost of maintenance are based
upon present experience.

to carry into effect its recommendations, we request that Section 100

To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
Brethren: In submitting my 10th annual report as Superintendent
of the Masonic Home at Decoto, for the year ending July 31, 1950, I
am pleased to report that conditions, generally speaking, are very good
and with few exceptions the morale of the Home has been satisfactory
during the year.
There has been the usual routine in the management of the Home.
It has been our endeavor to operate economically and efficiently and to
provide every care and comfort for our residents.
Mrs. Virginia Lord, our Matron, has been successful in creating and
maintaining an atmosphere in the Home which has brought a large
measure of contentment in the lives of the members of our large family
who are enjoying the care and protection of the Home.
Our hospital department has been operating very efficiently under
the supervision of Miss Esther G. Payne, ably assisted by Miss Bess
L. Payne. At present there are 6i patients in this department who are
receiving, in a most efficient manner, that kind care, love and protection
which they require and so richly deserve.
At the beginning of the year we had 172 women and 123 men, the
average age for the women was 78,81 and for the men 77.95. During
the year 27 women were admitted. average age 76.48, and 26 men,
average age 76.92. We lost by death, during the same period, 21 women,
average age 87.15, and 26 men, average age 77.96, and 5 men and 2
women were withdrawn, leaving at the end of the year 176 women,
average age 78.85, and 118 men, average age 79.14. Included in this
number are 14 married couples.

The extensive building program which was undertaken some two
years ago is now completed. We find at the completion of this work
that the badly needed quarters in the main building and in the hospital
have been provided. The extra quarters in the main building have
eliminated the waiting list and should take care of our requirements for
years to come. The work in the hospital has provided not only extra
beds, but also provided facilities which enable the staff to render a more
efficient service to their patients. The alterations and addition to our
kitchen have improved working conditions in that department and the
new dining room for our employees is very much appreciated by them.
We owe Brother Skaggs and his able assistant Brother Montell a
debt of thanks and we shall be ever grateful to them for the excellent
work they did on our driveways.
There were 41 Masonic Jurisdictions represented among the 2693
who signed our visitors register during the past year. Included in this
number were Grand Lodge officers from China, Washington, Nevada,
Vermont, and representatives from Manila No. 1, Saipan No. 121, and
Pacific Lodge No. 2, New Zealand.
Since 1916 the East Bay Past Matrons Associations has been holding annually in August a reception at the Masonic Home for their Grand
Matron. This year on August 19th about 600 of these kind ladies journeyed to the Masonic Home to attend the reception and brought with
them a goodly supply of jams and jellies. After an informal luncheon
in the banquet room the ladies adjourned to the auditorium where Grand
Matron Margaret Hughes Lauritzen and Grand Patron Dr. Arthur J.
Hook and their Grand Lodge officers were received and introduced.
On August 14, 1949, the East Bay Masters & Wardens Association,
Dr. Robert H. Taylor, President, in company with about 125 members
of the Association made their annual visit to the Home, enjoyed their

usual barbecue and presented an excellent program in our auditorium
for the entertainment of the residents of the Home.
In addition to the above mentioned programs the members of the
Home have enjoyed many excellent programs which have been brought
to the Home by Lodges and various groups from the Bay area and as
far south as Los Angeles.
The following distributing companies are still supplying to the Home,
"gratis," excellent weekly programs which the residents of the Home
enjoy immensely and for which they are very grateful : R.K.O., Columbia, United Artists, Warner Bros., M.G.M., and Twentieth CenturyFox.
Our library is a very popular place, particularly for those who are
of literary inclination. This department is kept well supplied with periodicals and daily papers as well as a fine assortment of fine books. Being
a branch of the county library we are able to supply any book which is
desired even though we do not have it in our library.
Devotional services are conducted each Sunday. The Reverend
Geoffrey C. Hinshelwood, who was appointed Chaplain of the Home,
conducts services one Sunday each month and appoints a minister to
conduct services on the other Sundays.
Grand Secretary Lloyd E. Wilson and Grand Treasurer Francis V.
Keesling have, on many occasions, honored us with visits during the
year.
Our Trustees, individually and collectively, have visited the Home
quite frequently during the year. Their counsel is always helpful and
deeply appreciated. It is my desire to thank the Board of Trustees for
the kind consideration they have always given to the various problems
in the Home.
In conclusion the Matron joins me in expressing our appreciation
of the efficient and conscientious work on the part of our department
heads and our employees. Their earnest efforts in connection with their
department has been a factor in maintaining the high standard of service
which is maintained in the several departments of the Home.
Respectfully submitted,

J. R. EUBANKS,
Superintendent.

PROGRAM AND SUMMER ACTIVITIES

For the second year every boy and gir1 enjoyed a wonderful camping experience at San Clemente State Beach Park. Camp activities began
July 6 and ended August 20. Three camping periods of two weeks'
duration afforded the various age level individuals a speciaJizing of
interests. Surf fishing, deep sea fishing, swimming, hiking, campfire
programs, horseback trips, overnight "sleepouts," the Laguna Art Festival and many other excursion trips were planned and supervised by a
trained and competent staff. Our healthy, happy youngsters are living
proof of a successful summer camp. This experience is never to be
forgotten in the minds of the children and serves as a stimulant in our
routine school program. The educational and inspirational influences of
such activities have a far reaching effect upon the normal growth and
development of our children. Instruction in ceramics has been added to
our program, aUowing for self-expression and individual attainment by
even our youngest girl. In addition to individual musical instruction such
as piano and voice, a girls' choral group has been formed. Vigorous
athletic activities, allowing for group and individual participation, are
a motivating factor toward the maintaining of a healthy body in support
of an active mind for many a boy and girl.
Highlighting the Home's program this past year has been the organization of a 4-H Club. This group, composed entirely of Home membership of intermediate boys and girls, has very aptly selected as their
name "Masonic Pioneers.'' Each member has been afforded an opportunity to purchase and maintain an animal or home-making project. The
products of their endeavor are purchased and consumed within the
Home. Entry into the 4-H Fair, held at Pomona, California, witnessed
the children receiving twenty-one ribbons and awards for their efforts.
Of more importance than the educational value, is the straightening of
stature that accompanies pride of ownership in the reaJization of personal
accomplishment.

HEALTH PROGRAM

It has been a very gratifying year in the operation of our health
program and we are grateful to our doctors and nurses for their help
in keeping the children in good health. One hundred and sixty-one
children were admitted to our Home hospital, with a total of nine
hundred and seventy-six hospital days. Four thousand eight hundred
and ninety-three Home clinic treatments were given and prophylactic
treatments numbered two thousand one hundred and three. Physical
examination of the children was made at regular intervals by Dr. W. P.
Magan and his associates, whereby an accurate record of the health
progress of each child was maintained by our head nurse. Correct
dietary values through careful menu planning, special nourishment and
rest when needed, vitamin supplement, and smallpox and triple vaccine,
all play an important part in keeping the children well. Dr. Ellwood
Laine, our visiting dentist, gave two hundred and twenty-five treatments
in the Home dental clinic during the year. Eight children are receiving

FARM AND GROUNDS

Farm activities continue to move in the direction of our long range
plan, whereby the Home, supplemented by the Masonic Pioneers' 4-H
Club live stock and poultry projects, will raise the necessary amount of
beef, pork, rabbits, and poultry for Home consumption. Under the
direction and guidance of our farm supervisor we are making good
headway and have during this past year butchered approximately three
hundred ninety-four pounds of dressed beef; two thousand five hundred
sixty-two pounds of dressed pork; one hundred seventy-eight pounds of
dressed rabbit; one hundred fifty-three pounds of dressed duck and one
thousand two hundred seventy-nine pounds of dressed chicken, all of
which was consumed at the Home. Part of the pork was converted
into hams and bacon.
The planting of shrubs and flowers has added to our landscaped
area. Under the trees on the west side of the athletic field a complete
picnic barbecue has been installed. Cooking facilities and tables with
benches will accommodate two hundred persons and a storehouse to
protect movable barbecue equipment has been built close to the area.
A careful study has been made of the groves because of quick decline
of trees in our area and as a result a program of partial re-plant and an
organization of cultural practices has been undertaken. Supervision and
guidance of this survey has been graciously forthcoming from Mr. W. J.
(Bill) Williams.
HOME ALUMNI

The fourth Sunday in September, which each year is set aside as
Alumni Home-Coming Day, is an exciting time for the children at the
Home. They enjoy meeting the former residents and their children.
Last Alumni Day was well attended, as was the Annual Alumni Dinner
in San Francisco. Invitations to these affairs were mailed to all Alumni.

INVOCATION
Oh, God, source of compassion and comfort, lift up our thoughts to
the Eternal Hills of Light, where dwell with Thee the heroes, the
martyrs, the saints, the good folk of all time. ·
We are met in this solemn moment to remember our Masonic Broth.
ers who have heard a Divine Summons and have passed beyond the
portals of our human lodges. As we walk in memory's hall, we recall
their virtues as true men and Masons and we give thanks to Thee for
their lives of uprightness and honor. We rejoice in the confident faith
that they, having lived well, do now dwell with Thee in a land fairer
than our dreams. ·
Help us to know that there is "no lost musk and no lost goodthat Life is ever lord of Death and love can never lose its own."
Bring to all our hearts the assurance that death is not the end, that
indeed it is the beginning of a new and more wonderful adventure with
Thee, 0 God. Whisper to our hearts that always Thou hast something
richer and better out ahead for us.
Soon or late, we all will have a rendezvous with Death. Let us not
be afraid of it. Rather, let us face it with the anticipation that Thou
hast a greater life for each of us. So in this quiet moment of memory,
may we gather fresh strength to live bravely and nobly. May we face
the future with smiling faces and hearts that are unafraid, praying only
that at the end of life's last long mile we may hear the Supreme Grand
Master say, "Well done. Enter into the celestial lodge to dwell with
thy brothers and with me forever." Amen.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY
The flat of nature is inexorable. Death is the portion of every
living thing. Awake or sleeping, it is our constant companion. Its call
may come to us at any moment and, be we prepared or not, the summons
cannot be denied. Death strikes so often and time passes so swiftly,
that it will not be long before this great celebration of the 1OOth anniversary of the founding of the Grand Lodge of California will be only a
pleasant memory to the few, and just another historical event to the
many.
The names of those we lament here today will be to those who come
later only a part of a record, and when we, in our turn, respond to the
final call, our names and our records will, in such a very short time,
be found only in the dusty archives. These truths should not depress
us for it is God's way, and it is in God that we are and have our being,
and we do not doubt, nor argue, nor quibble with His wisdom.

In the past 52 weeks, 280 Masters and Past Masters, members of
this Grand Lodge, have responded to the final call. Schofield Lodge
No. 443 of the Territory of Hawaii suffered the heaviest loss, five of
its Past Masters being summoned to the Grand Lodge above. Fidelity
Lodge No. 120, and South Pasadena Lodge No. 367, lost four each.
Six lodges lost three each, 48 lodges lost two each, and 153 lodges lost
one each. Long and faithful service is a characteristic of those who
serve Free Masonry, and in the past year eleven lodges have each lost
a Past Master whose activities in the Fraternity covered fifty years or
more.
Our Fraternity is accustomed to events of unique and distinctive nature, and in the passing of Adrian Benjamin Barnett, Past' Master
of Elsinore Lodge No. 289, something unusual has been added to the
record. Brother Barnett served his lodge as Master in 1914 and again
in 1940, an interval of 26 years elapsing between his first and second
installation.
}AMES HAMILTON LASH

The Grand Lodge of California in its long and eventful history has
been honored by the services of many great men. The office of Grand
Chaplain has been occupied by outstanding spiritual leaders. One of
the most learned, beloved and admired men to direct our religious
services died December 17, 1949 at his home in Hollywood, California.
Dr. James Hamilton Lash was born in Athens, Ohio, June 18, 1872.
From his early childhood the stories of the Bible fascinated him. His
regular attendance at Sunday school and church functions gradually
brought the realization that his life should be dedicated to the service
of his fellow man and the spreading of religious knowledge. Accord-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

157

ingly his education was directed along those lines. He studied at Hillsdale College and Hillsdale Theological Seminary in Hillsdale, Michigan, graduating with high honors. He also studied at the Union Theological Seminary. He was an active member of Delta Tau Delta
Fraternity.
After ordination Dr. Lash accepted pastorates in Indiana and later
in Minnesota. Coming to California, he became pastor of the Congregational Church at Rialto. His success at that church was recognized
and he soon received a call to the Lake Avenue Congregational Church
in Pasadena, where he served for nine yars.
When Brother Lash became pastor of the Hollywood Congregational Church on Hollywood Blvd. in 1919, services were being held in
a womens' clubhouse across the street from the location of the present
church. He immediately began a building program and before the year
y.ras out, officiated at the cornerstone rites for Woodruff Chapel, out of
which the new sanctuary stemmed. He resigned his pastorate early in
1949 but despite his relinquishment of active duties he was called upon
in November to lay the cornerstone of a new structure, thus terminating
the building program begun by him so many years before. His labors
were responsible for the magnificent buildings which now form the
church.
Despite the heavy responsibilities of his official position, he found
time to serve as moderator and president of the board of directors of the
Southern California Congressional Conference in 1914 and 1915, and
as a director from 1932 to the time of his death. He also served as
President of the Association of Ministers of Los Angeles and vicinity
in 1934. On several occasions Dr. Lash was speaker at the Easter Sunrise Services in Hollywood Bowl, a religious service that is broadcast
not only through the United States but throughout the world.
He was active in civic affairs and as chairman directed the affairs
of the Community Chest in 1929-1930-1931. He was a member of
Hollywood Rotary Club, and served one term as president.
It was only natural that one of so deep religious understanding
should become interested in Free Masonry. In 1923, he petitioned
Hollywood Lodge No. 355. He was initiated November 10, 1923,
passed December 13, and raised December 27 of the same year. He
was also a member of Hollywood Council No. 33 Royal and Select
Masters; Hollywood Chapter No. 120 Royal Arch Masons, and Hollywood Commandery No. 56 Knights Templar ..
At the 96th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of California, held in the City of San Francisco in October, 1945, the newly
elected Grand Master, Most Worshipful Lawrence C. Kelly, appointed
Brother Lash to the exalted position of Grand Chaplain. Only 12 days
after his installation, Grand Master Kelly was taken by death, and the
Deputy Grand Master, Right Worshipful Arthur W. Brouillet, sue-

ceeded to the office of Grand Master. Brother Brouillet recognizing, as
had Brother Kelly, the exceptional ability of Brother Lash and his devotion to the Fraternity affirmed the appointment, and Brother Lash
served with great honor to himself and to the Fraternity.
Brother Lash is survived by his widow, the former Frances Rebecca
Colyer, to whom he was married in 1906, and by their daughter, Mrs.
Frances Switzer, Corona, California.
Our present Grand Chaplain in speaking of the passing of Dr. Lash
said: "With love and honor, . we salute the memory of th~ gallant

JOHN SCALMANINI

The Grand Lodge of California has five lodges working in languages other than English-two work in French, two in German, and
one, Speranza Italiana Lodge No. 219 of the City of San Francisco,
working in Italian. Speranza Italiana Lodge on July 22, 1949, lost one
of its most beloved Past Masters, and one who served as Inspector for
17 consecutive years.
John Scalmanini was born March 1, 1861 in Tesserete, a village in
the Italian speaking section of southern Switzerland, a short distance
· from the Italian frontier. The spirit of adventure so dominant in youth,
and the fabulous stories of the American West then so current in
Europe, caused him to seek his fortune in the new world: He arrived in
California in October, 1878, and finding San Francisco exactly to his
liking he spent the balance of his life as a resident of that city.
In his business career Brother Scalmanini was part owner of the
newspaper Elvezia, a periodical devoted to the interests of · those of
Swiss ancestry. He was active as an insurance broker, and for 30 years
was secretary of the Colma Vegetable Growers Association.
He was a charitable man and had a deep feeling of understanding
and sympathy for those less fortunate than himself. He furnished the
funds to found a hospital in Tesserete and his efforts assured its maintenance. He organized the Swiss Relief Society of Mutual Help and
served as its secretary for many years. At his death he left substantial
sums to the Shrine Hospital for crippled children and also to the American Cancer Society.
Brother Scalmanini was made a Master Mason in Speranza Italiana
Lodge No. 219 in 1883. He held the exalted position of Master for
the Masonic year 1887-1888. Elected secretary of his lodge in December, 1900, he discharged the duties of that office for more than 30 years.
He was a trustee of the lodge from 1920 until his death. Inspector of
the 115th District from 1904 to 1921. Received the 50 year emblem
from Grand Lodge on his birthday, March 1, 1933. His other Masonic

On November 2, 1949, George E. Delavan died at his home, 912
South Plymouth Blvd. in the City of Los Angeles, at the age of 69.
George was born at Green, Iowa, the son of Sarah Inger and George
E. Delavan, natives of New York State.
Brother Delavan received his early education in the public schools
of Green and Estherville, Iowa. Following graduation from high scheel,
he attended Grinnel College, and later obtained his law degree from
the University of Iowa.
For reasons of health, George came to California in 1904, selecting
Los Angeles as the field for his future activities. Desiring to become
better acquainted with the community of his adoption he worked for
several years as a clerk in the offices of outstanding law firms, and when
he felt that his understanding of local conditions justified his actions,
he opened his own law office and practiced his profession with distinction until his death.
George Delavan was one of the pioneers of the suburban movement.
When Los Angeles began its phenomenal increase in population he
became a commuter, establishing his home at Manhattan Beach. He
immediately became interested in the problems of the village, and his
ready solution of many vexing problems so impressed his fellow citizens
that they elected him Mayor and he served in this position for 8 years.
For 6 years he presided as President of the Redondo Union Board of
Education, and much of the success of that educational district -is due
to his efforts. The Community Chest of Manhattan Beach claimed his
attention and for several years he was its chairman.
George Delavan was a deeply religious man and one of his first
acts upon arrival in California was to affiliate with the Pico Heights
Congregational Church, where he taught Sunday school, organized the
boys' band, established the annual reunion of former Sunday school
students, which organization is now in its 37th year. He also assisted
in the work of the choir of the Manhattan Community Church.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It was only logical that one so deeply immersed in religious matters
should become interested in Free Masonry. and, in 1909, he applied to
Sunset Lodge No. 352. Being initiated into the several degrees, he was
raised August 31 that same year. He occupied the Oriental Chair for
the year 1913. He gave unstintingly of his time, his efforts, and his
substance to further the interests of the Fraternity and as a result he
was honored by Grand Master Leon 0. Whitsell with the appointment
of Inspector of the 73rd Masonic District. Succeeding Grand Masters
renewed his appointment and he served until a short time before his
death, when ill health forced his resignation. He also gave valuable
service to the Scottish Rite Bodies of Los Angeles, being a member of
the class graduating July 16, 1915. He was a member of Al Malaikah
Temple of the Shrine.
His wisdom, counsel and guidance were an inspiration to his legion
of brethren, and Masonry is better because he served her so well.
George is survived by his widow, Louise, and by two daughters.
George Delavan was a grand man, with a fine personality, a radiance, a magnificent sense of humor. We miss him greatly.

He also directed the campaign in this area to raise $10,000,000 to

As a civic and religious leader he served for many years as an elder
of the Calvary Presbyterian Church. He was active in Islam Temple
and a staunch supporter of the Shriners Hospital for Crippled Children,
which he dedicated in 1923.
In 1948 he was elected president of the Civic League of Improvement Clubs, and at his death was honorary president emeritus of the
organization.
He was a past grand patron of the Order of Eastern Star in California, a past master of Bethlehem Lodge No. 453, F. & A. M., a
member and past commander of the Golden Gate Commandery of the

He was a past president of the St. Andrews Society, a member of
the Caledonian Club, Union League Club, and the San Francisco and
American Bar associations.
He was a leader of the California bar. He represented the Golden
Gate Bridge and Highway District from 1940 until his death. Earlier
in his career he was one of the first and most successful attorneys for
the Chinese and was instrumental in bringing peace among the tongs.
He was counsel for the Chinese Six Companies for many years.
One of his brothers was Gavin McNab, one of California's leading
Democrats. The brothers were vigorous opponents in many state and
national political campaigns, but this did not affect their close and affectionate personal relationships. John L. was largely self-educated. He
attended public schools in Mendocino County and attended Oakland
high school for two years, leaving at the age of 18. Deciding on a legal
career, he went for advice to his older brother, Gavin, already a successful lawyer. His brother's advice: "Read Blackstone 12 times." He
did, over a period of three years and together with considerable other
studying. As soon as he reached his 21st birthday, he took and passed
the State Bar Examination. He returned to Ukiah and established a
successful practice. Almost immediately he entered politics and while
still in his early 20' s became one of the youngest members of the Republican State Central Committee.
His first political activity of scope came in 1899 when, at the age of

Aside from his family, there was nothing nearer to Brother Osterholt' s heart than Free Masonry. He was initiated in the first class after
the institution of West Lake Lodge in 1908: was Master in 1914, and
it was during his term as Master that the present West Lake Temple
was built. He was later elected secretary, and served in that capacity
for 28 years.
The Osterholt family has held a unique place in California Masonic
history, for exactly 25 years to the day from the time Bill was installed
Master of West Lake Lodge, he had the privilege of installing his son
Allen in the same office. Later Bill had the pleasure of assisting Allen in
the conferring of the degrees upon Allen's two sons. Thus three generations of the family were members of the lodge at the same time. In addition to these unusual circumstances, Bill also gloried in the raising of
his second son, Breese.
Bill did not confine all his labors in Masonry to the Blue Lodge, for
on September 11, 1909, he graduated a 32nd degree Mason of the
Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite. His interest and enthusiasm for
this organization was recognized by the Supreme Council, and in October 1915, he received the decoration of Knight Commander of the Court
of Honor. His activities in these bodies continued until his death.
. It was only natural that one so interested in the Fraternity should
turn his thoughts to the Grand Lodge, and his work there was outstanding. He gave most appreciated service to the Committee on Credentials.
In 1942, the then Grand Treasurer, the very Worshipful William P.
Filmer, being confined to his home by illness during the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, the Grand Master, Frank M. Smith,
appointed Brother Osterholt Grand Treasurer Pro Tempore.
Bill is survived by his widow, Mrs. Nellie Osterholt, his two sons,
Allen and Breese, and two grandsons, Dick and Bill.
Brother Osterholt' s life was a rare combination of sincerity of purpose, one of modesty and humility, and the desire to do right. We are
proud that he was our friend, that he was our brother.
As we pay this tribute to our departed brethren let us not forget
that their lives were in no great measure different from our own; that
they in their earthly experience had the same hopes, the same fears, and
felt the same uncertainties that are the common lot of men.
They were mature men, men who from experience knew the beauties
and glories of life. They also knew from experience the eternal struggle
between good and evil; the ever present conflict between health and
disease; the never ceasing competition between light and darkness. They
knew that life under the best of circumstances could be exceedingly
difficult-yet they met life with the courage of free men, each receiving

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRIEVANCES
To the ft/lost Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
There has been referred to the Committee on Grievances a total of
47 records. This report to Grand Lodge by your Committee will deal
with 32 of these records. The remaining 15 records will be covered by
separate reports, due to the fact that they involve appeals, Petitions for
Restoration, or some other situation which, in the opinion of your Committee, requires them to be separately considered.
In presenting this, our so-called omnibus report, two matters appear
to your Committee again to require special mention. Reviewing these
records, year after year, there is impressed upon our attention the fact
that altogether too many Masonic trials, or the preferring of charges
for Unmasonic offenses, arise from matters occurring either prior to the
presentation of the Petition for Degrees or in connection therewith.
Prior criminal records of a petitioner and false statements contained in
Petitions for Degrees can usually be quite easily uncovered by proper investigation of the petitioner. We therefore strongly urge that the officers
of the constitutent lodges exercise greater supervision over the efforts
of investigating committees to the end that the unworthy character of a
petitioner may be discovered prior to his receipt of the Degrees of Ma- .
sonry, thus avoiding the necessity of trial procedure thereafter.
Many Masonic trials arise out of matters which have been the subject of criminal court procedure, resulting in a conviction of the accused.
In such cases, in the preparation of Masonic charges, where automatic
expulsion under Section 332 is not available, the offense committed by
the accused should be charged rather than the fact that the accused has
been convicted of the offense. It is the commission of the offense which
constitutes unmasonic conduct rather than the conviction therefor. To
charge the conviction rather than the offense itself is to plead a result

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

177

rather than the cause. Because of the frequency with which this error of
pleading offenses of Unmasonic conduct occurs, we deem it appropriate
to call this matter again to the attention of the Grand Lodge.
Your Committee proposes to recommend to Grand Lodge the affirmance of the result reached in the following trial records:
No. 1125-(Retrial). A member of Palms Lodge No. 512. Suspended
December 1, 1947.

made application for the Degrees of Masonry. Section 332 reads in part
as follows:
"In the event any Mason who is a member of a Lodge
under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California shall
suffer a final judgment of conviction of a crime classified as a
felony under the law, and be imprisoned in pursuance thereof;
or shall be adjudged an habitual criminal; it shall be the duty
of the Secretary of the Lodge of which such Mason is a member, upon learning of such conviction, to procure, at the expense
of this Lodge, two certified copies of such final judgment of
conviction, one of which certified copies shall be filed in the
records of the Lodge."
In a strictly grammatical sense, the phrase "in the event any Mason
.. . shall suffer a final judgment of conviction" standing alone conveys an
idea of futurity. The natural meaning of the phrase "shall suffer" ordinarily applies to the future. It is true that the phrase or its equivalent
is frequently found in statutes and in some cases it is applied to past as
well as to future actions. The majority of this committee feel that the
reasonable interpretation of Section 332 makes it applicable to contingent future events so that automatic expulsion can be used only when a
brother is convicted and imprisoned after he becomes a Mason. It does
not mean that a person convicted of a felony before he applied for and
was accepted in Masonry would not be subject to expulsion. It is the
opinion of the committee that, if the facts warrant the same, steps to
expel A. H. W . should be taken by the regularly prescribed procedure
for a masonic trial and automatic expulsion under Section 332 is not
permitted. In the event charges may be preferred, they should charge a
Masonic offense, occurring either after accused has become a Mason
or in the course of his application for Masonry.
We, therefore, offer and move the adoption of the following resolution that the action of Ja mes Foshay Lodge in suspending A. H. W.
from all the rights and privileges be reversed and set aside and that the
case be remanded to the lodge for such action, if any, as the lodge may
determine.
.
Adopted.

on the 18th day of April, 1930, and was sentenced to imprisonment at

certified copy of conviction was g.iven to the accused under the terms of
Section 332 of the Ordinances, and the accused did not demand a trial.
He was, therefore, automatically expelled by the lodge at the designated
stated meeting.
The question presented in this trial record is whether a Fellowcraft
Mason can be automatically expelled under Section 332 for the conviction of a felony and imprisonment thereunder which occurred before he

of a brief one-half page statement by the Secretary concerning the eviden<:e presented. It does not incorporate any of the exhibits presented
by the Accuser or the Accused and is not sufficient to permit a proper
review of the proceedings.
The Secretary's brief summary does indicate, however, that up to
the present time the widow has paid to the Accused over $3200.00 on
loans totaling $775.00.
The Commissioners did not ballot separately on the specifications
and on the charge of unmasonic conduct. They took but one ballot,
lumping all the specifkations and the charge of unmasonic conduct
together, the result being "guilty" three and "not guilty" six.
The Accuser has attempted to appeal from the decision of the Commission and has presented to the Grand Master a statement which, if it
had been properly taken and authenticated as pres<:ribed by Section 339
of the Ordinances, would support the specifications concerning fraudulent overcharges. The appeal is apparently directed to the Grand Master
instead of the Grand Lodge. There is no evidence that notice of appeal
was given to the Master of the Lodge as required by Section 338 of
the Ordinances.
·
Section 316 of the Ordinances provides, in part : "All oral testimony,
direct and cross, shall be written out in full by the Secretary or stenographer, and certiA.ed as correct. The documentary testimony shall 'be
made a part of the record by incorporating it or a copy of it therein."
Section 323 of the Ordinances provides that the record of proceedings shall include the testimony of each witness "exactly as he gives it
in his own words, giving all the questions and answers."
Section 322 of the Ordinances provides with reference to balloting
by the Commissioners as follows: "After sufficient consultatjon and
deliberation, a vote for 'guilty' or 'not guilty', by ballot shaU be taken
upon each speciA.cation, and each such vote shaU be recorded: and a
similar vote shall thus be taken upon the charge of unmasonic conduct
and be thus recorded, as it might be that the facts proven and found
did not constitute an unmasonic offense."
None of these provisions of the "Ordinances were complied with.
Obviously the failure to keep and supply a record of the testimony
is a denial to Grand Lodge of its right to review the proceedings and to
determine whether there has been any miscarriage of justice.
For the foregoing reasons your committee believes that the matter
should be sent back for a new trial and that if such action is taken the
specifications should be amended so as to definitely describe the acts of
the Accused which are alleged to be unmasonic offenses, giving the dates
thereof. Each specification should in and of itself allege a Masonic
offense.
We therefore offer and move the adoption of the foUowing resolution:

Adopted.

Trial Record No. 1203
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1203, reports as follows:
Accused, W.P.S., a member of Temple City Lodge No. 612, was
convicted in the state courts of extortion, a felony, and was sentenced
to state prison, but this sentence was suspended and he was placed on
probation for five years with the first six months to be served in the
county jail. This was such imprisonment in pursuance of a final conviction of a crime classified as a felony to make possible automatic
expulsion from the lodge under the provisions of Section 332, Constitution and Ordinances. Proceedings were had under that section and
he was declared expelled.
·
All . the proceedings were regular except that the notice required
under Section 332 was mailed to accused by registered mail at his former
home address in El Monte. The secretary states that the wife of accused
resided there and receipted for the registered letter containing the
notice, a nd that the accused was confined at the time at one of the many
county road-camps used in connection with the Los Angeles county

191

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

jail, and the lodge feared the letter would pass through · more strange
hands if sent to accused through the county jail.
However, we have always held that the last known place of address
referred to in Section 332, where an accused is being imprisoned for
crime, is the place of his imprisonment and not his former home. A
notice addressed to his former home may he withheld from him out of
mistaken kindness or desire to save him from grief. The receipt in this
case was signed by the wife of accused, and there is no certainty that
he himself ever received it.
For failure to mail the notice to the last known place of address,
which was then the Los Angeles county jail, this expulsion must now
be set aside and the case reversed.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved that the action of Temple Lodge No. 612 in expelling
W.P.S. under the provisions of Section 332, Constitution and Ordinances, be reversed and the matter sent back to the lodge for proper
proceedings.

notice.
For failure to mail the notice to the last known place of address,
which was then the State Prison at San Quentin, California, this expulsion must now be set aside and the case reversed.

Trial Record No. 1224
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1224, reports as follows:
Accused, J.F.L., (a member of Park Boulevard Lodge No. 568) was
charged on October 21, 1949, in three specifications as follows:
1. That in March, 1949, he accepted from a man who desired to
petition for the degrees in Park Boulevard Lodge No. 568 a check for
$100. made payable to accused together with an application for the
degrees and had not to the date of the charges turned the application
or money over to the lodge.
2. That early in 1948 accused borrowed $50.00 from a Master
Mason and had never repaid it.
3. That in November, 1947, accused borrowed $250.00 from the
wife of a Master Mason and had never repaid it.
Failure to pay a debt, in the absence of fraud or misrepresentation,
or misuse of Masonic standing or name, is not a Masonic offense, and
the second and third specifications herein are not considered in this
report although they were fully proved at the trial.
In this matter the record is very incomplete. There is no certificate
of service of summons and charges, but the secretary, now deceased,
typed in one place on the record that "the accused left for parts unknown, something over a year ago and so far as we can determine, no
one knows his present address." The master at the start of the trial
stated that the secretary had mailed a copy of the summons and charges
to accused at his last known place of address and that the trial would
proceed ex parte. The record does not show any other facts amounting
to due diligence in the effort to locate the accused to justify an ex parte
trial as provided for by Section 308, Constitution and Ordinances. The
commissioners were elected on November 25, 1949 and the trial there-

192

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

upon was set for Dec. 12, less than 20 days later. When the secretary
mailed the letter to accused, if he did, is not shown in the record before us.
At the trial on December 12th testimony was given by the man
involved that in March, 1949 he had requested from accused a petition
for the degrees, that accused a few days later came to his home with a
blank which he thought was such a petition, (although he said he
thought it was white, rather than blue, and was not the form shown him
at the trial, said form being an authentic blank petition). He filled out
the blank presented to him and accused took it saying he would get the
other signers, and a check was made out in the name of the accused for
$100.00 and delivered to accused. The witness stated that accused suggested that the check be made payable to him so he could turn cash into
the lodge with the petition. The check was introduced into evidence,
although we do not find it in the file herein. It had been cashed by
accused soon after he received it.
The witness stated he had asked the accused several times as the
months went by as to any action on his petition and accused told him the
lodge had a long waiting list of petitions and that his would he reached
in due time. Finally word got to the master of the lodge and investigation showed that no petition had ever been turned in. In fact, it appeared
that accused had never received a blank petition from the secretary, who
keot all such blanks in his locked desk so no member could get a blank
without his knowledge.
·
The wife and another relative of the man involved were in the house
when accused received the check and corroborated the testimony in part
in that they both heard the men discussing the matter of the application
for the degrees, although they were in an adjoining room, and they saw
the witness sign and deliver the check for $100.
The trial record herein shows nothing of the balloting on the specifications or on the question of unmasonic conduct, but the minutes of the
masters report to the lodge stated that accused had been found Not
Guilty of all three specifications and of unmasonic conduct.
This matter must be reversed because no jurisdiction was established
to try the case. It is evident no personal service was had and accused
did not appear at the trial. Whether the summons mailed to him at his
last Oakland address less than 20 days before the date of trial ever
caught up with him is not known, and probably makes no difference.
There was no showing that he was within the jurisdiction of the lodge,
i.e. in the City of Oakland, so that service could be made either personally or by leaving at his home ?ddress. The time was too short for
service by mail if accused had been elsewhere in the state or in another
state, and his address known. The ex parte trial was not justified by
any due diligence shown in ascertaining his then present address.
In sending the case back to the lodge we wish to state that the

uncontradicted evidence on the trial strongly supports a finding of guilt
of the first specification and the conduct of the accused set out in that
specification would certainly be unmasonic conduct. The trial commissioners in finding accused Not Guilty may have been influenced by .
the evidence tending to show that it was not an actual petition for the
degrees which accused had the witness sign when he got the $100. check.
Regardless of that fact, the evidence does show that the $100. was
being taken as the fee to accompany such an application and the failure
of accused to apply it for that purpose for at least seven months thereafter, without some excuse offered, would be unmasonic conduct.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption :
Resolved that the action of Park Boulevard Lodge No. 568 in adjudging J.F.L. not guilty herein be reversed and set aside, and the
matter sent back to said lodge for further trial on the first specification
set out in the charges filed, after proper service of summons on the
accused or a sufficient showing of inability to learn his address to justify
an ex parte trial.

The Accused C.L.S. was charged with unmasonic conduct in that

The Homes Trustees have appeared before your Committee on
Policy and General Purposes and convinced us of the propriety of their
recommendation. What is known as the Resident's Monthly Grant
Fund was established some years ago for the purpose of providing a
monthly spending allowance to residents.
The original fund was
financed by income from the Flint Trust Fund. At present the fund
consists in large part of proceeds realized from assignments executed
by residents at the time of their admission to the Home. The fund has
grown in proportions not anticipated at the time of its establishment;
so much so, in fact, that in 1949 the sum of $100,000.00 was transferred
from it to the Building Fund. The balance in the fund as of March 1,
1950 was $64,621.29.
That the Monthly Grant Fund is far more than capable of continuing the monthly grant to residents and also absorbing the charge of
$150.00 for each funeral is obvious. The execution of the proposed
funeral policy would not only be pleasing to residents of the Home,
but would also provide relief to the Lodges. Moreover, all Lodges
would be treated alike.
Your Committee therefore recommends the approval of the recommendation of the Homes Board as it is above set forth.

HOMES BURIAL POLICY

In the annual report of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes, it is
pointed out that under Sections 440 and 717, Edicts and Resolutions of
the Grand Lodge, it is the responsibility of each Lodge to bear the
funeral expense of any of its members or their widows who pass away
while a resident of the Masonic Home. The Board recommends the
adoption of legislation permitting the Board of Trustees to pay the
necessary burial expenses of residents of the Home who die while under
the supervision of such Trusttes, an allowance of $150.00 in each instance being made. This would relieve obligated Lodges to this extent.

Adopted.
ALLOCATION OP FUNDS TO ENDOWMENT FUND

There was referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes a recommendation by the Trustees of the Masonic Homes that the
following language relating to the $25.00 from initiates be deleted from
Section 100 of ordinances:
"When the amount thus collected and so held shall be more
than sufficient, in the judgment of the Trustees, to provide
for the maintenance of the Homes and for such improvements as are then in progress. or contemplated for the
immediate future, the surplus shall be by them allocated
to the Endowment Fund."
The Trustees report that the foregoing provision places a restraint
upon them and prevents them from holding funds collected during the
good years for use during declines when it would be unwise to further
increase the per capita tax. They state that under this provision funds
amounting to $300,000. have been allocated to the Endowment Fund
during the last five years. They declare that if the Homes had been
permitted to hold this $300,000. in reserve there would be no occasion
to restore the per capita levy against the lodges for some time to come.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is in agreement
with the recommendation of the Trustees, and therefore, recommends
that the language quoted be deleted from Section 100 and that the

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

matter be referred to Jurisprudence Committee to prepare the legislation.
The Committee on Finance concurs in this resolution.
Adopted.

PUBLIC LIABILITY INSURANCE

Your committee on Policy and General Purposes to which was
referred that portion of the report of the Grand Secretary relating to
the procuring of public liability insurance by our constituent lodges has
had the same under consideration and begs leave to report.
It appears that a program of liability insurance prepared by insurance counsel was approved by the Grand Master and put into operation
as an administrative action. The program has been made voluntary
since Grand Lodge only has the authority to make it mandatory.
Whether such a program should be made mandatory has been submitted to this committee for consideration. Your committee is of the
opinion that a study of the ancient history of lodges in this jurisdiction
and other pertinent facts is essential before a proper decision can be
made.
We therefore recommend that the incoming Grand Master be requested to appoint a spedal committee to study the question and report
at the next annual communication.
Adopted.
QuoRUM OP GRAND LoDGE

There has been referred to your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes a recommendation of the Grand Master that Section 11 , Article
IV. of our Constitution, relating to the requirement that representatives
of seventy-five lodges must be present to constitute a quorum for the
transaction of the business of Grand Lodge, be amended to provide that
in the event competent state or national authority shall prohibit seventy-

198

199

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

five or more persons from assembling, then the Grand Master, Deputy
Grand Master, Grand Wardens, and Junior Past Grand Master may
exercise the powers of Grand Lodge to appropriate money, to tax constituent lodges, to approve acts of constituent lodges, and to review
trial records, and, furthermore, that the elective officers of Grand Lodge
shall continue in their respective offices until the annual communication
next following the repeal of the prohibition.
During the period of active hostilities in World War II, there were
imposed wartime restrictions on travel and public assemblages which
prevented the normal functioning of Grand Lodge. The primary purpose of the proposed amendment is to forefend against a recurrence of
such restriction.
Since this nation is now engaged as a member of the United Nations
in the Korean conflict, and there exist at this time other threats of war,
it seems wise to make provisions in the event such wartime restrictions
are again imposed. We believe the policy of some such emergency
legislation should be adopted for the reasons stated, but recommend
that it should be provided that in the event competent state or national
authority shall prohibit seventy-five or more persons from assembling,
then a majority of the Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Grand
Wardens, Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary and Junior Past Grand
Master may exercise the powers of Grand Lodge to appropriate money,
to tax constituent lodges, to approve acts of constituent lodges, and to
review trial records, and, furthermore, that the elective officers of Grand
Lodge shall continue in their respective offices until the annual communication next following the repeal of the prohibition.
We, therefore, recommend the adoption of the policy as thus recommended and that the matter be referred to the Jurisprudence Committee for drafting of the legislation.

FORT CROOK

There has been referred to your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes a resolution offered by Fort Crook Lodge No. 575, Fall River
Mills, California, proposing that our laws be amended so as to permit
plural membership in lodges in this jurisdiction.
The reason assigned by the proposer is that at times in some small
lodges their own .brethren are not willing or capable of assuming the
duties of office, and that available brethren of other lodges living away
from their home lodge are not premitted under our laws to serve.
Your Committee has given the proposal careful consideration but
believes that it would be impracticable in operation. There would be such
serious questions of allocating demands or duties of relief. and of administrative and disciplinary control and of divided allegiance and loss
of membership in the home lodge, as to make such an amendment inadvisable.
We therefore recommend that the proposal be not approved.
Adopted.

CHANGE OF CEREMONIES

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Recommendation No. 7 in the Grand Master's message is:
"That the incoming Grand Master be requested to appoint a
special committee to consider the written ceremonies of the Grand
Lodge and report at the next Annual Communication".
This recommendation is preceded by a discussion relative to the
Masonic funeral service and a suggestion that it might be desirable to
have two approved forms of this service.
It seems desirable to consider the general recommendations under
two heads:
.
1. Shall we commit to a special committee the writing of an additional
Masonic funeral service and/ or the revision of the present funeral
service.
2. Shall we commit to a special committee the revision or complete
re-writing of the written ceremonies of the Grand Lodge other than the
funeral service, meaning thereby the ceremonies of the "Installation of
Grand Lodge Officers, the Institution of Constituent Lodges, the Constitution of Constituent Lodges, the Laying of Cornerstones, the Dedication of Masonic Halls, and the Dedication of Masonic Burial Plots.
We shall so treat them, as we have separate recommendations to
make for your consideration.
FUNERAL SERVICE

1. Shall we commit to a special committee the writing of an additional Masonic funeral service and/ or the revision of the present
funeral service:
After several years of study. the Ritual Committee revised the Masonic funeral service and in 1946 this form was approved by the action
of Grand Lodge. The form was prepared with the active cooperation of
our late P .G.M. Dana R. Weller, who for more than forty-five years was

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

201

actively associated with matters of our Ritual and who had more continuous personal contact with more of our constituent Lodges than any
other Mason in California. He was acquainted with the high. the low,
the rich and the poor. He_knew the city Mason and the Brothers on the
mountains and in the valleys.
The members of the Ritual Committee likewise had a wide personal
contact with the Masons of California. In addition to the attention
given to the words of the ceremony, the form was checked with many
Masons who were morticians or the owners or operators of chapels,
crematoriums and mausoleums. The instructions adopted as a part of the
ceremony were made sufficiently flexible to use in any chapel or in connectiC'n with any church service, if the family of the deceased so desired.
Thereafter, with the approval of Grand Lodge, the memorizing of
the Funeral Service was assigned as one of the requirements for a Master's qualifications of office. Now in every Lodge there are several
Brethren and in all California there are more than 2000 Masons who,
on very short notice can prepare themselves to render the funeral service
in a manner that is a credit to the Fraternity, and no Masonic Funeral
need now be held and then be followed by apologies either to the family
of the deceased, to the profane or to our own Brethren.
The words of commendation have been far more numerous than the
few dissenters who have raised their voices. There will always be some
dissenters for that is the nature and the privilege of democracy.
Why should we throw all these valuable accomplishments out the
window and start all over again.
To have two separate and distinct funeral services will add to a
Master's memorizing problems and create confusion not only in the
minds of the Master endeavoring to keep the two ceremonies distinct
during delivery but also confusing in the minds of the profane as to why
we have two distinct funeral services.
We meet upon the level. Let us depart the same way as well as upon
the square.
We recommend that Grand Lodge do not consider even the possibility of a further revision of the Masonic Funeral Service, or the
writing of an additional service, and that such matter be not submitted to
a committee for further consideration.
We move the adoption of this portion of the report.
Adopted.

2. The written ceremonies which are used by Grand Lodge when
convened or by Grand Lodge Officers when performing some Masonic

Except for the re-editing in 1947 of the instructions of use these
ceremonies have not been reviewed, modified or re-written for many,

many years. They at least need a re-examination and study .. In the case

With the exception of a very few of our Grand Lodge Officers, these

·
If it had not been for a report of a special committee made and adopted last year, which report apparently unintentionally divested t.he Ritual
Committee of all its authority to stµdy and make recommendations relative to our ceremonies, the Ritual Committee would undoubtedly have
proceeded to review these ceremonies and would have presented in due
