have in the past, take to themselves suitable assistance and also graciously receive and carefully consider all suggestions that any Brother
desires to offer in the premises.
We therefore recommend that the ceremonies used by Grand Lodge
while convened as such and those used by the Grand Lodge Officers in
the performance of their official duties be referred to the Ritual Committee for review and report to Grand Lodge.
We move the adoption of this portion of the report.

To PERMIT PuBLICATION oF CANDIDATES

There has been referred to your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes a resolution proposed by Bro. Ralph C. Hine, Past Master of
Magnolia Lodge No. 242 and ·Bro. Gustaf A. B. Quick, Past Master of
Santa Paula Lodge No. 291, permitting Lodges in this jurisdiction to
print the names of candidates in their regular Lodge bulletin, provided
such bulletins are enclosed in envelopes and mailed only to Master
Masons.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is of the opinion
that the disadvantages heavily outweigh the advantages of such a program. There are instances where harm might result if the bulletin was
to fall into hands of the profane. There are other times when such information obtained through the medium of bulletins carelessly discarded
could result in an embarrassing situation arising at a man's place of employment and which might result in great harm befalling the individual
through no fault of his own.
We therefore recommend that the resolution be not approved.
Adopted.

COMMITTEE REFERRAL

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has given consideration to the matter referred to it under the title of "Recommendation
No. 4" in the Grand Master's Message and offers the following report.
The Grand Master recommends that business of every kind shall be
referred to and reported upon by a committee before it can be finally
acted upon, unless by unanimous consent and whenever referred to more
than one committee, all such committees shall report thereon before any
vote shall be taken in the Grand Lodge.
Section 69 of the Ordinances, as now written, while requiring that
all business be referred to and reported upon by a committee, implies
the original intent that the "final action" taken pursuant thereto would
be upon the item of business referred and not necessarily upon the committee report as such.
A committee report might be received or accepted without a vote if
it contains only recommendations by the committee that the Grand
Lodge take certain action, but if the report should contain a proposal to
amend the resolution or item of business under consideration it would
then necessitate independent action notwithstanding prior or subsequent
reports from other committees. The long established custom in Grand
Lodge of terminating committee reports with a motion to adopt the
report may sometimes be highly desirable but, in case of multiple referral. would be rigidly prohibited by the legislation proposed.
Your committee is entirely in accord with the desire of the Grand
Master to avoid the time-consuming practice of taking a vote two or
three times on the same question with the possibility that the results may
not be the same on each vote, but is reluctant to recommend legislation

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

204

205

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

which might tend to inhibit the freedom of judgment on the part of thr
presiding Grand Master as to the propriety of entertaining a motion to
adopt any individual report of committee. We therefore recommend that
Recommendation No. 4 be not adopted without further consideration.
Not adopted.
Bro. Jameson moved that the above recommendation be adopted as to
policy. Motion carried.

foreign ritual in a California Lodge. under specific conditions, and this
recommendation is designed only to eliminate the contradiction now
existing between Section 192 and Section 247 your Committee recommends its adoption.
Adopted.
PUBLICATION OF HISTORY

We have considered the report of the Committee on the publication
of the History of Masonry in California. The report shows that the
work is rapidly nearing completion and the books will soon be ready for
delivery. Approximately 1000 sets have been subscribed for and it is
expected that many more will be sold as soon as deliveries can be made.
Last year we recommended to the Grand Lodge that two thousand sets
be printed at a cost then reported to us by the History Publication Committee of $43,200.00. It now appears that the total cost of this program
may exceed that amount.
It is not yet possible to determine the exact cost but it does appear
that it may be necessary for additional funds to be provided.
At the last Communication of Grand Lodge your Finance Committee did not recommend any appropriation but stated they believed
the publication should not be delayed through lack of such appropriation and recommended that the Grand Master be authorized to proceed
with the publication. Any funds used for this project should be returned to a great extent by the sale of sets.
Your Committee on Finance therefore recommends that the Grand
Master be authorized to make available for the purpose of finishing

the publication of the history such funds as may be necessary to carry
the project to completion.
COPIES OF HISTORY TO FOREIGN JURISDICTIONS

In connection with the publication of the History. this Committee is
in accord with the recommendation of the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes adopted by the Grand Lodge yesterday providing
for complimentary distribution of copies of the history when completed
to foreign grand jurisdictions.
Adopted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS

Since their institution, Orinda Lodge has raised 7 Master Masons,
accepted 20 members by affiliation and has 8 awaiting Degrees.
The Lodge has a satisfactory meeting place, all necessary regalia and
is in a sound financial condition with adequate cash on hand, and all
bills paid. The meetings of the Lodge have been conducted on schedule
and in a proper manner, and the attendance reflects the interest and enthusiasm of the membership.
The healthy growth of this community, the important part a Masonic
Lodge plays in its growth and the hearty co-operation of the adjacent
Lodges, convince your Committee that Orinda Lodge should join the
family of regularly constituted Lodges. It therefore recommends that
a Charter be granted to Orinda Lodge No. 704, in the County of Contra
Costa.

WESTCHESTER LoDGE U. D.

Westchester Lodge was granted a dispensation on the 18th day of
June, 1949, and was instituted by the Grand Master on June 18th, 1949.
Because of the comparatively short time this Lodge had been in existence, Grand Lodge continued it under dispensation for the current year.
This Lodge is located in the rapidly growing Westchester district of
southwestern Los Angeles, which prides itself as being the center of the
aircraft industry. The Lodge has built its strength to the present mem~ership of 96 members, having accepted 42 as affiliates and 30 as petitioners. They have a backlog of 28 degrees to be conferred. Their financial situation is comfortable with the sum of $3,624.00 in cash. While
the j,resent meeting place is not large or commodious. with the growth of
the area it is anticipated that a larger meeting place would be forthcoming in the near future. We desire, however, to compliment the members of this Lodge for their many ingenious ways in which they have
overcome the inadequacies of their hall and for the excellent feeling of
fraternalism exhibited therein, and for the comprehensive and excellent
report on the Lodge's activities submitted to your committee.
While the fact that Grand Lodge at its last communication did not
grant a Charter was a source of disappointment to the members of this
group, your Committee is impressed by the zeal and energy of these
good brethren in firmly establishing a Lodge which we are confident will
always be a credit to Masonry.
We therefore recommend that a Charter be granted to Westchester
Lodge No. 703 in the County of Los Angeles.

u. D.

This area is famous for its scenic splendor and as a mecca for summer visitors, but the winter season renders the district generally inaccessible, thereby depriving Masons living there, of Masonic communication with their brethren.
.

and healthy growth of a Lodge. While this Lodge may never be large
in numbers, its financial needs are modest and your committee's analysis

Lodge will not become a financial burden either to its membership or to
Grand Lodge. It is quite evident that the present officers and members

render a real service to Masonry and to the communities along the Lake.

ample cash in hand, and its records being found complete and in order,
your committee recommends that a charter be granted to Lake Tahoe
Lodge No. 707 in the County of El Dorado.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LODGE FINANCING
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Lodge Financing has just completed its busiest
year. More than sixty applications have been acted upon. Approval has
been given for the building of nine new Masonic Temples, for the acquisition of six Temple building sites, and for the incorporation of fourteen
Masonic Temple associations.
It is interesting to note that where applications were made for permission to construct new Masonic Temples, the large majority of requests involve the single purpose type of lodge building. A great deal
of volunteer labor is employed and the financing is taken care of. in
most part, by the members of the respective lodges.
The members of your Committee deem it a real pleasure to have
been able to approve the requests for permission to erect these several
new Masonic Lodge homes, and it has been a real inspiration to your
Committee Chairman to observe the brethren of some of these Lodges
building Masonic Temples with their own hands. Men, many of whom
had never driven a nail or wielded a paint brush in their lives, work
joyously and efficiently during all their leisure hours to complete the job.
There is something fundamental in the philosophy of Masonry which
impels men to do the things they do to further its cause. To illustrate
the point: About a month ago your Chairman journeyed to El Segundo
to watch the progress of the work on the new El Segundo Temple. On
that occasion, four past masters of the Lodge, all of whom were retired
from their employment and businesses, were on the job, working under
a blazing sun, tying steel in forms preparatory to pouring concrete for
the East wall. No amount of money could have hired these worthy
brothers to do this work. On telling this story to an inspector of a
Masonic district in that vicinity he suggested that they were working
for Master Mason's wages, which, after all, is more precious than any
other kind of pay.

213

As in the past, after your Committee has acted upon an application,
a complete file on each case, including the details of the request, necessary resolutions, financial statements, comments by Committee members,
together with copy of written consent is filed in the Grand Secretary's
office as a part of the records of the Grand Lodge.
The following Lodges and Temple associations received Committee
consent to erect Masonic Temples:

HISTORY
Although the beginnings of our Homes occurred early in the history
of Grand Lodge, it was many years before the seed was sown for the
Endowment Fund. Early contributions by individuals and appropriations of Grand Lodge were used for the acquiring of land and for a
building program. It was not until I 910 that the trustees, after the
accumulation of some $17,000.00, established what they termed a "permanent improvement fund." However, our records show that the previous year a bequest was made to Grand Lodge by Brother Jacob Hart
Neff (who died March 26, 1909) consisting of the residue of his estate,
amounting to $12,688.97, with the recommendation that said money
should be placed in a "permanent endowment fund." Grand Lodge then
ordered that the previously designated Improvement Fund be added to
the Neff legacy. Thus was our permanent endowment fund started, and
proper tribute was paid to the good and thoughtful brother in the following words:
"Thus a nucleus is created for a fund which we trust in time
will grow to such proportions as will take care of our Homes.
and the cherished name of the honored and loyal Mason, which.
in life, was written in our book of gold as 'one who loves his fellow man' and as 'one whom love of God hath blest.' Will forever in this greatest of Masonic charities lead all the rest."
At this juncture of our history, an Endowment Fund Committee
was created ( 1910) and small sums were added from time to time, which
were invested in sound. interest-bearing securities. It was in 1932 that
a real impetus to such a program was given. By action of Grand Lodge
(Constitution and Ordinances. Article V) a Masonic Home Endowment Board was established. The purpose of such a Board was definitely
set up, "to study. devise, and carry out plans for the securing of adequate endowment for the Masonic Homes of California."
The Board is composed of fifteen members, five appointed each year,

PROGRAM
A review of the Board's activities shows that it has consistently
followed a program in accordance with its established purpose. It has
been truly a continuous educational one. Such a procedure has demanded several definite approaches. It has been their responsibility to inform
not only the officers, but endeavor to reach every individual Mason by
some manner that he may be made aware of the splendid service of our
two Homes, how they are operated and the privilege he may share by
participating in their support. Over eighty thousand bulletins have been
distributed to the membership during the past year-an all-time record.
In accordance with past custom, the Grand Master designated May as
Endowment Month, a time when special thought and consideration
might be given to our Endowment program.
The splendid cooperation and assistance by the Most Worshipful
Grand Master throughout the year has been of invaluable assistance.
The thoughtful consideration by our _busy Inspectors has been most
appreciated. Particularly we are gratiAed by their cooperation in a new
redistricting program for our work during the past year. A member of
the Board has assumed responsibility to contact and cooperate with
certain definitely assigned districts. In general. this plan has proven
particularly helpful and has brought the message of the Endowment
J3oard much closer home and has given those lodges a clear insight in to
their opportunities and privileges. Chairmen for such, as well as lodge
officers, have aided materially in evolving this procedure and to them
great credit is due.
Informative talks have been given freely on request, pictures have
been shown and other means of disseminating information have been
utilized more freely and advantageously by the lodges. All correspondence and questions have been given prompt attention and in general we
have every reason to believe there is a much ·b etter understanding and
a more smooth operation of our educational program.

220

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

ACCOMPLISHMENTS
Every year shows a new record of achievement. The list of Honor
Lodges-those contributing two dollars or more per member-is a stimulating influence and gratification to your Board. The large number of
individual contributions is material evidence of the understanding and
appreciation on the part of approximately twenty-five per cent of our
membership. It is to be regretted that although the total individual contributions shows an increase over last year, the added amount is not
proportionate to the increased membership. The number of individual
members contributing has decreased from last year's figure of 52.998
to 49,233. We earnestly hope that the current year will witness an increased realization of responsibility and will result in total contributions
and total number of contributors proportionate to our membership. The
number of bequests is lasting evidence of the interest and appreciation
of those farseeing brethren who have realized that " I am my brother's
keeper." We commend a careful study of the detailed financial report
for a full understanding of accomplishments.
THE FUTURE
No goal has been set by Grand Lodge, unless it be, "a sufficient
endowment, the income from which should care for our Homes." Wise
planning and judicial action by those in charge of our Fund has given
us safety above all. They have taken their trust seriously and protected
your principal with the greatest possible income. The upkeep and
maintenance of our Homes has risen rapidly and may continue along
such lines for some time. We want them to ever be a welcome rendezvous for those entrusted to our care.
Our task is not too difficult, but some responsibility rests upon the
shoulders of each and every member of the Craft. A kind word, a wholesome thought. a dissemination of knowledge, a willing contribution by
those who are able, a planned bequest, are all involved when we say:
"Let every Mason in California today, share in endowing forever,
that which California Masons have built during the past one hundred
years."

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC INFORMATION

While questions and answers, to be etfective, must be brief and, therefore, leave much to be desired for thorough information, there is a psychological principle of value to be observed. It is that one learns a
fact better and rettains the knowledge longer, if he first has a question
in his mind about it.
Accordingly, your Committee presents herewith "707 Questions and
Answers about Freemasonry" which are divided by subjects, accompanied by a table of contents, listing eighteen heads and subheads. It
is not to be inferred that there are only 707 facts worthy ·Of note about
Freemasonry, nor that all of that number as set forth are necessary or
desirable.
.,.
In the preparation of this mater.ial, your Committee has had carefully in mind, just as it did in the preparation of the booklets above
mentioned, that it is no part of your Committtt's functions or privileges
to interpret the symbolism, ritual or rites of Freem,.~onry, or to indulge
in implications as to their origin or meaning as so often.appears to be the
tendency in such enterprises. Any references tb such subjects ·h ave been
confined to generalities or exoteric matters.
Your Committee recommends:
1. That there be appropriated the sum of $4,000.00 for printing a
supply of the four booklets for use during the coming Masonic year.
2. That this report and the manuscript of the 707 Question and
Answers be referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes
and to the Committee on Ritual for their examination and recommendations, and to the Committee on Finance as to the requested appropriation.
3. That your Committee be continued and that there be appropriated for the general expanses of your Committee during the ensuing
year, the sum of $500.00.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic Information reports as follows:
The Books of the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason which were
first recommended by your Committee at the 1948 Communication were ·
finally approved and, early in the present year, were printed and distributed to the lodges, together with reprints of the Address to the
Candidate and Book of the Entered Apprentice. We express our appreciation to the Grand Secretary and his Assistant for their cooperation
in the printing and distribution of these booklets. They will endeavor
to keep account of the number of initiations, passings, and ralsings in
the various lodges and to see that each Lodge is kept supplied with a
sufficient number so that there will be no break in the program of having
each candidate receive one of them at the proper time in his advancement. Should there be any oversight in this respect, your Committee
requests that the Secretaries of the lodges promptly notify the Grand
Secretary in order that the candidates may not be slighted. ·
While the primary purpose of these booklets is to instruct the candidate as he progresses through the degrees and the general distribution of
them to all members of the lodges has been thought inadvisable, many
lodges have purchased quantities of them to be sold to such as want
them at ten cents per copy. This has produced a revenue of $240.50
during the current year.
Many expressions of approval of the booklets and this system of
instruction have been received from Masters and Secretaries and in the
opinion of your Committee, this part of its program has been quite
successful and the distribution of the four booklets should be kept up
consistently and regularly.
The first printing of the booklets this year was insufficient to meet
the demand so that a reprint of 5,000 copies was necessary, which supply
is now approaching exhaustion.
Your Committee would appreciate any comments or suggestions
that may occur to the brethren at any time as to the nature or usefulness
of this method of instruction and, particularly, of any improvements
that can be made in it.
It has been repeatedly suggested to your Committee that there should
be prepared questions and answers to accompany the four ·booklets,
based, in part at least, on their contents, and a number of requests for
material of that sort have come to your Committee from the lodges. Of
course, questions and answers are not good merely because they are
questions and answers, for the question should be on a point of some
importance and the answer should be correct so nearly as we know how
to make it, or, if there is doubt about the fact, that should be stated.

Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON TAXATION

The amendments to the Social Security Act are so recent that authoritative interpretation has not yet been formulated by the Internal Rev,enue Department. In the event of any material deviations from the abo~e
by such interpretation of the Department before the next communication,
the Committee will make a special report to the Grand Master.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Special Taxation Committee has continued to function under
the membership of Robert R. York, James E. Hammond and R. P. Wisecarver.
The Committee during the past year has given advice repeatedly to
the subordinate lodges and to the various committees of Grand Lodge,
The scope of the advice covers not only taxation, but various phases of
insurance coverage, closely related thereto. The Committee has also
prosecuted an app~al with respect to the Fresno Board of Relief and
Employment .with the California Department of Employment, and has.
successfully maintained the status of that and similar organizations, as
being wholly charitable.
: 'For the past two or three years we have been awaiting action by
Congress on the many bills pending before it, purporting to extend the
coverage of the Social Security Act and to expand its pension system.
Congress finally passed a bill known as Public Law 734 of the 81st Congress. materially expanding the scope and coverage of the Act. It would
appear that so far as Grand Lodge and the subordinate lodges are concerned. the Act does not materially alter the tax status with the exception that the minimum salary of those coming under the Act, has been
increased from at least $45.00 per quarter to those receiving $50.00 per
quarter. The rate is also increased to 1Yi%. with provision for additional increases in the future.
With reference to organizations coming under the exemption of
Section 101-6 of the Income Tax, which relates to charitable. religious,
scientific, literary and educational organizations, an amendment was
made. allowing such organizations to elect to come under the Social
Security Act for a minimum period of at least ten years, providing that
at least two-thirds of the employees join with the employer in electing
such coverage. The Boards of Relief and Employment could therefore,
with the co-operation of the employees, if they so desire, elect to come
under the Social Security Act, as to all of such employees so electing.
Employees wQo do not join in the election would not be under the Act.
All new employees hired after the election would automatically be under
the Act.
This amendment is of importance because for the first time, the
Social Security Act allows an election to come under its terms.
To recapitulate: Grand Lodge and all subordinate lodges are under
the Social Security Act and the State Unemployment Act, subject only
to specific exemptions of certain employees who are either ritualistic
officers or whose wages are less than $50.00 per c~lendar quarter.
The charitable organizations and corporations may elect to come
under the Federal Social Security Act and the State Unemployment Act

R. P. WISECARVER
JAMES E. HAMMOND
ROBERT R. YORK .

REPORT OF 'COMMITTEE ON CONSTITUTION MONTH
OBSERVANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Constitution Month Observance is pleased to
submit herewith the report of its activities for the year. We are particularly pleased to advise you that much interest has been created throughout the entire jurisdiction in the matter of this observance and information received from every portion of the jurisdiction indicates that the
observance of the natal day of our Constitution throughout the month
of September was the most successful in the history o~ such observ~n.ces.
Activities incident to the observance were outstanding, and ambitious
programs of merit and unusual interest were presented by the various
constituent Lodges.
Your committee has been gratified t'hat in so many instances the
observance on the part of the constituent Lodges was open to the general
public. Statistics gathered by your committee from every quarter of the
state indicate the most universal recognition of the Constitution this ye.ar
of any previous time. This is a wholesome.and compell~ng sign and o~r
fraternity may well take unto itself a considerable gortion of the credit
for such a state of affairs.
This year the constituent Lodges paid special tribute to the Bill of
Rights which includes the first ten amendments to the Constitution. T~­
day in a troubled world there is only one Government on the .face of this
globe than cannot do what it pleases, and that Government is the Government of the United States of America. This is a remarkable fact to
chronicle when you cast your eye about the rest of the world and note
what governments are capable of doing. This status on our part is ma~e
possible through the fundamental principles expounded in the Consh•
tution of the United States to the end that life, liberty and property
might be preserved. We note that assaults are being promulgated
against this document from many sources. Not only from abroad, but
from within the confines of our own country as well. If any person has

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

231

any doubt as to the wisdom of this statement that the Constitution is a
precious heritage. let him take down the musty records that tell the story
of the governments t'hat have gone, or peruse our newspaper files covering the last fifteen years of world history for proof of these fundamental principles that were incorporated into our Constitution.
During the year your committee secured and made available for
distribution among the constituent Lodges o.f the state, 25,000 copies of
the Bill of Rights and in addition printed copies of the Constitution itself
were secured for distribution to the constituent Lodges as well. We
believe that the motif for the creation of the committee is of sufficient
importance to warrant the committee functioning throughout the entire
year and not simply as a prelude to t'he observance during the month
of September.
The committee also recommends that a suitable appropriation be set
aside for the activities of the committee including the printing of a
brochure setting forth with particularity the Constitution of the United
States, the Declaration of Independence and other patriotic documents,
for there has been a general demand throughout the jurisdiction for
some such information.
Your committee also wishes to express our appreciation to the many
members of the fraternity who gave unstintingly of their time in addressing numerous constituent Lodges throughout the jurisdiction. In view
of the fact that we have had many distractions this year which have
had a tendency to divert our attention from other important tasks, the
unusual interest and success attending the current observance of Constitution month has been most heartening and the members throughout
the jurisdiction are to be commended for their every effort expended
toward acquainting our fellow men with the many blessings conferred
upon us through the medium of this immortal document.
Since so many of our fundamental privileges as citizens are embodied within the Bill of Rights, the tribute which we paid to this particular
portion of the Constitution has impressed all of us that we are possessed
of a precious heritage which we should hold inviolate and pass on
unsullied to posterity.
The Constitution of the United States has been the powerful force
in the lives of all of the people of the world and of all generations of
people ever since the adoption, even though its authority does not
extend beyond the borders of our own country.
No nation in the world can in war or peace matc.h our production
under our system of free enterprise, with its incentives and rewards for
effort. This is only made possible under our system of government which
has in turn given us the highest standard of living ever known and
opened the way for our amazing progress and for opportunity, happiness and blessings not enjoyed anywhere else in the world. Such a

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

system of government certainly is worth saving for us in America,
because accepting the substitute, a planned society, it is necessary to
surrender the right to think, to surrender the mind which controls the
free actions of men. In a planned society education is controlled, freedom of speech is abridged, freedom of the press is abridged, freedom
of assembly is abridged. The control of the mind of man for the maintenance of the plan is not economic democracy. It is not social justice.
It is tyranny-blind tyranny-the darkest, blackest tyranny that the
human race has ever seen.
Under our American Constitution the cause of human freedom has
been served. Human rights, the right to life, freedom of thought, religion, residence, press, assembly. petition and action, civil liberty and
property, are promulgated and perpetuated by this ~o~s~itution wh!ch
promotes the welfare of the individual as one of many md1v1duals makmg
up the nation.
Government exists for only one purpose-the protection of these
rights. Its exercise of power is limited by a written constitut~on. in
order that it may never curtail these rights. As long as the Constitut10n
lives, America need not dread the heel of the dictator of the disorder
of anarchy.
As America faces the future, let us pause to recollect that the farseeing vision of our constitutional fathers resulted in an instrumen~ of
government which no foe of human rights has penetrated and survival
of which has met every challenge to the natural rights of man. Our
most formidable fortress of defense in time of stress still remains the
Constitution of the United States.
Respectfully submitted,
WILLIAM R. McKAY
}AMES T. FRASER
LEET. MULLEN
DUDLEY H. NEBEKER

. PUBLICATION OF HISTORY

\Ve have considered the report of the Committee on the publication
of the History of Masonry in California. The report shows that the
work is rapidly nearing completion and the books will soon be ready
for delivery. Approximately 1000 sets have been subscribed for and it is
expected that many more will be sold as soon as deliveries can be made.
Last year we recommended to Grand Lodge that two thousand sets be
printed at a cost then reported to us by the History Publication Committee of $43,200.00. It now appears that the total cost of this program
may exceed that amount.
It is not yet possible to determine the exact cost but it does appear
that it may be necessary for additional funds to be provided.
At the last Communication of Grand Lodge your Finance Committee
did not recommend any appropriation but stated they believed the publication should not be delayed through lack of such appropriation and
recommended that the Grand Master be authorized to proceed with the
publication. Any funds used for this project should be returned to a
great extent by the sale of sets.
Your Committee on Finance therefore recommends that the Grand
Master be authorized to make available for the purpose of finishing the
publication of the history such funds as may be necessary to carry the
project to completion.

GENERAL ADMINISTRATION EXPENSE

Your Committee on Finance has reviewed the General Administration expenses for the past year and has consulted with the Grand Secretary concerning the probable expenses. for the current fiscal year;

For several years it has been the practice for Grand Lodge to assume
the entire cost of Social Security and Unemployment ·taxes making no
deductions from the individual salaries. This policy was fixed several
years ago when the staff of the Grand Lodge office was much smaller
than it is today. While the expense involved is not large we believe that
the principle is wrong. We recommend therefore this practice be discontinued and that Social Security and Unemployment taxes be deducted from the individual salaries as they are paid. It is recommended
that a portion of the salary expense be refunded by the Masonic Homes
for the services rendered by the office of the Grand Secretary to the
Homes in such amount as may seem equitable but not less than $6,000.00.

as required by legislation adopted at this Communication. Inasmuch as
it is anticipated that the income from the Endowment Fund will derive

all of the income from the endowment fund is paid to the Homes it is

GRAND MAsTER's DECISION No. 7

This decision involves the advancement of an Entered Apprentice
and a Fellowcraft. The facts in each were submitted to the Grand Master by an inspector. Whether formal objection to advancement had
been made does not appear. The facts in the two cases differ widely.
The Entered Apprentice, apparently through sheer indifference and
neglect, permitted his status to continue for many years, during which

I

244

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

his health seriously deteriorated. Dependence was apparently imminent,
and physical handicaps, including partial blindness, destroyed his
capacity to normally proceed with the remaining degrees.
The Fellowcraft' s affliction, on the other hand, apparently overtook
him without warning, while he was in due course proceeding with his
advancement.
Difference in the facts engenders doubt as to whether the two cases
may properly be disposed of by a common decision and suggests the
necessity for more complete and detailed information.
If formal objection to advancement is interposed in the respective
Lod5es, the matters may be disposed of without further consideration.
Meanwhile, your Committee recommends that the Grand Secretary
obtain from the inspectors referred to complete statement of the facts
in each case, including present status of the advancement proceedings,
and submit the same to the Jurisprudence Committee for further consideration.
Adopted. ,

DECISION 11

From this decision it appears that a petitioner for the degrees to
Menorah Lodge No. 623 was made an entered apprentice mason. In
his petition he had answered "no" to the following question eight:
"Have you ever presented a petition to any Masonic Lodge--if so when
and to what lodge?"
After his initiation · the following discoveries were made: ·
1. The petitioner had, before his application to Menorah Lodge
presented to a lodge in Missouri, a like petition, which had been read
to the lodge but, at the petitioner's request, was withdrawn before any
ballot thereon:
2. The petitioner had, also before the petition addressed to Menorah
Lodge signed and handed to a friend and member of Los Angeles Lodge
No. 42 a like petition. The petition was later returned to him with
statement by his friend that the latter refused to present the same.
In view of the making and withdrawal by the petitioner of his
petition to the Missouri Lodge, the answer to question eight was patently untrue. Furthermore, this untruth would amply warrant objection
to his advancement, to be disposed of as prescribed by Ordinance
No. 238.
In connection with such objection the facts with reference to the
petition to Los Angeles Lodge No. 42 might well be material on the
question of the wilfulness and intent of the applicant in failing to disclose his petition to the Missouri Lodge in his petition to Menorah
Lodge.
Your committee believes that the parts of Decision No. 11 as to
what constitutes "presenting" to a lodge of a petition for the degrees

DECISION 12

Without reciting particular facts, this decision states that in three
instances to lodges, each of which had caused a Temple Association
to be incorporated, the Grand Master had advised:
"A Master of a Lodge, as such, cannot direct the acts of an incorporated Temple Association unless provision for such control is contained
in the articles or by-laws of the corporation."
The decision, as an abstract statement is correct. Your Committee
deems proper, however, warning against any implication therefrom that
a corporate instrumentality formed for the convenience of a Lodge in
the holding of title to Lodge property or the officers of such instrumentality are beyond the control of the Lodge. The facts of each particulal' case require careful consideration in determining ways and means
for asserting and maintaining lodge control. While a Master, as such,
may be without the power specified in the decision he is a proper medium
through which the . Lodge may convey and exercise its deliberate
determination.
Adopted.

REVISION OF SECTION 100

Your Committee has given careful consideration to the request of
the Trustees of the Masonic Homes Board relative to repealing the
portion of the language in the second paragraph. section 100 of Ross
Digest reading as follows:
"When the amount thus collected and so held shall be more than
sufficient, in the judgment of the Trustees, to provide for the maintenance of the Homes and for such improvements as are then in progress
or contemplated for the immediate future, the surplus shall be by them
allocated to the Endowment Fund."
Your Committee respectfully suggests that the foregoing sentence,
by its very language, now empowers the Trustees to set aside from
said funds more than a sufficient amount, limited only :by their discretion, for maintenance and improvements. Then, too, if this language
be repealed, there will be no requirement or authority of any excess.
however great, to ever go into the Endowment Fund.
Your Committee therefore presents the following resolution:
RESOLVED:
That the recommendation of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes
Board relative to repeal of a portion of Section 100 of Ross Digest be
not adopted.

SUSPENSION OP MASTER

At the Grand Master's suggestion, his action in suspending the
Master of Sequoia Lodge No. 349 for the period of three months from

253

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

May 1 through August 2, 1950, has been ref~rred to and considered by
your Committee on Jurisprudence.
Because Brother Earl Warren is a member of Sequoia Lodge and
Brother Clinton T. Duffy's name appears in the proceedings in question, and both said brothers are members of this Committee, they asked
to be and were excused from participation herein.
Subdivision 8 of Section 34 of the Ordinances authorizes the Grand
Master:
"to suspend the Master of any Lodge from the exercise of the powers and duties of his office for good reason shown until the next Annual
Communication."
The Grand Master's action is thus stated, under the heading, "Discipline," on page fifteen of his message:
"Contrary to our custom and the proclamation of the Grand Master
one of our large lodges held a major entertainment on the regular meeting night during Public Schools Week and a public schools meeting
two nig?,ts later. I suspended the Master from office for the next three
months.
The Master states that he had no notice that the matter was under
consideration by the Grand Master, or opportunity to present his
version of the matter in advance of the Grand Master's order.
This Committee has not heard, and is not authorized to hold a
hearing to determine the facts. Informally and without attempting to
·
verify the entire accuracy thereof. the facts appear to be:
For many years it has been the annual practice of Sequoia Lodge
No. 349 to hold a public entertainment called "Stag Night." Before
announcement of the Public Schools Week Proclamation, the 1950
Stag Night had been fixed for April 25, and the program, including an
address by Brother Clinton Duffy. Warden of San Quentin Prison,
partially arranged.
Sequoia Lodge is in the District of Inspector Brother Harry S.
Savage, Jr.
Following the Public Schools Week Proclamation the Master consulted Inspector Savage as to the propriety of making a joint affair of
the Stag Party and Public Schools meeting stating that previous Public
Schools Observance meetings had been slimly attended, that Warden
Duffy was well qualified to impress Masons and non-Masons with the
importance of the Public Schools, and that the Stag Party entertainment
would insure the large attendance which Public Schools Observance
warranted.
The Inspector replied that a joint meeting could be held if it fell
within the terms of the proclamation "That no meeting other than a
Public Schools Obesrvance be held by any Lodge." The Master stated
to the Inspector that the meeting would conform to the proclamation.

Brother Duffy was informed of the change and of the Inspector's
advice and assured the Master that his address would stress the importance of education as an element in crime prevention.
A Lodge bulletin was then issued announcing "plans to observe the
31st Annual Public Schools Week, April 24 to 28" by visiting the
Schools; it stated that Sequoia Lodge, "at its sixteenth Annual Stag
Night, on April 25th, in observance of Public Schools Week, would
be addressed by Warden Duffy, who will impress you with its significance in relation to Public Schools; also that Sequoia Lodge would
join the other local lodges on April 27th in a joint Public Schools Meeting and an address by the Manager of the Oakland Board of Education.
Sequoia Stag Night meeting, with entertainment and the addres~
by Brother Duffy, was held as scheduled on April 25, and was followed
by the joint Public Schools Meeting on April 27.
Under date of April 30th the Grand Master wrote the Master of
Sequ~ia~ Lodge questioning the propriety of the Stag Party during
Public Schools Week and, among other things calling attention to newspaper quotation attributed to the Master about the contemplated stag
party which contained no reference to Public Schools Week. The
Grand Master concluded:
"I hereby suspend you from office as Master of Sequoia Lodge No.
349. You are ordered to exercise no power, function or privilege of
that office and to take no part in any ritualistic work in that or any
other lodge during the ninety day period from May 1 through August
2, 1950,'' and directed the Senior Warden to take over during the time
specified.
The Master's reply to the Grand Master gave his version of the
facts, protested his innocence and stressed the absence of opportunity
to be heard. He assured the Grand Master that the order would be
obeyed. It was carried out.
The Master stated to the Committee that he was not correctly
quoted in the newspaper article referred to by the Grand Master and
was in no way responsible for its publication and again protested that
he had had no opportunity to justify or explain his action, or defend
himself against the accusation or order made against him.

There is thus presented the important and delicate task of defining
the powers of the Grand Master in the matter of the suspension of a
Master of a Lodge. The equally important rights of the Master of the
Lodge, as against an order of suspension, are also necessarily involved.
We are impressed by the steadfast desire of the Grand Master to see
to it that no deviation from the spirit of the Ordinances or the established practice of adhering strictly to the educational program of Public
Schools Week, be permitted. On the other hand, the Master of the .
Lodge in question has steadfastly asserted his good faith, his desire to

My conclusion is that the order of the Grand Master should be

Several decisions have been ca11ed to attention, involving suspensions of Masters by the Grand Master, wherein the action of the Grand
Master has :been approved by the Grand Lodge. No decision, however,
involving a situation identical with that here presented has been called
to our attention, nor any in which the power of the Grand Master was
challenged or a request made for hearing by the Master involved.
In view of the repeated approvals of the Suspensions of Masters by
~ the Grand Master. we believe the Grand Master was warranted in concluding that he had the power to make the suspension which he here
ordered.
On the question of the Master's right to present his defense, we are
of the opinion that he has that right and to now deprive him thereof
would be a grave injustice. We believe that proper procedure is for
this Grand Lodge to refer the matter of such hearing to.the Committee
on Grievances. or such other Committee as it may designate, for a
complete hearing of and recommendation to the Grand Lodge upon the
Master's defense.

DECISION No. 1

A dispensation was requested of the Grand Master by a certain
Lodge to hold a special meeting in the same city but in a Masonic
Temple other than its own. The Grand Master correctly held that a
dispensation in such circumstances was unnecessary, but his decision
was not limited to a special meeting. We therefore :believe that the
word "special" should be inserted in his decision and recommend that
his decision read as follows :
"Under Section 121 of the Ordinances a lodge may hold a special
meeting in any suitable building in the city, town or community named
in its dispensation or charter without a dispensation from the Grand
Master."
Adopted.

CENTENNIAL CELEBRATION
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of California officially celebrated the Centennial Anniversary
of its organization during the 101 st Annual Communication held in San
Francisco, October 9-13, 1950. The complete record of the celebration
will be set forth in the volume to be published under the direction of the
Grand Secretary, and the purpose of this record is merely to set
forth the highlights of the celebration and officially record the special
addresses which were delivered by the Grand Master and distinguished
guests.
Plans for the celebration were inaugurated during the terms of
Grand Masters Chester H. Warlow and Edward H. Siems and carried
to completion during the term of Grand Master E11sworth Meyer. The
committee which developed the plans and carried them out was under
the general chairmanship of Most Worshipful Francis V. Keesling.
Past Grand Master and Grand Treasurer, who presided at the numerous
official committee meetings and who gave unstintingly of his time and
great talent in planning and carrying through to completion the genera]
program and the tremendous amount of detail which resulted in an
outstanding celebration. Serving with Brother Keesling on the Executive Committee were Harvey E . TeUer, Vice-Chairman, Henry. C.
Davis, Herbert R. Hargrave, Earl B. Myers, Carl Olsen and Cyril L.
Weeks. To this Committee is due the thanks of Grand Lodge for a
celebration entirely in keeping with the dignity of Grand Lodge and
traditional California hospitality.
The observance of the centennial year officiaUy opened on April 19,
1950- the exact one hundredth anniversary date-with a statewide
broadcast by Most Worshipful Ellsworth Meyer, Grand Master. The
address delivered on that occasion appears in this account as Exhibit A.
Grand Lodge was opened in ample form on Monday, October 9,
promptly at 10:00 A. M .. and in the afternoon the Grand Master formally and officially received the folJowing distinguished guests:

Brother Keesling introduced the Grand Master as follows:
"We are gathered here this morning in tribute to a great man. Also,
there are in attendance direct descendants of this distinguished man.
Thomas Starr King-ordained by God-a great churchman, and inspired by God-a victorious marshal of the forces of freedom-was one
of the two most distinguished citizens of California honored by a place
in the Hall of Fame. He, in turn, placed his stamp of approval on the
Masonic institution by uniting with it as a member of the fraternity and
is the most distinguished Mason of the jurisdiction of California.

the week, and on Monday night twenty-two hundred delegates enjoyed
the Fellowship Dinner at the Palace Hotel. At the same hour a dinner
at the St. Francis Hotel was attended by more than 600 wives of
Masters of Lodges, Grand Lodge Officers. Past Grand Masters, and

at the dinners assembled at the Civic Auditorium for the Grand Ball.
One of the outstanding features of the entire week was the premier
performance in San Francisco of Mozart's opera "The Magic Flute,"
presented by the San Francisco Opera Association with its full cast of
operatic stars.

were presented.

EXHIBIT A

A CENTURY OF MASONRY IN CALIFORNIA
By MOST WoRSHIPFUL ELLSWORTH MEYER
Grand Master of Masons in California
(As broadcast over KNX on April 19, 1950)
This day is of particular significance to the Masons of Calif pmia and
Hawaii. One hundred years ago on April 19, 1850, a group of Master
Masons who had gathered in Sacramento .ompleted their preliminary
work, and. at high twelve, opened the first communication of the Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons for the State of California.
It might be said they were a bit optimistic in the selection of a name,
for California was not admitted to the Union yet and did not become a
state until five months later.
The California in which they lived was a very different California
from that which you .know. There were no railroads, no broad highways,
no rapid means of communication, no bridges across rivers and swift
mountain streams.
The population was concentrated, but not at the location of our
modern, great cities. Instead. it was to be found in narrow canyons by
the American and Feather Rivers and on the banks of the Sacramento.
These California communities were known by such picturesque
names as: Coloma, Hangtown, Angels Camp, Grass Valley, Chilli
Gulch. and Rough & Ready.
Within the year, thousands of men had come to these communities
and other thousands were on their way across the Rockies, by way oi
Panama, or around the Horn. Around the world had gone the cry of gold
-gold in California, and the greatest migration in history was under
way.
The stories of hunger, thirst. hardship, of heroism and cruelty dur~
ing that migration are well known, but it is not so widely known that
despite the haste of departure and the feverish desire to reach the
gold fields time was taken by Masons to obtain charters and dispensa~
tions from twelve eastern Grand Lodges for the establishment of fifteen
Masonic Lodges in this fabulous El Dorado.
From Connecticut to Florida, from the District of Columbia to Mis~
souri, issued proper authorization for the establishment of lodges in
California.
The Masons who were assembled in Sacramento one hundred years
ago today, belonged to lodges which had been established in Sacramen~
to, Benton City. Benicia, and San Francisco.
They were motivated not only by their affection for the fraternity,
but by the suffering occasioned by the epidemics which had swept
.

I

266

267

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

through the camps and towns, the poverty of those who had come inadequately equipped, and wide-spread disregard for the hallmarks of civilization.
They recognized the necessity of banding together the good men
and true of different cities who had knelt at Masonic altars, who were
disciples of brotherly love and temperance in thought and deed; men
who understood and practiced charity.
In that first Grand Lodge session were men from Sacramento who
established the first hospital in California, who nursed the victims of
the several cholera epidemics, buried the dead, and expended more than
$33.000 of personal funds for the relief of the needy and the afflicted.
In the fever for gold, other men might become calloused, turn from
the hungry. the widow, and the orphan, but to these men of Masonry.
our doctrine of the Fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man was
no lofty preachment, no sounding pretensions; it was a way of life.
The presiding officer of the two-day convention which preceded the
formation of the Grand Lodge was Charles Gilman, a San Francisco ·
lawyer of note. who had already served one year as Grand Master in
New Hampshire and six years as Grand Master in Maryland. He was
the logical choice to be the first Grand Master in California, but intended
to return east shortly and deferred in favor of Colonel Jonathan D.
Stevenson. his law partner, whom President Polk had sent to California
in command of the first New York Volunteers on the outbreak of war
in Mexico.
Colonel Stevenson had brought his troops around South America in
three ships in 1847, and. as with many other easterners, he came to
California and stayed.
Early California Masonry had within her ranks many other colorful
men: Sam Brannan, who founded San Francisco's first newspaper, was
the first to broadcast the discovery of gold, preached the first Protestant
sermon in California, and was the subject of the state's first jury trial.
John W. Geary. who came to California after service in the Mexican
War, became the first Postmaster and the first Mayor of San Francisco,
and later a Brigadier General. and then the Governor of Kansas and the
Governor of Pennsylvania, and Robert Semple who presided over the
Constitutional Convention, and, with Hastings, conditioned Californians
for wide-spread public education.
To chronicle the names of prominent men who have sat in California
Masonic Lodges during the past century would be to call the roll of mos~
of those who have left their names as noble legacies to the state, and of
those who are recognized as leaders today.
.
I shall mention but a few of those whose names stand like mountain
peaks high above the past: Commodore Sloat, Kit Carson, the renowned
Indian scout; Mark Twain, who gave the world "The Jumping Frog of
Calaveras County"; Stephen J. Field, who served longer on the Supreme

Court of the United States than any other justice; Thomas Starr King.
one of the two Californians in the Hall of Fame in Washington, and
who was serving our Grand Lodge as Grand Orator at the time of his
early death; Peter Lassen, named as an officer in the charter issued by
the Grand Lodge of Missouri, and for whom Mount Lassen and Lassen
County were named; Don Benito Wilson, who located Riverside, was
Mayor of Los Angeles in 1851, and for whom Mount Wilson was
named; Lester A. Pelton, who made hydroelectric power possible by inventing the Pelton water wheel; Leland Stanford, railroad president,
Governor, and United States Senator, who gave Stanford University;
and Luther Burbank. who unfolded so many of nature's secrets. These
are but a few of the great names in a century of California Masonry,
and I have purposely omitted the names of those still living who are a
credit to Masonry, California, and these United States.
The Grand Lodge founded in that upper room at the corner of Fifth
and "J" Streets in Sacramento has, in the century of its progress; spread
to the Oregon and Mexican borders and crossed the Pacific to Hawaii,
where the first Masonic Lodge had been established by the Grand Orient
of France and over which two Hawaiian Kings had presided as Masters.
It has grown until its membership today is the fifth largest in the United
States and the seventh largest in the world. If we were to add to its
members, the thousands of Masons who reside in California, but maintain their membership at their former homes, the number would probably
not be surpassed by any other American Jurisdiction, but California
Masonry is not interested in mere numbers.
Unlike many organizations it can invite no man to take its degrees.
He must seek admission of his own free will. It does not sit back in smug,
self-satisfaction as it reviews its record on this Centennial Day. It is
proud of its history, but not boastful. As individuals. its members are
serving in every cause which is building a better state and a better society, and they will continue to serve.
The Grand Lodge of California today touches life at each level.
Through its home for children at Covina, it cares for orphans and hal£
orphans from the first grade of grammar school through graduation from
high school. By means of its club houses at Berkeley and Los Angeles
campuses of the University of California, it is an influence during the
collegiate years. Its lodges inspire during the active, adult years, and its
Home for the Aged at Decoto, in Alameda County, is a haven for 300
in the late afternoon of life.
Masonry is not a religion, but it is religious. It does not require a
particular church affiliation and only asks a candidate whether he believes in a Supreme Being and some form of future existence.
It is not a political organization, but it does impress upon its members that they have civic duties to perform through channels of expression outside its lodges.

268

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

It is not a benefit society. It offers no form of insurance, but it need
yield to none in works of charity.
.
It has no fancy uniforms, and the only badge of a Mason is the
apron, which is never worn in public except for the funeral of a brother,
or the performance of some other strictly Masonic duty.
It does not seek the front page, but it does not shun the light of
inquiry.
It is a secret society as to its modes of recognition and pass words,
but there is no secrecy as to its organization, principles, or purposes.
It denies the claims of dictators, political or religious, but it is loyal
to governments established by free peoples.
It recognizes familiar tones in the Declaration of Independence and
the Constitution, and it has seen many of the signatures on those two
documents on the rosters of its own lodges.
Masonry was a stabilizing influence in the rough and ready days of
'49. It is an anchorage in the present and for the days to come.
It has helped to build California, and it will not now lay down the
plumb, the square, or the trowel. For a century in California, and for
many centuries elsewhere, Masonry has united at its altars of reverence,
men of good will who have striven by every resource of their art to make
tangible, the power of brotherhod, the worth of virtue, and the reality of
the ideal.
Masons will continue to build the temple of humanity among the
nations and in the hearts of men.

THOMAS STARR KING
Address by ELLSWORTH MEYER, Grand Master,
'
Masonic Memorial Services
San Francisco, October 8, 1950
'

Eighty-six years ago, Grand Master Belcher and the officers of the
Grand Lodge of California stood where we stand this morning. With
solemn rites they here laid to rest the mortal remains of a young man,
iJlustrious and beloved-.
How different, indeed, was the scene and tempo amid which they
assembled to perform the last duty to our brother.
San Francisco was already a thriving community, but it and California bore the impress of the Gold Rush Days. The nation had but
lately been extended westerly to touch the shores of the Pacific and it
was just emerging from the long and difficult struggle between the
North and the South. Freemasonry was ancient and honorable, but the
Grand Lodge of California, as with the state, was in only its fourteenth
year.
Since that day in March of 1864, wooden 11tore buildings have
given way to towering sky-scrapers, great cities have risen where was
naught but rolling hills and barren land, the stage coach and horseman
have been surplanted by the airplane and telegraph, historic markers
now stand where then were populous mining camps and nature has
covered the scars on the field of Gettysburg. Freemasonry is still honorable, but the Grand Lodge of California has completed a century of
existence.
Notwithstanding all these other changes, the name of our brother
is still illustrious and beloved and the citizens of this great state have
judged Thomas Starr King one of the pre-eminent men of his adopted
common wealth.
lt is fitting that we should gather here as Masons in the first act of
our centennial session to pay our humble words of tribute to this illustrious citizen and Mason, for it was he who declared of Masonry, in an
address on May 16, 1863: "This is the most remarkable social organization of the world."
Thomas Starr King was born in New York on December 17, 1824
and his youth was spent in Portsmouth, New Hampshire and Charlestown, Massachusetts. He was planning to enter college, but the death
of his father, when the son was but twelve years of age, necessitated
his working as a clerk and schoolmaster for the next eight years and
he pursued his theological studies as best he could.

271

PROCBBDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The first pulpit he filled was that which his father had occupied
in Charlestown and he did not come to California until 1860. In the
shadow of this church he has remained. Although ·his life in California
covered but four years, such were his deeds. so distinguished his services to the nation, so eloquent his oratory that Californians have decreed
that his statue shall stand as one of the two from this state in the Hall
of Fame in the national Capitol.
We are proud that he was a devoted Mason and twice was appointed
Grand Orator of the Grand Lodge, which post he was holding at the
time of his demise. We recognize his brilliance as a clergyman and that
to him, more than to any other, is accredited the preservation of California to the Union during the Civil War.
With the outbreak of hostilities a division of public opinion and
sympathy began to appear in California. Many had come but recently
from southern states, there were those who favored the extension of
slavery to California and many advised a course of temporizing with
the secession. Impassioned oratory on behalf of secession and the
Confederacy was heard.
Suddenly, there was heard the voice of one man speaking with logic
and eloquence against slavery, against vacillation and for the preservation of the Union. His words were not wavering, they were not
susceptible of two interpretations, but rang out like the hammer blows
of a mighty smith. They came from a man frail of body, but strong of
heart. A man of indomitable courage. for he not only spoke from his
pulpit, but went into other towns and the lumber and mining camps.
wherever danger appeared or the cause of the Union could be served.
Frequently, he was promised assassination and it has been said that
on occasion guns were drawn while he spoke, but neither threat nor
danger could intimidate him or silence his voice.
Before the tide of battle had turned, he had turned the tide of public
opinion in California and his words had echoed across the nation. He
then :b ent his efforts toward material assistance by way of relief for
the victims of the war. California had not been called upon to furnish
fighting forces for the conflict, but Thomas Starr King called upon her
and Oregon to furnish funds with which to care for the wounded, the
widow and the orphan. More than a million and a half dollars was
raised, a huge sum for that day, which nearly equalled that raised by
all the other states combined.
It was not given to any of us to hear his voice, for it was stilled at
the age of thirty-nine, but his contemporaries of that time when eloquence was in full flower judged him pre-eminent, the results he achieved
are testimony and the poet Whittier has penned his praise.
Californians have not been content merely to erect his statue, but
they have given his name to public schools, a giant Sequoia and one of

the domes in Yosemite. These two are fitting monuments · because he
was a man of intellect and his name stands high above the wintry past.
inviting us to leave our names as worthy legacies to our country.

270

It has been said that to live in the hearts ·of those we leave behind,
is not to die. Of Thomas Starr King, we say: He yet lives in the hearts
of Californians, he yet lives in the hearts of Masons.

As Grand Master of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Connecticut, I bring you the warm fraternal greetings of all the Masons of
Connecticut and their heartiest felicitations, to this, your Masonic
Centennial.
I want to thank all of you here in California for the splendid arrangements made for our comfort and the hospitality shown to our Grand
Secretary, M.W. Earle K. Haling, Mrs. Haling, Mrs. Hesselmeyer and
myself.
I know what it means to plan a celebration such as this, long and
tedious hours of work and painstaking effort. This planning reminds
me of a story I heard recently. It seems two elderly ladies were having
a very confidential conversation. One of them had been married four
times, first to a banker, whom she divorced: secondly to an actor, whom
she divorced: then to a clergyman whom she also divorced, and now
she was married to an undertaker. The other asked her, "Sally, how
did it happen that you married men of these varied professions?" And
without hesitation Sally answered, "I planned it that way : one for the
money, two for the show, three to get ready, and four to go."
I am particularly happy to be here as the Grand Master of Masons
in Connecticut, as our Grand Lodge was instituted in 1789, and later
as you know, the brethren of Connecticut were instrumental in helping
establish Masonry here in California.
In Connecticut we are proud of Hiram Lodge No. 1, of New Haven.
Connecticut, which was first chartered in 1750. On November 29th of
this year I am planning to be present and to help it celebrate its 200th
Anniversary. I quote from the history of Hiram Lodge No. 1:
"A Connecticut Lodge in California. The members of Hiram
Lodge have done a great deal of pioneer work in organizing
Lodges in unoccupied territory. A remarkable instance of this
kind occurred in 1849, when several of the brothers had a severe
attack of the gold fever and were about to start for California.
They petitioned the Grand Lodge for a Charter, and Hiram
Lodge recommended them as worthy brothers. The Grand Lodge
met in special session at New Haven on January 30, 1849, and
organized Connecticut Lodge, No. 76, with Caleb Fenner, a Past
Master of Hiram, as Master.

WHAT IS MASONRY?
While acting as Master of my lodge, Day Spring No. 30 of Hamden,
Connecticut, in 1929, and being much younger than I am today, I thought
I knew the answer, and the same was true when I was District Deputy
of the Fourth Masonic District of Connecticut in 1931 and 1932. For
the last eight years I gradually advanced through our Grand Lodge Line
and became Grand Master this last April. Within the last few years as
I started to visit other jurisdictions and had the opportunity to hear
others, much better informed than I, speak, I began to wonder what
Masonry really was. I gradually, subconsciously, started to analyze
the whole institution.
The first question that suggested itself to me was, "ls Masonry a
social organization?" Masonry promotes sociability. Every Grand Master urges his lodges to close at a reasonable hour so that the brethren
may have a social hour. Fellowcraft and Square Clubs and other allied
organizations promote entertainments and other social events. One
hundred years ago, at least in the east, sociability was promoted much
more than it is today. Going through the history of Masonry · in this

274

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

country, as we all know, the early lodges met for the most part in inns,
and the flowing cup was nothing unusual, even in a Masonic meeting.
One of our oldest members is now ninety years of age, and when talking
of his early days in Masonry he remembers when a bucket of beer with
the necessary ladle was kept in the ante room, so that all could refresh
themselves as the occasion and spirit required. We can well therefore
understand, with the change in all this that has taken place, as now of
course no alcoholic beverages, not even beer, are allowed in any Masonic
Temple, why the old fashioned eloquence that we hear so much about
has disappeared from the lips of our officers and speakers. Masonry as
it is practised in this country today promotes sociability, but it is not a
pure and simple social organization . .
Is Masonry an educational organization? Masonry teaches through
symbols, the greatest of which is the letter "G," which stands for the
Great Architect of the Universe-God. Every Grand Lodge encourages
its lodges to carry on educational activities, and we are doing our best
to help our members learn as much about Masonry as we possibly can,
yet Masonry is not purely and simply an educational organization.
Is Masonry a secret society? This has changed a great deal in the
last one hundred years. In certain parts of Europe, at least before
World War II, Masons could not let it be known to the profane that
they were Masons, but in this country this veil of secrecy is for the
most part a thing of the past. You can come to the Grand Lodge Office
in Hartford and the Grand Secretary will be glad to give you a book
containing the name of every Master Mason belonging to the lodges
9f our jurisdiction. Again, you will find a copy of that on file in the State
Capitol in Hartford. It is true that we have a few things in our work
that are secret, but the greater part of M~sonry is not secret, and therefore Masonry is not today a so-called secret society.
Is Masonry a political society? It teaches that its members shall obey
the law of the land and constituted authority. They are also taught not
to enter into political controversy as Masons. I wonder sometimes if
we as Masons fully realize what it means to respect constituted authority.
We hear many good Masons, without provocation unjustly criticize our
government leaders, where instead of that they should keep quiet as
Masons, and support them while in office. The Masonic organization
was thrown into politics well over one hundred years ago, which resulted
in the formation of the Anti-Masonic Party and caused the cessation of
Masonic work in most jurisdictions. I have reference to the Morgan
Episode and what followed. Masonry is not a political organization
and will not enter into any political controversy.
Is Masonry a religious organization? It is true that the Holy Bible
is on the altar of all of our Masonic Lodges. It is true that most of our
teachings come from the Old Testament. It is true that our ritual is

full of religious expressions and dogma, but Masonry is not a religious
organization. Rather than to oppose any church, it is a helpmate of the
church. Masonry is sometimes accused of keeping its members from
church membership. This again is not true, for a good Mason is a good
church member. I so stated at a banquet somewhat over a year ago. and
apparently put some of the brethren on the spot, for thereafter brother
after brother, on meeting me, told me that I should not have said that
as their wives were present and now they were losing sleep as they had
to go to church regularly, as each Sunday morning the wife reminded
them of the fact that the then Deputy Grand Master told them that a
good Mason was a good church member.
If Masonry is not a social organization, educational organization,
secret society, political organization or religious organization, what is
it? It has been defined as a philosophy of life. That is true, but that
definition docs not satisfy me as it is too vague. A leading Masonic
writer defines it as a progressive science based on morality and taught
by symbolism. This again is true, but it seems to me is incomprehensible
by the average Master Mason. I have adopted a definition of Masonry
for myself and I give it to you for what it is worth. "Masonry is based
on the four principal virtues of antiquity: temperance, fortitude, prudence and justice, together with the three theological virtues of faith,
hope and charity, and its principal tenets of brotherly love, relief and
truth. These cardinal virtues and tenets Masonry teaches to its votaries
by symbolism with the hope and endeavor, the better to fit them as living
stones for that spiritual building, that house not made with hands, eternal
in the Heavens."
FREDERICK C. HESSELMEYER

Grand Master, Connecticut

Masons everywhere, who may have the privilege of becoming acquainted with that splendid address. In determining how true we and other
Masons are to our principles, I should like to ask a few questions; and

ADDRESS OF MOST WORSHIPFUL ALBERT J. DeLANGE
Grand Master of Masons of the Grand Lodge of Texas
M. W. Ellsworth Meyer, Grand Master, Grand Officers and Members
