and Brethren:
It is a rare privilege for me to bring you, on this great occasion, the
greetings and best wishes of the two hundred thousand Masons of
Texas. We congratulate you of the Grand Lodge of California on
your first century of great accomplishments; we rejoice with you, and we
are proud of the outstanding position which you occupy in the Masonic
world. May I express my personal appreciation of the many courtesies
which have been extended to me by your Grand Master and all the
brethren of your Grand Lodge from the time that Brother Patterson and
his charming wife met me at the airport and extending throughout my
visit here. These many courtesies cause me to regret-almost-that in
Texas we sent the "patrol wagon" for Brother Meyer (or thus it seems
from his description of the conveyance). Though my friendship with
Brother Meyer is of a few years, when measured in units of time, his
many sterling qualities, both of mind and of character, have endeared
him to me, but the treatment he has accorded me, which you have all
witnessed, brings forcibly to my mind the old warning: "The Lord
protect me from my friends, I will take care of my enemies." You will
notice the adroitness with which he presented his claim that Brother
Ted Doss had kept your Grand Master "off the streets" during the
Grand Master's trip to Washington. His claim calls to mind our Texas
definition of an alibi, namely, proving that you weren't there when you
did it. His own reports show that Tennessee handled him with finesse
and Texas with "frazzling."
Texas has always felt and had the closest ties of friendship and
kinship with California and the sister states in our area with which our
history has been so closely associated. For Texas started the procession
to the West. The Battle of San Jacinto, fought on soil within view of
my own Lodge. was one of the.decisive battles of the world, one of the
momentous decisions which yet profoundly affects the history of the
world, and the progress of mankind. It secured benefits now enjoyed
not alone by us but also by the descendants of those who were then our
opponents, but are now our closest neighbors and our warmest friends.
When the Republic of Texas annexed the United States we gave the
United States as war surplus our western wastelands, from which were
later created the States of California, New Mexico, Colorado, Wyoming, and the neighboring states. Sutter's gold accelerated the rush

280

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

to the golden west. We now see the teeming cities, the multitudinous
industries, the great agricultural activities, the commercial. and the
cultural development of California, and are filled with amazement and
a feeling akin to incredulity. We are astounded that you have done
so much with so little. Perhaps within a short time, when your taxable
values justify it, Houston will reverse the action of 1846 by annexing
you. As it is, Houston considers California as only an outlying district
of Houston, though there are some who maintain that nothing can
"out-lie" Houston.
Masons throughout our broad land, indeed, Masons everywhere,
are proud of the part which the Masons of California have had and
are having in the writing of the proud history of your State, and we hail
with great satisfaction the pre-eminent position you now hold.
Gra~d Master Ellsworth Meyer has asked me to address you briefly
on a subject of my own choosing. I realize that no subject chosen by me
would add to the present knowledge of those present, particularly your
officers, the Grand Masters, and other distinguished guests. Accordingly, I am making no effort to inform or educate you. I seek only to
direct your attention to matters already well known to you. Earnestly
I seek to focus your attention on the need of adherence to the fundamentals of Masonry.

Ancient Craft Masonry is basic or fundamental Masonry. Each
Grand Lodge is sovereign. Full and complete attainment of the privilege of Masonic membership is in no wise dependent upon the Mason
joining any other Body. A proper study of the history, biography,
philosophy, principles, and purposes of the Order is entirely sufficient
to occupy all the available time of any earnest Mason, no matter how
great his capability, learning, and energy. And the application of such
principles is a life-long endeavor. Yet there is a mad rush to join other
"branches" of Masonry, or, more often, some organization predicating
its membership on Masonry. A recent pamphlet by the Masonic Education and Service Association of the United States lists some seventyseven groups or degrees, constituting branches of Masonry or Orders
predicating their membership on Masonry, including the androgynous
degrees or so-called adoptive Masonry, and the organizations for those
under age. The neophyte in Masonry is hardly started on his way when
he becomes the target of a number of membership committees or others
seeking to secure his application for membership in such other Orders.
He is made to believe that his entrance into Masonry is not complete
with the Master's Degree. The zeal of the solicitors is founded on a
misapprehension of the fundamental and true purposes of Masonry and
causes the frustration of those purposes and the loss of the principles.
One reason that we have lost sight of the fundamentals of Masonry
and the basic purposes for Masonic organization is the emphasis or

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

281

over-emphasis which we have placed on learning and exemplifying the
esoteric work, or perhaps I should say upon the failure to properly
point out and emphasize the true purposes of "Such esoteric work. In
Texas, we require a considerable knowledge of the esoteric work of
each degree before the candidate can advance to the next degree and
we require that he pass a satisfactory examination in the Master's
Degree within ninety days after receiving it. Because of the large number of candidates applying of recent years, and the extensive knowledge of the work required of the candidates, the active members of the
Lodges have been busily engaged in the teachins:r of such work to the
neophytes and the perfecting of themselves and others as certificate
members. The constant effort required for these detailed duties has led
to their occupying a paramount place in the minds of the active workers
and this impression has persisted until many active workers have subconsciously looked upon the teaching of the esoteric work as the primary
function of Masonry and perfection in it as the final accomplishment of
the individual Mason.
It is within the tiled walls of the Lodge that we must determine
whom we shall admit at the West Gate; it is before our altars that we
must obligate those whom we have approved; it is within our Lodge room
that we form the friendships which "unite us into one sacred band or society of friends and brothers": and therein, over the years, we must become completely indoctrinated with the principles and purposes of the
Order. But all this effort is completely wasted, all such activity entirely
sterile, if Masonry begins and ends within the Lodge room or if its
primary functions are those performed within the Lodge room. 'Unless
the principles there taught are carried outside, at the fireside, the workshop, the market place, the public schools, the civic forum, the place
of worship, in all the manifold activities of life, then the labor is fruitless, the so-called accomplishments are vain. Our real ends are attained
as the result of every member having a true conception of our principles
and by his proper application thereof, not by the display of emblems and
jewels, nor by the empty preaching of Masonry, nor by the holding of
membership or offices in multitudinous organizations claiming to be
Masonic.
A true realization of these fundamental principles and objectives will
give us a clear perspective and a deeper appreciation of Masonry. A failure to keep such guideposts in view will inevitably lead to confusion, a
straying from the path, a missing of the true destination.
At this time, we are almost in the position of the illiterate colored
man who, when asked whether he could read the road signs, replied that
he "could read how fur but not where to".
The Grand Lodge of Texas has recently increased the waiting period
between degrees from one lunar month to two lunar months and has

prescribed a six months' waiting period after attaining the Master's
Degree before the Mason can apply for membership in any Body, Masonic or non-Masonic, which requires of its members that they hold
membership in a Masonic Lodge. We hope that the learner or newlymade Mason may devote himself exclusively to study of Blue Lodge
Masonry during these waiting periods without the pressure of invitations or solicitations to join other organizations; that he may find time,
opportunity, and inspiration to make a study of the fundamentals rather
than the forms of Masonry. There is no expectation that he can attain
any great proficiency during these maturing periods. It is hoped that his
feet will be set on the right path and his viewpoint properly fixed; in
other words, that he will be properly oriented, be basically sound, and
later make solid progress. To this end, a program of study has been
prepared by our Committee on Education and Service and will soon be
released to the Lodges. We shall endeavor to prevent this becoming
fixed or static, and will currently supplement all material with new
studies and suggestions. I invite and earnestly solicit any listening to me
to send to me at Houston, Texas, any suggestions that you may have,
with any pamphlets, studies, or other material that will aid in this work.

to create these new organizations is based upon the false premise or
thought that the esoteric work itself is our primary purpose, or upon the
misconception that there must be a multitude of social or similar activities to engage the attention of the members, ~n alleged matter "of holding interest" or an opportunity for more emblems and jewels. Any who
can be bound to our Order only through such means are of no aid or

282

In bringing to the attention of our members the sovereign position
of our Grand Lodge, and the character of Ancient Craft Masonry, and
in requiring a period of service to the Blue Lodge, it is not the purpose
of our Grand Lodge to imply that we are in any manner opposed to
either of the Rites or any of the truly Masonic Bodies. In fact, it is my
sincere belief, and I know most of the leaders of our Order in Texa~
join me in the belief. that to the properly educated and guided Mason,
the additional light and inspiration of the Rites and other recognized
Masonic Bodies will :b e of great aid; practically all of us of the "Grand
East", including the Past Grand Master, belong to both Rites and are
thoroughly convinced of their value to the Craft. But the lessons of the
Rites are as useless as those of the Blue Lodge when falling upon ears
that in truth cannot hear. And the leaders of both Rites in Texas are in
full accord with the program of our Grand Lodge, and feel that the reresults will be, and are, very beneficial to them, furnishing the Rites
applicants or members who are in fact Masons and not simply members
of the Masonic Order.
As to the non-Masonic organizations which require Masonry as a
predicate to their respective memberships, I personally am very definitely of the view, and I believe that it is shared by all the leaders and the
vast majority of the members of my State, that a halt must be made to
the multiplicity of such Orders. The great number of such Orders. the
multiplicity of the "projects" sponsored as a means of securing members
or of giving some purpose to the several organizations, and their varied
activities are but "confounding the confusion". Let me repeat, the desire

And the organization of such splinter groups detracts from the principle of the universality of Masonry. It results in a fragmentation of
Masonry. . It encourages diversity of interest and foments internecine
strife. It dissipates our efforts and confuses our viewpoints.
Our Grand Lodge has very definitely opposed and prohibited the
formation of groups of Masons into clubs or organizations within the
Order, based, for 'example, upon trades, professions, attendances at
particular institutions, and the like. Even study clubs at universities
can be organized only under the auspices of a constituent Lodge and
under its ultimate control and supervision. Article 10 of our Laws provides: "This Grand Lodge alone has power and authority to establish
and disseminate the esoteric work of the first three degrees of Ancient
Craft Masonry in this jurisdiction." This has been construed by our
Committee on Purposes and Policies; and the construction being approved by our Grand Lodge. to prohibit such ancillary organizations,
(which have been denominated, in some reports, as "appendages" of
Masonry), hence such groups are not permitted in our State. Hardly a
year passes, however, without one or more applications being made to
the Grand Master for authority to organize such a club or group or to
permit the entry of one or more local chapters of such organizations
recognized or permitted in other states. These applications are invariably and promptly refused.
There is a very definite feeling in Texas that a number of the activities of some organizations, which predicate their membership on Masonry. including some which have been in existence for many years, are
often detrimental to the interests and reputation of Masonry. Because
such organizations appear in public on many occasions and make many
demonstrations, whereas Ancient Craft Masonry and the Rites refuse
to so appear, and because such organizations require that their members
first have membership in the Blue Lodges and perhaps one of the Rites,
the public generally has a tendency erroneously to view these groups as
the uppermost Bodies of Masonry and even our members who know
better, or should know better, hold the same misconceptions.

284

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Let me say without equivocation that, in my opinion, a number of
their activities have been very detrimental to' the interests of Masonry
and I, for one, am thoroughly convinced that unless their practices come
to harmonize with Masonic principle, and remain in such harmony,
legislation must be taken by Masonic Bodies to prohibit or restrict right
of its members to join such organizations. In other words, such incompatability will force a juridical divorce of this common law marriage.
I regret that very recently it has become necessary for me as Grand
Master of the Grand Lodge of Texas to institute a Court of Inquiry with
respect to the activities of a local group of one such organization. This
action is not taken on any premise that the Grand Lodge is directing, or
will direct or interfere with, the activities of such organization, but upon
the concept that Masons are subject to, and must obey, all Masonic
laws of conduct on any and all occasions, and are subject to the discipline and judicial processes of the Grand Lodge if they fail to refuse
to do so. The inquiry is also conducted for the purpose of obtaining information from which to determine whether an edict should now go
forth, or recommendation be made to the Grand Lodge to enact a law,
prohibiting any further joining of such organization unless and until its
practices are bettered.
Another clear indication of the failure of the officers and brethren
to realize and maintain the sovereign and independent nature of Ancient
Craft Masonry and its entire separation from and independence of all
other Bodies has been the use, clearly unlawful in Texas, of letterheads
and other printed matter jointly with other Masonic Bodies or Bodies
composed of Masons. This has been definitely stopped in Texas. Such
use was, I am sure, more negligent than wilfully violative of the law,
though I fear that in some instances at least, there was deliberate intent
to impress the newly made member with the thought that a joining of
the other Bodies was necessary for the completion of his Masonic education. Whether intentional or unintentional. such was the effect. I am
pleased to be able to say that there has been complete cooperation by
all Bodies, and an unreserved recognition of the necessity of the abandonment of the improper practice.
The urge to embellish the emblems of Masonry, and the constant extension of the use of such emblems on every possible medium, are more
indicia of the deplorable tendency to accept the form and neglect the
substance. This perversion had been carried so far in my State that one
of the large and influential Lodges had a large picture of an animal's
head (signifying name of the Lodge) thrust through and looking from
the letter "G", this distortion or perversion being used in the Lodge
notices in the newspapers, in the Lodge stationery, and in other printed
matter. Following the emphatic mandate of our Grand Lodge, I have
required every Lodge to desist from such misuses, to bring all its printed

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

285

matter in line with the applicable laws, and to refrain from any embellishments. The District Deputy Grand Masters have been assiduously
ferreting out all violations and immediately stopping them.
The Laws of the Grand Lodge of Texas positively prohibit any constituent Lodge supporting or sponsoring any other organization of any
character. As I have always been so thoroughly convinced that the
Order of De Molay and Order of Rainbow for Girls are doing an outstanding work for young men and women, I long felt that such policy
was wrong in its application to be named orders. I am now thoroughly
convinced that the "hands off" policy is entirely correct. I am convinced
that individually and as individual Masons we should support the named
organizations in their fine work and I have always encouraged them.
But I am likewise completely convinced that any differences of opinion
that may develop within such organizations (or any other Order based
directly or indirectly on Masonic membership) as to management, control. or procedure or in other particular, should not be brought into
Masonic Lodges as they invariably will be if there is any sponsorship
or direct relationship. Too often we are having dissentions brought into
our Lodges from the subsidiary organizations which are not recognized
as Masonic but to which a large number of the Masons belong.
As a corollary to the proposition that we should have and teach the
true principles and purposes of Masonry is the determination that only
authorized Masons or Masonic organizations should be permitted to
speak for Masonry or to speak or publish anything that the uninitiated
might consider the authoritative words of Masonry. Accordingly, our
Grand Lodge publishes its official organ, the Texas Grand Lodge Magazine. It attempts no editorials or editorial policy and accepts no advertisements. Our Grand Lodge permits constituent Lodges to publish and
distribute to their own members, news of such Lodges but without editorials or advertise.men ts. Recently an effort was made .:by a Master
Mason and his blood brother, an Entered Apprentice Mason, to establish a magazine, of character similar to that published by such publishers'
blood relatives in another State, which magazine purported to be for the
information of Masons and to carry news of interest primarily to Masons. One number only was published. The publishers were tried and
expelled, and such sentences were upheld by the Grand Lodge. The
Grand Lodge strengthened its laws to proscribe not only any participation in the publication of such a magazine or advertising therein, but
also any subscribing thereto. The publishers were informed that legal
action would be taken against them and any advertisers would be persistently informed that the publication and all advertisements in it were
entirely offensive to Masons. Such publication ceased after the first
number.

And may I turn seriously to the history of my own State to present
a symbol of active applied Masonry. To us in Texas, the Alamo is the
cradle of liberty. It does not evidence any enmity against those who were
our enemies more than a century ago. and whose descendants are our
nearest neighbors and now our warmest friends. It is a symbol of Adel~
ity to duty and devotion to Country. Besieged by overwhelming numbers. William Barrett Travis, the commander of the gt;lrrison-and a
member of our Craft-sent his . last message . containing the immortal
statement:
"I shall n@ver surrender nor retreat".
His fearless band perished to the last man, holding back the invaders
until Sam Houston-who later presided over the meeting organizing the
Grand Lodge of Texas--could form the army of defense. A monument
was erected to commemorate the fidelity of the heroic defenders of the
Alamo. I do not now refer to the fine monument of enduring Texas
granite erected in the Capitol grounds at Austin upon which is inscribed
the proud line:
"Thermopylae had its messenger to defeat, the Alamo had none."
I refer to the smaller monument. erected shortly after Texas independence was won. This unpretentious memorial was built of the broken
stones, the rubble, and the debris of the Alamo itself, those fragments _
thrown down in the struggle. And upon one face of the modest monument was engraved the line:
"Erected as an altar to the God of the fearless and the free."
Masons of every clime could well consider this line engraved upon
the altar of every lodge as a constant reminder of the inescapable Masonic duty of service to Country.
I close with a repetition of my expression of warmest fraternal
friendship and good wishes from the Grand Lodge of Texas and all its
members to the Grand Lodge of California and all other jurisdictions
represented here.

ADDRESS OF MOST WORSHIPFUL
WALLA CE E. CALDWELL
Grand Master of Masons of the Grand Lodge of North Carolina
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Masonry is a beautiful system of morality veiled in allegory and
illustrated by symbols. This is important because allegory and symbols
talk a universal language meaning the same thing to men of many lands
and different tongues. At the same time, their meanings are so rich and
so varied that they appear differently to any one Mason at different
times.
One night too tired to go to sleep I began running over the ritual and
came to think of one of our ancient brethren who became weary and sat
down for a rest. As I saw him sitting there I said, "Move over, brother,
and make room for me." Then I thought more. He had gone on a long
and difficult journey on a quest that must have seemed well nigh impossible and with a stern sentence hanging over him if he failed. Finally,
exhausted, he sank down for a rest. But he got up again, called to his
companions and they returned. Had he not arisen or had his companions
not returned, his end would have been sure. But he did get up, his comrades did come back and victory, success. was at hand.
Now, my brethren, we have a task to perform. The ruffians of greed
and violence and materialism are abroad in the land and we must overcome them. Self-seeking men are setting money, position, or power as
their goals and not considering the means by which they secure them.
They deny God, spurn religion, and laugh at altruism, asking only
"What is there in it for me? What am I going to get out of it?"
Masonry provides the spiritual power for overcoming them. First it
reminds us that we are individuals who entered the fraternity at our own
.request and were received and treated as individuals as we advanced in
it. It asked us one question only which had to be answered correctly for
it is obvious that no atheist can be a Mason. Beyond that it told us that
we were entitled to our own interpretation of our answer, our own
religious views, political affiliations and occupations. It gave us a position of dignity and security. There is represented in every regular and
well-governed lodge a certain point within a circle. The point represents
the individual brother, the circle that boundary of his duty to God and
man beyond which he is not to.allow his passions, prejudices or interests
to betray him on any occasion. What is more dignified than the center
of a circle or what more secure. I like to think of myself as standing .
there. The circle is around me consisting of my brethren in Masonry,
wherever I inay be, at home in Chapel Hill, in North Carolina, here in
California, or anywhere else in the world where there are Masons. As

288

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA
PROCEEDINGS OP THE

long as they are there I know there will be those who will assist me,
pray for me, keep my secrets, give me good counsel and protect me from
danger. What greater security could I ask. Yet if I am to stand there I
must remember that I must be worthy. I must use the working tools Masonry has provided upon myself that my actions may stand the test of
the square in the hands of the Supreme Grand Master, that I may walk
upright before God and man and meet all men on the level. I must also
remember that if I am to stand in the center so I must also take my place
in the circle around every other Mason, using my trowel to spread
around them that cement of brotherly love and affection which unites us
into one sacred band or society of friends and brothers. Should I get
angry or prejudiced or greedy and break the circle, what have I done?
I have reduced myself to a point, no longer the center of a circle, just a
point which has neither length, :breadth nor thickness, the nearest to
nothing in all mathematics. I have simply destroyed myself.
.In all this I must remember that the powe~ comes not from myself but
from the Supreme Grand Master, source of all Masonic light and power,
the spiritual force of Masonry itself. Masons know, I do not say believe,
that God is. No man can go through the ceremonies of Masonry thoughtfully and sincerely without feeling His presence. Knowing that God is,
they know that they are the sons of God and therefore brother. There
can be no brotherhood of man without the fatherhood of God. This, the
fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man is the great tenet of _
Masonry. On this foundation it unites men of every country, sect and
opinion, and conciliates true friendship among those who might otherwise remain at a perpetual distance. This is the great task of Masonry
to spread these principles abroad. By this means we may overcome the
ruffians of our day. It is tempting to say we have done our work when
we have received the degrees, when we have served as Master or even
as Grand Master, that we are tired and wish to rest. But the task is not
done, our quest ·not ended. We must b~ up and at our work as Master
Masons.

ADDRESS OF MOST V/ORSHIPFUL J. H. MORGAN
Grand Master of Masons of the Grand Lodge of British Columbia
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I come from the Land of the Maple Leaf; from that New Nation of
the twentieth century-The Dominion of Canada, that Country which
shares with your United States of America the great portion of the
continent of this New World of North America-a Country separated
only from that of yours by a common line fence, by a line fence many
thousands of miles in length,-from Cape Breton and Newfoundland
on the Atlentic to the shores of Vancouver Island and of the Queen
Charlotte Islands on the Pacifk,-a line fence over which the spirit of
peace and good will has resigned for almost a century and a half. Truly,
I come from a land whose people believe, above all else, that "It is good
to live in unity and in harmony with ones neighbors." And all over that
Land, the Institution of Freemasonry is on the march. There are nine
Grand Lodges in Canada, one in each of the nine older Provinces, and
all in a most healthy and flourishing condition. In Newfoundland,
Canada's newest and youngest Province, there is as yet no domestic
Grand Lodge,-there, there are many Lodges, some of them of old age,
but all operating with Charters from and under the jurisdiction of either
the United Grand Lodge of England or the Grand Lodge of Scotland.
I am indeed greatly honored and very much privileged, this morning,
to bring to this Grand Lodge and to all its Freemasons the warmest
congratulations and felecitations from all the Freemasons of Canada
upon this-your Centennial Festival.
However, it would be presuming if I were to spread my wings or
range too far from my home territory, or embrace too much of the geography of my Country. It would not do for me to encroach upon the
preserves of my other Canadian friends and colleagues who are here
representing the Freemasonry of the other Canadian Grand Jurisdictions. And so perhaps I had better stay in British Columbia.
It is my special desire to present the compliments of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of British Columbia, to extend to this Grand Lodge
of California our fraternal greetings, our congratulations upon your One
Hundredth Anniversary, and may your glorious past be reflected in a
more glorious future. Also, I wish to say a word of personal thanks for
all the wonderful hospitality which has been extended to Mrs. Morgan
and to myself. The graciousness and the kindness of the Grand Master
and associates is so very much appreciated. We will not forget this visit
to California.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Perhaps, it might be interesting if I told you something of the origin
of Freemasonry in British Columbia, and of how it happened that
brethren from California formed the nucleus of a group to establish the
first Lodge at Fort Victoria, in the Crown Colony of Vancouvers Island,
(now Victoria, British Columbia).
It all started with the first Gold Rush in 1858. In California, the
frenzied activity that followed the gold rush of 1849 had died down.
The time when gold was to be had for the taking, had passed, and men
were looking for a new Eldorado. The California mines had moved into
the big business stage. In 1857 rumors were .current that g~!d had ~een
found in the North on a hitherto unknown River called the Fraser . It
was said that the Hudsons Bay Company was digging out millions, that
it was a second California. In 1858, 800 ounces of flne gold was sent
down by the Hudson Bay Company to the mint in San Francisco. Not
a large amount, and certainly not much in today's dollar terms, but it
then was enough to start a rush for the North. Gold seekers sailed from
California for Fort Victoria, and thence to the Fraser River, and up that
River they found gold at Fort Hope and Yale. The excitement had started. A City of shacks and tents soon was clustered around the Hudson
Bay Company's fort at Victoria, a City sprung up over night. There
were many· Freemasons among the newcomers,-most of them, whether
citizens of the United States or of other countries, had learned their
lessons in the then Lodges of California,-and as soon as they became ·
settled they wanted a Masonic Lodge in their new home. Men like J. J.
Southgate, an Englishman, came from California; Geo. Pearkes, a solicitor a Canadian from Port Hope, Ontario, practiced law in San Francis~o. and was a member of Occidental Lodge No. 22 of San Francisco;
Capt. Jeffray, another Californian; Jas. N. Thain, from Davy Crocker
Lodge No. 7 of San Francisco; Amor De Cosmos, a newspaper man,
whose real name was William Smith, but which he changed because I
suppose there were too many Bill Smiths in California; Richard Lewis,
an architect, is listed as a member of Golden Gate Lodge No. 30; and
there were others. It was these men who, joining with some earlier arrivals in the Colony, laid the foundation of Freemasonry in our present
day British Columbia.
.
- -In 1858, an application was made to the United Grand Lodge of
England for a Charter. After much delay and mu~h c~rres~ond~n~e
the application was granted and a Charter was received m Victoria m
March, 1860. Thus Victoria Lodge No. 1085, G. R. of U. G. L. of England the flrst Lodge in British Columbia, was established. So you will
see, ~hat we, in British Columbia, can date at least a part of our origin
back to your California.
From that small beginning in 1860, with a handful of members in one
Lodge, Freemasonry has grown and expanded until today in the Grand

Lodge of British Columbia there are some 18,000 odd Freemasons inhabiting some 130 Lodges. And it holds a great future. British Columbia
is a great Province, a land of opportunity, a growing land, a big land
with a future unlimited. Perhaps I should not permit myself to :boast,
but you in this Country are accustomed to seeing and hearing of big
things, and I know you will pardon me if I raise my voice just a wee bit
to boost of my own country.
Why just yesterday, I heard the Master of Texas speaking in most
glowing terms of the vastness, of the bigness and of the greatness of his
State of Texas. Would I be going out on a limb, if I requested you to inform the Grand Master of Texas that within the boundaries of British
Columbia there is an area approximately 100,000 square miles larger
than his great State of Texas. I invite you to come up some time and ·see
this land of mine.
One hundred years of Freemasonry! What a great pride you must
have in your glorious past! 1850 to 1950.
Brethren, what are your hopes for the future of your Freemasonry.
In this year of 1950, what are you and I, and countless thousands of
Freemasons like us, doing with our Freemasonry or expect to do with
it. Is it not true that never before in the history of the world has life
been so thrilling and so well worth living? Never before so many oppor- .
tunities for the living of a full life, and for leadership in every good
cause. Never before has there been so great a need for the practice of
the Golden Rule, "Do unto others as though you were the others."
Never before so many opportunities to put Freemasonry to work.
The other day I read an article by a leading educationalist. He wrote
and I quote-"Never before in the history of the World has its people
stood at such fateful crossroads. One road leads definitely towards the
Brotherhood of Man, the goal of every religious and philosophic movement; the other towards a setting wherein man is pitted against man,
nation against nation, to the utter destruction of our way of life."
There is no doubt regarding the road which we, as Freemasons, must
take. Every humanitarian movement, religious, political. social and fraternal, must be used to draw men closer together, else all that we hold
sacred, our institutions and our inheritance will be destroyed. Therein,
Freemasonry is given a challenge. We can use Freemasonry in strenuous labor for the right. We can and must marshall all our resources
towards the successful accomplishment of the greatest task of all-the
establishment of a practical and working Brotherhood of Man. Our rewards will be great. We shall have communicated much happiness to
others, and certainly we will be happy ourselves. We shall be on the
right road, going forward at high speed, singing with full hearts, secure
in the knowledge that at the end we shall find a "New Heaven and a
New Earth."

Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California
September 29, 1950
San Francisco, California
Gentlemen:
We have audited the books of accounts and records of the Grand Lodge
F. & A. M. of California for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1950 and submit
herewith the following statements:
Consolidated Statements
Exhibit AA : Consolidated Statement of Assets and Liabilities, Owned or
Under Control of Grand Lodge, July 31, 1950.
Exhibit BB : Consolidated Statement of Cash Receipts and Disbursements, from Funds of or Controlled by Grand Lodge, August 1, 1949 to July
31, 1950.
Grand Locl~e
Exhibit A: Statement of Assets and Liabilities, July 31, 1950.
Exhibit B: Statement of Cash Receipts and Disbursements, August l,
1949 to July 31, 1950.
Exhibit C: Grand Treasurer's Statement of Cash Receipts and Disbursements, August l , 1949 to July 31, 1950.
Exhibit D: Grand Secretary's Resume of Cash Received.
Schedule 1: List of Securities, July 31, 1950.
Schedule 2: Statement of Grand Lodge per-Capita Dues Collected from
1949 Annual Returns.
·
Schedule 3: Statement of Masonic Homes per-Capita Due and $25.00
Contributions Collected during the Year 1949-50.
Schedule 4: Comparation of Budget and Expenditures, 1949-50.
Comments
The publishing costs of the Masonic history books up to July 31, 1950
amounted to $9,455.88 which has been listed as an asset of Grand Lodge on
Exhibit A as it is expected that all costs will be collected through the sales
of the books. The other expenses and appropriations paid during the year
exceeded the revenue by $25,590.62. The $12,578.00 advanced to Gravel Range
Lodge No. 59 in the previous year was written off this year in accordance
with the motion passed ·a t the 1949 communication of Grand Lodge, thus the
total decrease in the reserves of Grand Lodge for the year 1949-50 amounted
to $38,168.62.
Our Schedules 2 and 3 show proof of the revenue due from the Lodges
in accordance with their returns and the $25.00 Homes contribution reports
received up to July 31, 1950. The tot al revenue due, as shown, agrees with
t he total cash received from the Lodges by the Grand Secretary.
Cash recei.pts were accounted for and deposited in the proper bank
accounts of the Grand ';C'reasurer. Disbursements were made by checks and
supported by properly approved vouchers. The disbursements made by the
Grand Secretary were from his Operating Fund bank account. Reimburse. ments to the Operating Fund by the Grand Treasurer were not made until
we had audited and approved the bills, which was done monthly. During
the year, we found that no bills were paid by the Grand Secretary unless the
expense was provided for i_n the budget and the appro:priation had not been
exceeded, except when prior approval had been obtained from the Grand
Master.
Bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries. A
certified l~t of the securities :v_as received fro~ the An~lo-California National
Bank which holds the securities for safekeeping. All mterest and dividends
due were received.
Sotoyome Lodge No. 123 has fulfilled its agreement during the year·
$150.00 monthly was paid by Grand Lodge and $100.00 monthly was re~
ceived by Grand Lodge from Sotoyome Lodge.
In our opinion, the attached statements P.resent fairly the financial position of tl~e Gr~n9' .Lodge F. & A. M. of Califor!1ia at July 31, 1950 and the
result of its activities for the fiscal year 1949-50 m accordance with generally
accepted accounting principles.
Respectfully submitted,
BURROWS & PARKER
Certified Public Accountants
Walter A. Parker

COMMENTS
Cash:

The bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.
All interest and dividends due from investments and savings bank accounts
were received by the Grand Treasurer and deposited in the bank accounts
of the Masonic Homes. The total income received by the Homes from the
Endowment Funds amounted to $95,722.56.
Sec:urities:

Securities on hand that were ·a cquired in prior years are listed on Schedule 1. Securities received through contributions and bequests and bonds
purchased during the current year are listed on Schedule 2. Securities redeemed and sold during the current year are listed on Schedule 3.
Bonds purchased are listed at actual cost. Donated securities are listed
at market value when received, or at a nominal value of $1.00 if the actual
value is unknown.
Certified lists of securities held for the account of the Endowment iFund
were received from the Anglo-California National Bank. The records were
checked to these lists and the securities not listed were inspected by us at
the office of the Grand Secretary.
Increase in Fund:

All returns have been received and paid in full in accordance with
the amount shown by the returns as computed. The balance still due
represents errors made in various returns and are in process of collection.
Respectfully submitted
BURROWS & PARKER

Certified Public Accountants
WALTER A. PARKER

GRAND TREASURER'S REPORT-ENDOWMENT FUND

Other Endowment Assets:
The books of the Masonic Homes carry the records of the Harriet C. Wadleigh Endowment Annuity Fund. After the death of the beneficiaries of this
fund, the remainder will be transferred to the Endowment Fund. Schedule 7
of the Masonic Homes report shows that this fund had a balance of $21,794.42
as of July 31, 1950.
The Masonic Homes also hold several pieces of real estate for the account
of the Endowment Fund. Whenever a sale is made, the proceeds will be
deposited to the account of the Endowment Fund.
In our opinion, the accompanying statements present fairly the financial
position of the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund at July 31, 1950 in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles.

Investments:
During the year the Homes General Fund received from the estate of
Ann G. Luther stocks and bqnds which had a market value of $26,357.63.
These securities together with the government bonds purchased by the
Homes in prior years are listed on Schedule 1. The securities were verified
by a certified list from the Anglo-California National Bank which holds them
for safekeeping.
Properties:
The value of the properties as shown on the Balance Sheet, Exhibit A,
is the cost of the two homes at Decoto and Covina owned by the Masonic
Homes of California. During the current year $119,229.06 was disbursed for
the construction of new buildings, for improvements to the old buildings and
for new equipment.
·
Other Funds:
The Masonic Homes has numerous separate funds which have been
created for definite or special purposes. Some were created by donation and
by bequest to the Homes for a particular purpose, and others by action of
the Board of Trustees to set aside money that is to be used only for the
purpose indicated by the title of the fund. Full details of these funds are
shown on the attached statements, Schedules 2 to 12 inclusive.
All interest and dividends due on the investment of these funds were
received and deposited in the proper bank accounts. Payments of principal
and interest have been received on the notes and contracts owned by the
Monthly Grant Fund. Insurance premiums and taxes due on real estate have
been paid. Proper payments were made from the annuity funds in accordance
with the contracts and agreements.
All bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.
The securities were accounted for as held by the Anglo-California National
Bank or in the office of the Grand Secretary. Those held by the bank were
verified by a certified list from the bank, and those in the office of the Grand
Secretary were inspected.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ENTERTAINMENT

August 7, 1949: Barbecue Picnic
Dinner at Lake Park, Hutington
Beach, given by Huntington Beach
Lodge No. 380. Children and staff of
the Covina Home were special guests.
August 28, 1949: Junior and Intermediate Girls, with their houseparents, were guests of Bethel No. 4,
Order of Job's Daughters, at a picnic
on the Masonic Home Athletic Field.
September 25, 1949: Lamanda Park
Lodge No. 627 entertain the wards of
their Lodge, Roland and Lowell
Parker, at a picnic given at Farnsworth Park, Altadena. Harry and
Harold Eller (wards of Meridian
Lodge No. 667) were guests of the
Parker boys at this picnic.
October 9, 1949: The Junior Girls
and their housemother were guests
of Anchor Lodge No. 273 at a picnic
at Covina City Park.
October 20, 1949: A birthday party
for Roland Parker was given by Lamanda Park Lodge No. 627, at the
Senior Boys' Building.
November 19, 1949: Twenty-five
children, by courtesy of the Covina
Legion Post, were guests at the annual American Legion Vaudeville
Show at the Hollywood Legion Stadium.
November 20, 1949: The Crown
City Modelaires Competitive Exhibition of one hundred Flying Model
Planes - on Athletic Field of the
Home.
November 27, 1949: Tickets for the
"First Annual Youth Football Frolic," by courtesy of the Los Angeles
Junior Chamber of Commerce.
December 3, 1949: The Junior and
Intermediate Boys and Girls, accompanied by their houseparents and
Mr. and Mrs. Henry, were guests of
Hollywood Lodge No. 355, at the first
Christmas party of the season.
December 16, 1949:· Christmas
. party given at the Home by Carmelita Lodge No. 599.
December 18, 1949: "The Toy Maker's Dance" was presented at the
Home by the Vera Baker School of
the Dance, sponsored by the Anzettes, Auxiliary to Anza Grotto, San
Bernardino.
December 21, 1949: Masonic Home
Christmas Party. The Southern Members of the Board of Trustees and
their families were special guests.

December 22, 1949: Monrovia
Lodge No. 308 and Sojourner Lodge
No. 607 held their twenty-seventh
annual Christmas Party for the children, at Monrovia.
December 23, 1949: Covina Home
Hospital held Open House and gave
Christmas Party for children and
staff.
December 24, 1949: Christmas
Party at the home of Mr. and Mrs.
Henry for children and staff.
February 1, 1950: Minstrel Show at
Pasadena Scottish Rite Cathedral.
February 4 and 5, 1950: Intermediate Boys and Girls spent the weekend at Lake Arrowhead, accompanied by the children's houseparents,
the nurse, and Mr. Henry.
February 16, 1950: Monrovia Lodge
No. 308 entertained a group of Intermediate and Junior Boys as "adopted
sons" at the Monrovia Lodge Father
and Son Dinner.
February 18 and 19, 1950: Senior
Girls, Junior Girls and Junior 'Boys,
accompanied by their houseparents,
Mr. Henry and our nurse, spent the
week-end at Lake Arrowhead.

Drama Guild of Pasadena Consistory were hosts to our Senior, Intermediate and Junior Girls and Intermediate and Junior Boys at a Minstrel Show at Pasadena Scottish Rite
Cathedral.
February 25 and 26, 1950: Senior
Boys' Snow Trip· to Lake Arrowhead, accompanied by Mr. Henry,
houseparents and nurse.
March 16, 1950: Senior, Intermediate and Junior Boys and Intermediate and Junior Girls were guests of
the San Bernardino Santa Fe Masonic Club at the National Orange
Show at San Bernardino.
April 1, 1950: The children and
their houseparents were guests of
Fezzan Grotto (Whittier) upon the
occasion of the Fezzan Grotto Hit
Show.

Club sponsored an entertainment on
the Home grounds, featuring wrestling and boxing matches, followed
by vaudeville acts.

Lowell Parker given by Lamanda
Park Lodge No. 627 at the Intermediate Boys' Building.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of Grand Lodge
of California:
FOREWORD
Once again your Committee on Correspondence has finished its
Cook's Tour of the Masonic Globe and has returned to the Temple to
make its annual report.
The several months spent in mental travel. first within our own
Golden Empire. disclosed that California in its Centennial year is Grand
Tiler of 606 Subaltern Lodges and some 197.000 Master Masons constituting their membership.
Your Committee realizes that a certain much is lacking in this report
-that Stalin and the Vatican. Tito and Franco still hold a tight yoke
on a great part of Europe and Asia.
Reports of a sort indicate that in Greece. France, and Israel the altar
with its Sacred Volume has been erected and maintained, while in the
Philippine Islands, Masonry again has been enabled to assume a
stronger hold. In Red China six Lodges manage to maintain their
identity, while in Japan two Lodges hold their authority for parentage
likewise from the Philippine Jurisdiction.
In South American Countries recognition generally is withheld either
because of the absence of the Holy Bible from the altar or because of
unfriendly church dominance. Masonry of a type is to be found but
it is of a clandestine sort.
And now after a long swing of years your California Committee on
Correspondence has altered its mode of report, changing from the
Topical to the Reportorial form of presentation by Jurisdictions. We
liked. in truth we rather preferred, the well established Topical style
of telling our story. California. as a jurisdiction, long has adhered to
this thesaurus of Masonic experiences and teachings. However. it
seemed best that with the growth and spread of Masonry some way
should be found whereby the burden might be carried more equitably
upon many shoulders instead of on one ·back. as the last steep editorial
grade hove in sight.
In searching the archives for a good and sufficient reason for the existence of a Committee on Correspondence. we came upon the following
answer to our query from the mind of Brother Jesse M . Whited, member
and Chairman of this Committee for over twenty years :
The functions of the Committee on Correspondence can be
traced back to Revolutionary days. In order to maintain contacts
between the various Colonies committees were appointed for this
purpose, and afterward this procedure among Grand Lodges was

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

483

adopted in order that the members might be informed of what was
transpiring in the different jurisdictions.
. The Chair~an'. or Correspondence Committee of any jurisdiction, aft~r ~eviewmg the Proceedings of the various Grand Lodges,
per~aps is in a better position to give to the Craft what has occurred
dur~ng the preceding year. Extracts from the forewords of the
chairmen o~ a n~mber of jurisdictions! are perhaps the best index
as to what is taking place in Masonry at ·the present time
The quotation is from the Foreword to Brother Whited'~ Report
of 1940.
B_efore takin.g this venturesome step we sought the good and wise
advice .?f ~ertam Masonic luminaries, and the most direct reply seemed
to be: Give _them something short-something that they will read."
As to brevity we fear again we have failed. As to its acceptabilitywe only can ask your kind indulgence, as we pause on the threshold of
a ·1ew Century.

Wyoming ····························-···········-· 76

Lee Garrett, Grand Master.
Joseph A. E. Ivey, Grand Secretary.
The Grand Lodge ( 67th) was opened with due ceremony April 27, .
1949, including the presentation of the Flag and the pledge of allegiance.
Following a trend now evident in other Grand Jurisdictions the
Grand Master recommended an adoption of a statement of principles to
which a foreign Grand Lodge must subscribe when it applies for recognition by the Grand Lodge of Arizona. The Grand Master also recommended that the Grand Lodge stop straddling the intoxicating liquor
issue and proposed a constitutional amendment clarifying the matter.
However, the committee to which it was referred, disagreed and as a
result no action was taken. We, in California, are in no position to
criticize.
We admire the spunk of the Board of Trustees in commenting on the
adoption by the Grand Lodge of a pet project of some of its members
which resulted in "spending a lot of money and getting a headache".
The Board also criticized the transfer of income of Masonic Homes
General Fund and Masonic Homes Endowment Fund to the Grand
Lodge General Fund to cover expenses. The adoption of a proposed
amendment to correct this situation would have increased the per-capita
tax from $1.50 to $3.32, consequently, the matter was deferred until the
next communication. The policy committee seemed to think that it was
entirely proper to tap the income of these funds.
The committee on Correspondence recommended that funds be made
available to permit publication of reviews of the proceedings of other
Grand Jurisdictions as part of the annual proceedings. Unfortunately,
the General Policy Committee recommended against the proposal and
· this Committee's recommendation was adopted by the Grand Lodge.
WILLIS R. PINKERTON, Grand Master
JOSEPH A. E. lVEY, Grand Secretary.
Next Communication, Flagstaff, April 24, 1950.
ARKANSAS
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of Arkansas met in the one hundred eighth Communication in the one
hundred eleventh year of its existence as a Grand Lodge, in the city of
Little Rock, on Tuesday, November 15, 1949.
The roll call showed a constitutional number of representatives of
subordinate Lodges were present, whereupon the Most Worshipful
Grand Master Brother C. Allon Clift, opened the Grand Lodge in ample
form, with a prayer by the Worshipful Grand Chaplain, Brother Arthur
Terry.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Brother W. A. Thomas, Past Grand Master, ·and Grand Secretary,
in his report shows that there are 379 chartered Lodges and 3 under dispensation in the Grand Jurisdiction with a total membership of 49,655,
a net gain over last year of 2,831.

COLORADO

490

Rising Sun Lodge No. 138 at Big Flat, Arkansas asked to have its
charter restored and the request was granted by the Grand Master. On
September 7, 1949 War Eagle Lodge No. 429 merged with Pea Ridge
Lodge No. 119 as provided by 'the laws. Hebron Lodge No. 299 being
inactive and having initiated only 3 .members in the last twelve years,
with membership decreasing until they now have only nine members,
and Falcon Lodge No. 67 holding only one meeting in 1949 and there
being no one raised since 1943, with a membership of 20 their charters
were suspended. North Star Lodge No. 729 being inactive, only two men
have finished the degrees in the past 14 years, with failure to hold meetings regularly, it was recommended that the charter be arrested.
The records of the Grand Lodge show that 4,000 men have petitioned for the degrees and been rejected by the Lodges, and also that on
October 1, 1949 there were 713 petitions for the degrees pending, 135
men who had been elected but not initiated, 982 who had been initiated
and not passed and 486 passed but not raised. During the year Fifty
Year Buttons were presented to 38 members.
The scholarship committee reviewed eleven applications, and finally
selected five of equal standing and agreed on two alternates.
There were eight emergent Communications for the purpose of Constituting new Lodges, laying corner stones and dedicating new buildings.
A report of the work done at the Masonic Building of the Arkansas
Tuberculosis Sanatorium covered the period from November 1, 1948
through October 31, 1949. At the beginning of the year, there were 81
children. During the year 144 children were admitted-76 girls and 68
boys. There remained on November 1, 1949, 107 children. In all 225
children have been hospitalized from 54 counties during this period.
Since the Masons gave the building to the Arkansas Sanitorium there
have been 3, 168 patients treated with 2,876 arrested results.

It is the opinion of the Home Committee that help for needy Free
Masons and benevolence to members of their families can be done with
greater satisfaction and contentment if extended to them in their own
homes and in their own communities where family and neighborhood ties
contribute to the happiness of those affected than to place them in a home.
Brother Charles Lester Hanna was elected ~-;;_d ~installecithe Most
Worshipful Grand Master of Masons in Arkansas, and after a few
timely remarks the Grand Lodge was closed in ample form to reconvene
again for their annual communication in November 1950.

Next Communication, Denver, September 19, 1950.
CONNECTICUT 1949

The One Hundred Sixty first Annual Communication of the Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted Masons of
Connec~icut, with a constitutional number of Lodges represented, was
opened m ample form by the Most Worshipful Louis Stevens Thomas~
Grand Master at 10 A. M. on Wednesday, April 6 A. L. 5949, in the
Masonic Temple, 201 Ann Street, Hartford. ·

492

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

The prayer was offered by the Grand Chaplain, Worshipful and
Reverend William H. Nicolas.
The National Colors and the State Flag were presented by the Senior
and Junior Stewards, and all joined in the Pledge of Allegiance followed
by singing one st.a nza of "America". The Flags were placed in the Grai:id
East, and all joined in singing three stanzas of "Faith of our Fathers",
as is their annual custom.
The Grand Master stated that in a few instances, some well meaning
but over zealous Brethren had been taking unwarranted liberties with
the candidates, in their eagerness to put on a good show for the sidelines
and attempt to create fun by introducing burlesque and other acts of outright clowning. These innovations together with unnecessary roughness,
destroy the impressiveness, the dignity and the true purpose and meaning
of the drama of the sublime degree of Master Mason. The Gral).d Master
said that there was a time and place for everything, even for fun, and he
hoped that there would be a prompt elimination of all improper acts. He
also stated that his principal objective was to spread brotherly love and
affection and thus bring about a closer bond of mutual understanding and
a greater spirit of sincere cooperation among the craft.
The Grand Master was especially interested in the DeMolay Boys
and Rainbow Girls, and other youth organizations, stating that these
boys and girls are doing a magnificent job to inculcate in the hearts and
minds of our youth, the love of the one true God, the love of Country
and the love of our American way of life.
He recommended that a survey committee be appointed to find out
why the Brethren do not attend Lodge more regularly; and what they
would like to have done to make the meetings more interesting. He also ·
urged that a committee on Public Relations to promote a better understanding of the principals of Masonry in the minds of the general public
be created. Whether Masonry wins favorable or unfavorable reaction
depends on the kind of information disseminated the Grand Master
added.
The Tw.enty five year button that is awarded by the Grand Lodge is

DELAWARE

There was no comment on California Grand Lodge or Correspondence Committee report. Grand Master James Carswell observed that
while it is regretable, it is nonetheless a well-known fact that it is becoming increasingly difficult, if not impossible, in many of our lodges to
accept the responsibility of performing the traditional burial service for
a deceased brother. Whether this is due to a lack of "brotherly love and
affection" or whether the complexities of the modern way of life do not
anticipate or provide for this eventuality, he did not wish to say, but
felt that some definite action be indicated to correct or relieve this situation.
Recommendation that the Committee on Work prepare an optional
condensed form of burial service ·b ased upon or consistent with the present service sanctioned by this Grand Lodge and report at the next Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge. Adopted.
The Grand Master was also convinced there is a netd of proper preliminary instructions immediately preceding the reception of a candidate
into Masonry.
Recommendation that the Committee on Work be instructed to prepare a suitable charge to be delivered by the Secretary of the Lodge to
the candidate immediately preceding his reception into the Lodge. This
charge should embody briefly the history and traditions of Masonry, the
responsibilities of the candidate and what he may reasonably expect from
his membership in the Fraternity. Report to be prepared and submitted
by the Committee on Work at the next Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge. Adopted.

The proceedings of this Grand Lodge show that the Grand Master
was exceedingly busy; there were eleven corner stone layings, five new
Lodges constituted and one dedication of a new Temple with the Grand
Master presiding at all but two of the ceremonies. There were also numerous appearances at subordinate Lodges in Georgia as well as other
public functions. M. W. Brother Moulton reported to his Brethren that
it had been his privilege and pleasure during his term as Grand Master
to have raised his only son to the sublime degree of Master Mason. In
his address to the Craft he asked this question "How Firm A Foundation?" and then proceeded to answer it as follows: "My Brethren it is
just as firm as we make it. Our founding fathers and Masonic predecessors, your ancestors and mine, wrought well. They established a
great country for us in which to live, love and enjoy. The fundamental
principles which they embodied in the creation of this great Nation were
firm and sound. The ideas of thrift. the right to work, free enterprise.
private property, separation of the Church and State, establishment of
the public school system for the education of all the children of all the
people, were part and parcel of the State and National Constitutions.
We as participants in the affairs of our Nation, must never allow it to
drift into planned economy-a welfare State. My heart goes out to the
people of the world who have had to live under this religious dictatorship
over the years, but against dictatorship either political. spiritual or both,
the Masons of Georgia must unquestionably stand. Support your
Churches and your public schools, by Brethren. Remember that children
are the mos~ important things on Earth. They are entitled to the rich
heritage which we enjoy. Guard it well for them as our forefathers guarded it for us. Hand it and our Fraternity down to them spotless and undefiled. Our Churches and our public schools are FIRM FOUNDATIONS."
.

IDAHO
The 83rd Annual Communication of Grand Lodge was opened on
September 20, 1949 with the customary presentation of the Flag of the
United States. We were pleased to note that the procedure in Grand
Lodge of Idaho resembles that in California with respect to Lodge
financing. On the petition of a Lodge for authority to borrow money, or
build a Temple, the Grand Master appoints a special committee to make
an investigation. and bases his opinion upon the advice and counsel of
this committee.
The matter of the physical qualifications of candidates again came
before the Grand Lodge and a resolution providing that the matter be
left to a decision by the Lodge involved, when the matter of the physical
qualifications of an applicant who was maimed while serving in the armed
services of the United States. was voted down.
The Committee on Masonic Education reported the adoption of the
plan of presenting degree pamphlets as candidates advance in the work,
and that many older Masons are obtaining the pamphlets for study.
This seems to be the absolute minimum that a Lodge can do in informing
its new members. Our experience in California would seem to indicate
that proper distribution of the pamphlets should be a requirement, not
a suggestion.
This Committee is disturbed by the lack of understanding of Masonic
law by Masters. Wardens and Secretaries. The suggestion that these
officers be required to pass an examination by filling out questionnaires
is timely. Digging into the fundamental law to find the ans~ers t? 40 ~r
50 questions has proved an invaluable aid to Lodge officers m Cahforma.
The novel review of the informal events of the communications by
the Grand Secretary, under the title "Sidelights" was exceedingly interesting and worthwhile.
The scholarly etymologist (he also understands German and Norwegian) who is the foreign correspondent, devoted two ~nd one half pages
to an entirely adequate review of the 1948 proceedings of our Grand

t~~! a possible eco~omic period of recession could be ~et, if the "mystic

time in the Lodge schedule should be assigned to each activity, all in
proper '~alanc~ to the whole scheme of things. such as a dignified but
mterestmg social program for the brethren, their ladies and their families.

The proceedings of 99th Annual Communications of the Grand

At the Grand Lodge opening the Flag of our country was presented
by color bearers from the Lodge at Fort Knox, Kentucky. The address

An interesting controversy over the activities of an auxiliary organization was reported. It appears that for many years this body had
conducted raffles, using Grand Lodge mailing lists; funds running into
thousands of dollars annually were thus raised for the Old Masons
Home, notwithstanding a section of the regulations prohibiting all forms

of gambling and specifying raffle~. The Grand Master refused to act

The Grand Secretary reported that 82 lodges collected dues of less
than $5.00 per member and paid the Grand Lodge $3.50 per member.
How do they do it?
The fear of legal, or at least moral liability, in the case of default
of a subordinate lodge in its financial obligation assumed in the construction of a Temple, if the Grand Lodge had approved and ratified the
Lodges' actions, caused the Grand Master to recommend, in effect, that
the assumption of obligations be left to the sound discretion of the
Lodges. In view of the disastrous experiences of many lodges throughout the country we wonder at the faith in the business judgment of all
Lodges.

In the opening ceremonies the Flag of our country was presented,

Although the completion of a new Infirmary at the Masonic Home

The Homes Endowment Fund was increased by $76,000 to $1 ,113,000. It is invested in a wide assortment of corporate securities, including co,mmon and deferred stock.
The Grand Master commented on the threat of bankruptcy of many
lodges arising from the issuance of life memberships and urged that the
lodges involved take steps to restrict the number of such memberships.
The Grand Master's message contained the best statement of current
Masonic problems we have seen.

The Grand Lodge meets on St. John's Day in Boston, to install

and December 8th.

At each quarterly communication the following statement appears
in the proceedings: "The Grand Master called attention to the presence
in Grand Lodge of the distinguished heads of the collateral Grand
Bodies in Massachusetts. Each of these Brothers rose as he was presented, and was heartily greeted by the Brethren."
The following quotations are from the Grand Master's Meisages
at the Quarterly Communications:
"I want to call attention to the fact that kneeling. as used in the
Masonic sense, means kneeling on the knee or knees-going entirely
down and not just a genuflection. Also, no covering should be worn
on the head in the lodge room except by the Master or Grand Master,
both of whom, as you know, have the privilege of remaining covered if
they so desire. The District Deputy Grand Master, on occasion, is
also covered."
" As many of you know, tomorrow, with my Marshal and Sword
Bearer, I go to New York and sail on Friday on the Queen Elizabeth
for England. On the 23rd of March, a new Grand Master, His Grace
the Duke of Devonshire, K. G .• is to be installed in the United Grand
Lodge of England. This is to take place at the Royal Albert Hall in
London.
"I am fortunate in the fact that my brother, the Honorable Gerald
Keith, is Consular of Embassy in London, and we are going to be able
to stay with him and make his home our headquarters. This should be
a delightful and unusual experience.
"Two of my predecessors in office during comparatively recent
years have been fortunate enough to be at similar ceremonies-Most
Worshipful Joseph Earl Perry was in England in 1939 and Most Worshipful Claude L. Allen in 1936, attended the installation of the present
King of England as Grand Master Mason of Scotland at Edinburgh.
It was a very short time after his installation that the abdication of the
King required the Grand Master Mason to resign that position before
ascending the Throne as King of England.
"I look forward naturally to this pleasant occasion and shall be glad
to report to you at the June Communication of our Grand Lodge."

The Grand Master in his report also had this to say:
"The legend of the Third Degree and the work at the three gates has
often been the part that makes or breaks the solemnity and effectiveness
of this very important lesson. You have heard my predecessors in office
discuss this subject, and I want again to point out that this part of the
degree should be handled in such a manner that there is no semblance
of a smile at any time. This work was exemplified recently for the
entire Grand Lodge of New York by their Grand Lecturer. If done
with the proper feeling and tone of voice, it can be exceedingly impressive. There is no need or occasion for force or roughness of any kind.
The di~~ity of this part of the work is entirely in the hands of the
Master.
There is no comment in the proceedings concerning any flag ceremony.
The M.'.W.'.Grand Master and R.'.W.'.Grand Secretary were
re-elected to serve for another year. It is the custom of the Grand
Lodge of Massachusetts to elect its Grand Masters for three succeeding
years. and during each year of his administration the Grand Master
selects a Deputy Grand Master to serve for that particular year only.
MINNESOTA
M:.W:.Grand Master. John Tomhave.
At the opening session in St. Paul several distinguished visitors
were introduced, including several Grand Masters from sister jurisdictions, as well as the Grand High Priest, the Grand Master of the Grand
Council, the Grand Commander of the Grand Commandery, and the
Sovereign Grand Inspector General of the Scottish Rite, all of Minnesota.
In his address the Grand Master made the following observation:
"To fulfill adequately the office of Grand Master. one should be an
idealist, a practical business man, a globe traveler, an office worker,
an editorial writer and a public speaker."
He called attention to a matter frequently neglected: "During the
year many letters have come to the Grand Master which would indicate
that the membership as a whole is not familiar with the fact that it is
un-Masonic to declare or suggest after any petitioner has been rejected
how he or any one voted upon the ballot."
The proceedings include an excellent oration given by the Grand
Orator Al L. Dretchko who asked a challenging question, "True
Masonry, in America, has enjoyed a large and rapid growth, new members have been taken into our ranks in ever increasing numbers and
every Lodge is financially sound, but I ask you, Brethren, what are we
doing for those thousands of initiates who in recent years have knelt
at our altars? What have we done to arouse their interest in our Fra-

506

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ternity? What effort has been put forth to acquaint them in what
Masonry really means, its noble and glorious history, its ideals and
inspirations, the measurements of which are taken from the Holy Scrip·
tures which lie open on the Altar of every Masonic Lodge? What
attempt is being put forth to awaken to active participation those of our
Brethren who have more or less drifted away but still maintain their
membership?"
In reviewing the proceedings of the different Grand Lodges, it is
interesting to note the various attitudes concerning the Order of the
Eastern Star, ranging from close cooperation such as is evidenced in
Minnesota, on down through a policy of no recognition and no official
contacts such as in our own jurisdiction, to the position of the Grand
Lodge of Pennsylvania which forbids its members from any contact
whatever on penalty of suspension.
A resolution was introduced appropriating not to exceed $25.00 to
be expended by the Grand Master in sending flowers in the name of the
Grand Lodge to a member of Grand Lodge during a serious illness.
$10.00 was finally appropriated. It is refreshing to observe such careful
use of the Grand Lodge funds.
There is no mention in the proceedings of any flag ceremony.

"Recently the Masonic War Veterans of New York have been incorporated under New York State laws and Grand Lodge auspices.
Every honorably discharged veteran of the Spanish-American War or
World War I or World War II, who is a Master Mason in good standing, is invited to join.
"One of the unique accomplishments of the year has been the successful launching of the corporate body known as the Masonic Foundation for Medical Research and Human Welfare. It has made initial
grants to certain institutions engaged in rheumatic fever research. It is
our earnest hope that out of this effort will come the answer to one of
mankind's most baffling ailments. Last year Grand Lodge voted that
the necessary Constitutional amendment be passed to make the formation of this corporation possible. I. therefore, recommend that this Grand
Lodge take the same action so that the necessary second vote to an
amendment to the Constitutions be secured."
As might be expected, New York Lodges have the largest membership in the country. The Grand Lodge there has a great many activities
under its charge. There is a committee on radio broadcasts. Two magazines are published: The Masonic Outlook, which has a subscription
price of $1.00 a year, and a total subscription list of 21,000, and a Masonic Family Magazine which goes to every member every two months,
and for which the Grand Lodge pays 25 cents per member per year.
Your reviewer has read these magazines during the past year and while
they are interesting, they do not seem to achieve the high standards of a
professional magazine which we would expect from a state like New
York. From various discussions appearing in the proceedings, it would
appear that the Grand Lodge of New York is not entirely satisfied with
its magazines and it will undoubtedly be ·possible to improve their quality.
Some of the activities of the Grand Lodge of New York have puzzled
Masons in other parts of the country. It employs a Director of Public
Relations and the following quotations from his report are offered without further comment:
"Our success in conducting the program has been on a ·professional
level but we have tried to keep the warmth and close contact in our
work that are particularly ours as a Fraternity. Our sincerest flattery
cam~ from the Grand Lodge of Missouri, which now wants to set up a
Public Relations Department of its own.
"The re-enactment of the First Inauguration of Washington, at the
Sub-Treasury Building, the site of old Federal Hall, was covered by
every newspaper in the metropolitan area. The Sun, the Times, and the
Herald-Tribune featured the story on the front page.
"The truth is that much of what is news today concerns Masons;
much that was news for the last two centuries in America has depended
upon Masons. It remains for Public Relations to tie up the news with the

in his address said:
"Are we really taking advantage of our opportunities to practice real
Masonry, striving for more friendship, more brotherhood and more
service to mankind? Are our lives an influence for good on those who
know us? If so, then we are contributing to our generation to the utmost
and will reap a reward which cannot be bought by any material recom-

In Ohio the Grand Master appoints twenty-five District Deputy
Grand Masters, each of whom has from fifteen to forty-three lodges
under his immediate jurisdiction. The Grand Master reported that each
deputy was requested to make all reasonable efforts to have all lectures
given by line officers and not to depend on past masters for such work.
The . Grand Master stated, "Some Lodges are not issuing Degree
Booklets to the candidates. This is part of our educational program for
the benefit of those receiving the degrees, and should be given in all
cases."
The Grand Master called attention to the Richly Memorial Hospital
in connection with the Ohio Masonic Home. It now can accommodate
307 patients and is filled to capacity. Over 50 per cent of the applications
for residence in the Ohio Masonic Home are now hospital cases. He
said, "It is my belief that we are better enabled to take care of these
hospital cases at far less expense than individual relatives in the home,
or Lodges can afford to do in rest homes or hospitals. and I further believe that with our personnel and with our highgrade equipment, we are
better enabled to bring comfort and happiness to these unfortunate residents who are in need of hospitalization.
The Grand Master reported that he was informed that Temple of the
Shrine in Akron, an organization basing its membership on Masonic
affiliation, was permitting the use of slot machines and other forms of
gambling in its Temple and was sponsoring bingo parties. After repeated warnings these practices were not stopped and the Grand Master
suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry the Potentate,
Chief Rabban, Assistant Rabban, and all members of committees involved. At the Annual Communication the Grievance Committee decided that the committeemen had been sufficiently disciplined but the
suspension of the three principal officers was continued until the Grand
Lodge Communication in October, 1950.
The Code was amended providing that in the absence of the Master
and both wardens by reason of their attendance on a session of Grand
Lodge. the Master may at a stated meeting just prior thereto, appoint
a past master to preside at either a stated or a special meeting.
There is no mention made in the proceedings. of any flag ceremony.

Master much pleasure to grant them."
In speaking of preparation of the candidate for the degrees, the
following statements were made:
"The candidate should not be given mis-information by lightthinking brethren so that he approaches the degree with fear and
trembling. He does not receive the full benefit of the great lessons
contained in the symbolism and the lectures of the degrees. The vast
majority have little or no knowledge of the manner in which they should
approach the degree, nor are they informed of the solemnity and real
spiritual uplift that is contained therein. We have long needed a
general plan of preparation of the candidate for reception into a lodge
of Entered Apprentices. After initiation, he then should be taught not
only the lectures of the degree but he should learn how he can practically apply them in his every-day life. He should be informed of what
Masonry stands for and its relationship to human society. He should
then be prepared to receive the great lessons of the Fellowcraft degree
by divesting him of all prejudices and informing him briefly of its
history and calling his attention to the real human values that he will
receive by a careful study and application of the lessons of the Fellowcraft."
In his Necrology report, the Grand Master gave considerable space
to John J. Pershing. General of the Armies, by sympathizing with the
Nebraska Grand Lodge in the loss of its most distinguished Mason,
on July 15, 1948.

As of December 31, 1948, this jurisdiction had under charter 1BO
Lodges and 2 under dispensation, with a total membership of 36,715
showing a net gain of 1,641 for the calendar year. During the year two
hundred ninety-six life memberships were issued, bringing the total
since the program was instituted to 4,383.
Ninety-six requests for courtesy work had been received from other
jurisdictions, and in return courtesy work in sixty instances were requested.
The state is now divided into thirty-two districts, 19 of which have
less than 1,000 members, seven better than 1,000 members, four districts
more than 2,000 members and two districts with more than 3,000
members.
