At the .quarterly session on June 1st a musical program was given.
It presented so extensive a selection of Masonic music that the program,
with its program notes, is worthy of reproduction:
·
1. (a) Masonic March ..................................................................Mozart
( b) "Within This Holy Dwelling".............................................Mozart
(By Brother Knodle, Organist)
Wolf gang Amadeus Mozart was associated with several Masonic Lodges in Vienna. One of them was the Lodge Zur
Wahren Eintracht (True Harmony Lodge). He composed for
Masonic use, instrumental pieces, songs and cantatas. His great
opera. the Magic Flute, has to do with ancient Egyptian mysteries, associated with the worship of Isis and Osiris. A competent critic observes that the brilliance given by the music to
the symbolism of the mysteries is founded upon Mozart's devotion to Masonic symbolism. ideals and philosophy.
2. "The Entered 'Prentices' Song"
(Also known as "The Freemason's Health")
(Chorus by Choir)
The words are credited to Matthew Birkhead. a stage singer.
The tune is an old melody and may be found in a book entitled
"Pills to Purge Melancholy" published in 1719. The words and
the tune are printed in the 1723 edition of Anderson's "Constitution of the Grand Lodge of England."
3. "The Warden's Song"
( Solo and Chorus)
The words by James Anderson, D.D.. and the music are printed
in the Anderson Constitutions of 1123. The words in metrical
form recite "another history of Masonry" in 13 stanzas of ten
lines each with a chorus repeated four times. It was directed
"to be played at the Quarterly Communication."
4. "Free Mason's March"
(Brother Knodle at the Organ)
This march was "composed by Mr. Dubois, arranged for the
Piano Forte by Mr. Meguin, and published by G. Willig, Market Street No. 185" in Philadelphia about 1798.
5. "The Master's Song"
( Solo and Chorus)
The words by James Anderson and the music of this Song are
printed in the 1723 Constitutions. There are 23 stanzas of eight
lines each with a chorus repeated four times. It is a metrical
"history of Masonry" and is directed "to be sung with a Chorus

when the Master shall give leave, either one part only or all
together as he pleases."
There are directions to stop the music ·~to drink the health"
following:
Part 1. "To the Present Grand Master."
Part 2. ::To the Mas!er and Wardens of this particular Lodge."
Part 3. To the glorious memory of Emperors. Kings, Princes,
Nobles, Gentry. Clergy. Learned Scholars. that ever
propagated the Art."
Part 4. "To the happy memory of all the Revivers of the ancient
Augustan Style."
Part 5. (There is no direction to stop the music at the end of
part five.)
6. "~e Prove;?Y Geometry, Our Rules Surpass the Arts They Teach
m Schools

The one hundred and thirty-sixth Annual Communication of the
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of Tennessee
was held in the Grand Lodge Building, Nashville, beginning at 10:00
A. M. January 25, 1950 and was opened in ample form, with the Most
Worshipful Grand Master Lucien Campbell Connell presiding.
The devotional service was given by the Right Worshipful Grand

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

529

Chaplain, the Reverend Ira Caldwell Cole, after which the Brethren all
joined in pledge of allegiance to the Flag of the United States.
· There were sixteen Past Grand Masters in attendance, and 374
·
Lodges represented out of a total of 376.
The Correspondence Review by Brother W. Phelan Douglas is unusually complete, covering the proceedings of 70 Grand Jurisdictions and
also those of the Grand Masters and Grand Secretaries Conferences,
and the George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association.
He also recommended the recognition of the regular Grand Lodge of
Italy, as having found it to conform to the fundamental requirements
of their Grand Lodge.
During the year the Grand Master issued 1, 126 certificates of proficiency on the recommendation of the two Lecturers, Brothers C. H.
Barber and W. B. Linton, who have rendered yeoman service this past
year. They have traveled more than fifty thousand miles, making five
hundred and three visitations, with an attendance at their meetings of
more than seven thousand Brethren. There is now a grand total of
2,978 certificates in force.
The Grand Master stated that in some instances Masonry is still
being made too cheap, and recommended that those Lodges which charge
less than fifty dollars for degrees and five dollars dues give serious consideration to increasing the fees and dues.
During the year forty-seven certicates and buttons were issued and
presented to Brethren who have been in the Fraternity for fifty years.
Brother Elbert Carlton Coleman was elected and installed Most
Worshipful Grand Master of the State of Tennessee and his appointments being approved the Grand Lodge was closed in ample form.

Orato.r Worshipful Brother Elliott W. Evans in his Grand Oration used
as his topic "Separation of School and Church." In talking on this
highly controversial subject Brother Evans told of the many efforts
that are ·being made to take advantage of our public school system
to foster religious teachings. Brother Evans also pointed out that in

531

some states children are released from public school to attend religious
training classes. most of these "released time" training classes are condemned because the program interferes with that of the public school. It
was also brought out that if "released time" is given to a student that
the public should not have to foot the bill and that no teacher should be
furnished by our public schools, no transportation should be furnished
and above all no public funds should be used.
Newly installed Grand Master Newall B. Dayton made a few remarks among which was one that is of extreme importance to all Grand
Jurisdictions. "The Masonic funeral service is beautiful and satisfying
to the family if properly conducted, but often fails because of lack of
interest or the inability of the officers in charge. Unless the Master and
other officers can appear in proper dress and conduct the service with
credit, a special team composed of Past Masters or others be developed
for this vital duty which affords the only opportunity for us to appear
formally outside of the lodge room." These remarks were indeed interesting to Californians who are required to pass a satisfactory examination..in funeral service before they are installed as Master of their Lodge.

the Masonic year it reviews. Not the least portion is that dealing with
Masonic statistics; the best compendium on Masonic membership figures
we have seen this year. The tables show a total Masonic membership
over the world of over 4,879,500."

The report of the Endowment Committee of the Virginia Masonic

Charles E. Webber, Grand Master, in his message to the Craft,
stressed the need of:
1. A closer fellowship among ourselves to promote goodwill and
brotherly love.
2. A greater interest in and understanding of the workings of
Grand Lodge.
3. Loyal support of our churches and a higher appreciation of
spiritual values.
4. Devotion to home and family.
Regarding membership and attendance at meetings he added:
"There is no substitute for personal work in building up our attendance and good fellowship at stated and special communications. I urge
every Master and Warden to select at least ten names from the roster
of his membership with whom he is not personally acquainted, and to
make a personal visit to each of them, telling them of the work his
Lodge is doing, and urging their attendance. In the larger Lodges, this
work should be extended to the Deacons and other officers."
As to newly raised Master Masons, the Grand Master stated:
"I request every Worshipful Master to make it his especial duty to
provide instruction for the new raised brother, relative to the business
procedure of his Lodge, and to acquaint him with the work being done
by our Grand Lodge. I would like to see our new members encouraged
to visit other Lodges, and to have impressed upon them the importance
of maintaining their Masonic relationship wherever they may be."

WASHINGTON
The ninety.second Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of Washington convened
in the Masonic Temple, Seattle. on Tuesday. the 21st day of June, 1949
and was called to order by the Most Worshipful Delos A. Shiner at
10:00 o'clock A. M. There were 17 Past Grand Masters present.
The address of welcome was given by the Honorable William
Devin, Mayor of the City of Seattle, although not a Mason, he com·
plimented the Order for the things they stand for and the things they
have accomplished. He also quoted from the Vision of Sir Launfal.
" He who gives alms serves three, himself, his hungry neighbor and me."
The invocation was given by the acting Grand Chaplain the Rev·
erend Dr. Cyrus E. Albertson.
The Grand Master in his message stated that Free Masonry is
on the march, that our members fully appreciate the gifts which have
come down to them from the past and are determined to protect and
defend them, that the precepts of Free Masonry are recognized tools
to teach men to become better men. and to prepare them for useful service
in the community. in the church, in the administration of Government,
in the guidance of boys and girls. and in like endeavors.
One of the Grand Master's greatest interests has been in the youth
of America, especially devoted to the Boy Scouts of America. As a
tribute to his outstanding work in that organization the National Council
conferred upon him the highest Regional Honor in its power to bestow,
the Silver Antelope.
In the Grand Master's report on the Washington Memorial Temple
at Alexandria, Virginia, the reports show that the total expenditures to
February. 1949 for building construction, grounds construction, admin·
istrative and general expetises, purchase of land and maintenance total
$5.025,435.94 and it is thought that an additional $1.000.000 will com·
plete the undertaking.
During the year there were 57 fifty year certificates issued, some of
them being presented for the Grand Lodge of Washington in other
Grand jurisrictions. There were three new lodges constituted, two new
lodge halls dedicated, and one lodge issued a dispensation.
The Grand Secretary, John I. Preissner's report shows that there
are 268 Lodges under charter and one Lodge under dispensation in the
Grand Jurisdiction, with a total membership of 59,488 members, an all
time high in the annals of Grand Lodge. There were 173 requests for
courtesy work from foreign jurisdictions; Washington Lodges requested
113 degrees from other jurisdictions.

Master was compelled in many instances to disapprove of by-laws or
resolutions which attempted to set up the personnel of committees, such
as a finance committee or a charity committee. Similarly, a by-law
which would compel the Master to appoint an officer, such as a chaplain or an organist, which is not a required officer, has been held to be
illegal. The Master has the right and power to appoint additional
officers such as a chaplain or an organist if he thinks wise, but it is not
in the power of the lodge to compel him to do so.

WISCONSIN
The one hundred and fifth Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of Wisconsin was opened in
ample form, in the Scottish Rite Cathedral, Milwaukee, Tuesday, June
14, 1949, by M.'.W:. Norman H. Smith, Grand Master.
The Flag of our Country was presented and ordered placed in its
station on the dais at the right of the Grand Master. With the guard
of honor and the assembly standing at attention, the pledge of allegiance was then given.
The Report of the Grand Master contained the following:
That there had been four quarterly conferences of all of the Grand
Lodge officers held throughout the State; that at all of these conferences
officers and members of the constituent lodges in the vicinity met with
the Grand Lodge officers and had a very frank and open discussion of
the problems of the Craft, which conferences were very helpful to the
Grand Lodge officers in enabling them to learn something of the problems and desires of the members of the Craft, which the Grand Master
believed the members of the lodges also found helpful and stimulating.
He heartily recommended the continuance of this practice of holding
regular and frequent meetings of the Grand Lodge officers in various
cities of the State.
That during the year the Grand Master made 46 visitations to
lodges; and that other Grand Lodge officers made similar visits, making
in all 219 visitations: that in the course of the last three years every
lodge in the state of Wisconsin has been visited by one or more of the
Grand Lodge officers.
The plans and specifications for building a few new temples and
for remodeJing others had been approved; that inasmuch as we might
be approaching a period of recession, and having in mind the unhappy
experiences of some of the lodges which acquired indebtedness in times
of prosperity, and inflation, and which was an unbearable burden in
normal or depression times, care has been taken to approve plans for
borrowing only within what is believed to be the definite ability of the
lodge to pay; and using as a rule of thumb a formula applied by the
predecessors of not authorizing indebtedness in excess of $50.00 per
member where the building has no income features and $100.00 per
member where the building does have income features; the rule was
applied in these instances.
As to by-laws of constituent lodges, insomuch as the Master is
responsible for the conduct of the lodge and he can be held responsible
only so long as he can control the committees and functions, the Grand

540

and belief "that the Mother Grand Lodge will see the error of her ways.
but at this time it would be most unwise to do anything which would
add fuel to the fire."
The Grand Master closed his report with the following i
"In my messages and in my visitations I have tried to emphasize the
spiritual content of Masonry. I have called attention to the great responsibility, as well as to the great privilege, of being a Mason. If during
this year there has come to any brother a finer and higher concept of
the great end and object of our Gentle Craft, a new realization of the
Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man, then it is just one
more proof of the goodness and kindness of a Heavenly Father Who
accomplishes His great purposes through humble and simple men."
WYOMING
The Seventy-fifth Annual Communication was opened at Laramie,
August, 1949 by M. W . Grand Master Carlyle D. Williamson.
Special Communications had been held throughout the State during
the preceding year.
At the quarterly communication in Torrington, on September 25,
1948, the brethren marched north from the Masonic Hall to the site of
the All Saints' Episcopal Church in the north part of the city, where
they laid the corner stone in accordance with ancient Masonic rites and
ceremonies.
At the quarterly communication held in Worland on March 19,
1949, the brethren marched east from the Masonic Hall to the site of
the new First Baptist Church where they laid the corner stone of the
said Church in accordance with ancient Masonic rites and ceremonies.
At the quarterly communication held at Thermopolis, Wyoming, on
May 19, 1949, the brethren rode in automobiles to the State Park in the
eastern part of the city to the site of the new Home and Hospital. The
Grand Master laid the cornerstone in accordance with ancient Masonic
rites and ceremonies.
The Seventy-fl£ th Annual Communication was opened at Laramie
on August 22, 1949.
In his Welcoming Address, Dr. G. D. Humphrey, President of the
University of Wyoming, stated this to be the 75th year of the Grand
Lodge of Wyoming, and therefore its diamond anniversary meeting,
adding:
"Our organization is the largest in the world, respected by the world
at large, and loved by all its members, not because of the badge we wear,
for the badge is merely a symbol, whether it be a plain pin or one set
with diamonds; not because of the lodge rooms in which we meet, for
whether it be a bare hall in a remote rural district or a magnificent city
temple, the word spoken and the work performed are no different: not

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

541

because of our hospitals and homes, for much of our charity is without
show or the knowledge of the world: but because the very name of Masonry breathes the spirit of fraternal love and gives to our symbol its
priceless value, making of our halls a sacred meeting place, bestowing
upon our institution that love and service not found in public life of like
character, and bringing to our side a brotherly helper wherever our
appeal for aid may be heard."
In response to the address of welcome, Glenn C. Templeman, Worshipful Master of Lovell Lodge No. 36 said:
"That early in the last decade it was decided the people of this country needed assistance ... The Government therefore undertook to correct conditions by deficit financing ... IS THIS WISE? ... have we
given sufficient consideration to the law of cause and effect? ... Like dope
or drugs, a little may work the first time, but under prolonged and continued use the desired results can only be attained by increased amounts
until eventually no effect is experienced . . . We as Masons should
understand these things for we are carefully instructed regarding them
in the second degree. Our Brothers who had a large part in the moulding
of this Nation used much of their Masonic knowledge in that founding.
I hold that we, their heirs, as well as their Brothers have a duty to perform in maintaining what they so well started ... Let us properly ponder
them in the light of our Masonic teachings," and Grand Master Williamson in his report asked:
"Are we correspondingly alert to the duties, privileges and opportunities for service to each other and our environment and do we possess
the foresight which they showed when they instituted this movement
devoted to the principles of brotherly love, relief. truth and social improvement? I hope that when this Grand Lodge meets seventy-five years
hence the judgment may be 'Yes'; but this will be only if we lay seriously to heart the great dangers we are in from the system of distorted
thinking, usurpation of excessive authority and disregard of individual
freedom which has been established in a considerable part of the world,
and which some of our people ... seem to see as the panacea for all that
is not to their liking ... We can prove ourselves worthy of this trust
only if we remove the scales from our mental eyes, discover clearly the
designs laid down on His trestle board by the Supreme Architect of the
Universe and perseveringly add our efforts-each in his own way-to
the upbuilding of the edifice planned by that Architect ..."

WESTERN AUSTRALIA
Communication from the M.'.W.'.Grand Master
Excerpts
To all the brethren I have selected from the many scores of worthy
Craftsmen, the thanks of Grand Lodge are due for their work in Free~
masonry, and for the standing and stability they give to the Craft. May ·
they continue to wield their influence in Freemasonry for many years to
come.
With three exceptions, who have been selected for special reasons in
the interests of the Craft, the average age of the brethren upon whom
P.M's rank has been conferred is over 70 years.
I have told you Grand Lodge is growing, and the opportunity of
serving as Grand Lodge Officers are limited. I have adopted the practice
of conferring Past Grand Rank on brethren who richly deserve it but
who, for various reasons, have had no opportunity of becoming Grand
Lodge Officers. We have reached the stage where about 230 to. 240
Worshipful Masters go out of office each year. The number of officers in
Grand Lodge is less than 60, so you will see we have an ever~increasing
burden. It has been my policy to overcome that as far as we can.
Membership
The progress of the Craft is again shown by the annual Statistics.
By a coincidence, the nett gain is the same as last year, namely 1,117,
making a total membership of 16,522. Thirteen new lodges have been
consecrated since the last Annual Communication, and several more are
in the process of formation, all of which shows a healthy state of affairs.
Golden Jubilee
On Thursday, 7th April last, Lodge Thistle, No. 180, celebrated
its Fiftieth Anniversary. To mark the event, I conferred the rank of
Past Grand Direetor of Ceremonies on Wor. Bro. E . H. M. Owen,
whose Patent of Office was presented by R.W. Bro. W. W. Raad,
P.D.G.M., who represented me on that occasion.
Whither Are We Drifting?
For any organisation that is spread throughout the world, and con~
sequently has a world outlook, the present situation is full of perplexity
and the future is both doubtful and disturbing. During the last world
war, one of the questions inost frequently asked was: what are we fight~
ing for? The late Archbishop Temple said that it was not a dog~flght be~
tween national imperialism; it was a struggle between two incompatible

544

545

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

ways of life. Surely it would be reasonable to suppose that those who
fought side by side in the allied cause were desirous of that kind of victory that would bring happiness back to the world? And yet today that
incompatibility is just as great between Western and Eastern ideologies
as it was during the war between the Allies and Germany. We fought
for victory, certainly, and obtained it. But surely victory meant more
than merely subduing the enemy. Surely we did not mean it to be barren
of any results. In a book published in 1941 by W. E. Sangster, the
author set out the opinions of various statesmen as to what they envisaged in the word victory. Mr. Churchill said we were fighting for security, and the present Prime Minister (Mr. Attlee) that we were fighting
for peace; Arthur Greenwood for a new order, and Lord Halifax for
progress; Stanley Bruce for justice, and Anthony Eden for freedom; Sir
Archibald Sinclair for decency, and McKenzie King for democracy.
When we look over the world and world affairs today can we honestly say that we have achieved any of these results? Are not the differences
and dissensions amongst nations still as great as they have ever been?
and is not that altruistic desire for a hightr and better civilization rapidly
giving way to the same selfish materialism that so largely helped to throw
the world into the cauldron of war for two generations? We are all perplexed and sometimes despairing. If victory in two world wars cannot
give us that security, peace, freedom and democracy that we fought for,
what can?
Is there any ground for hope? If not, what relief is there from despair?
I think the remedy lies in our own hands. If, as individuals, peoples and
nations we could turn our minds from the drab and selfish materialisms
of life, and look towards those things that are of God and from God, our
difficulties could be solved and the attainment of universal peace an1
brotherhood might be assured.
Two thousand years ago a still, small voice sought to change man's
attitude toward life from a state of harshness, selfishness and nationalism
to one of love, thoughtfulness and brotherhood. This new religion, beginning in the East, rapidly spread westward, and European political
structures were built upon it. Nowhere did those principles take root
more deeply than in Britain and, as the world grew, amongst Englishspeaking peoples. We have not always followed the teaching with that
sincerity that we should. Down through the centuries there have been
periods of forgetting God, but still all the time there has been an advance
on part of Western European peoples towards that higher civilization
envisaged in the Sermon on the Mount. In fact, until about sixty years
ago, the teachings of the Man of Galilee were perhaps vaguely the basis
of all civilised political structures. Then there arose an atheistic and
tyrannical movement that neither believed in God nor respected the
sanctity of human life. That movement, cradled in one Great Eastern
European Nation, has spread, principally through illiterate poople, be-

yond the confines of its own country. And so the world is faced ·today
with one of the most deadly human ideologies, which is infiltratiing its
theories into every phase of human activity. With that infiltration in other
countries we are perhaps only remotely concerned, but we are very
deeply concerned with its effect on our own Commonwealth. This evil
influence has already infiltrated itself into many activities and institutions
throughout the world and in our own Commonwealth. There are creeping
in subversive elements that would set up a tyrannical form of government, destroy the rights of citizens, and make of any country, in which
they get the upper hand, a country where life itself would be reduced
to a condition of slavery. We are liable, in Freemasonry, just as in any
other institution, to have to face such an infiltration. It, therefore, becomes of paramount importance to remember the tenets and principles of
Freemasonry and the obligations that we took when we entered the
Craft-to believe in God, to honour the King, to obey the laws, to allow
freedom within the law to our fellow men, and to be true to the ideals of
our native or adopted land.
We are reaching a stage in the history of the community as a whole
when this ideology which is destroying the Body Politic must be opposed
with all our heart and soul and strength~ I am not talking about politics;
I am talking about those things that are sapping the vitality of our Commonwealth, and that should be opposed, not only by every right-thinking
man in our own country, but by every right-thinking man in every country in the world.. As far as Freemasonry is concerned, the tenets and
principles to which we have pledged ourselves are those of Sincerity,
Charity, Tolerance, Humanity, Brotherhood and Peace. Are we going
to allow any subversive elements to come amongst us and by their actions
take away all these qualities and leave us, more or less, in a state of
slavery? Are we to be at the domination of any outside force or are we
to live as the Great Architect intended we should live as human beings,
serving God, doing justly to man and preserving peace?
I am speaking seriously, because I believe that the time has arrived
when it is necessary for everyone with a desire for the well-being of the
community to speak seriously if the canker in our midst is to be removed.
I believe, seriously, that this Commonwealth is in danger of the invasion of subversive elements. I believe that they have made their
presence felt in other institutions throughout this Commonwealth. They
may get into Freemasonry. Every one of us should be up and doing to
see that they do not. Freemasons should stand four square for all that
is true and honourable, and strive to do their best for their. fellow men,
and so endeavour to make the world better for the fact that they have
been privileged to live upon this earth. Its influence should be turned
against any movement wherehy the people, as a whole, would be called
upon to suffer because a few have the desire to secure all power and
authority. Think it over.

546

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The challenge comes to Freemasonry, as to every other respected
institution, to carry out its principles and take care that within its ranks
there shall be no subversive elements to upset the happiness of the com~
munity in which we all dwell. With the Church, our task is to keep things
on an even keel, so that by God's Grace and by the dissemination of.
high principles we can wipe out the evil influence that is trying to spread
its wings over the Commonwealth of Australia.

Grand Lodge throughout the world should prove that quality has been
sacrificed to quantity; no other feature of present trends in Freemasonry
presents more pressing need for careful attention by Lodges in all Jurisdictions. Second, is the note of warning that may be read into the statement which appears in the "Report of the Board of General Purposes"
to the United Grand Lodge of England, under date of 1st June, 1949.
We quote, p. 3: "During the past ten years, while the expenses of every
Institution have been growing, we have been fortunate in the fund of
General Purposes to have had increases in revenue which have taken
care of increases in expenditure. That is, until last year. In June of last
year it became apparent that this fortunate position was not continuing,
that expenses were continuing to grow, but that there was a diminution
in the recent great influx into Masonry and that we could not therefore
expect any further increase in expenditure to be covered by a revenue
which seemed to have reached its peak, and perhaps in s<:>me respects
to have started to decline." (End of quote.) In New South Wales,
though the influx into Masonry is still great, Lodges may well take
warning from the foregoing statement, that now is the time to consolidate their positions.
The numbers of Lodges and their members on the register of the
United Grand Lodge of England has reached an all~time high peak. In
the United States and in Canada, Grand Lodges continue to gain in
membership; and in every land in Europe, where democracy is practiced, Freemasonry is being re~established. Prior to three years ago,
Freemasonry in Continental Europe, was practiced only in Sweden and
Switzerland. In all other places in Europe organized Masonic life was
either destroyed or cancelled. By 1948, Lodges had been re-established
in Norway, Finland, Denmark, Holland, Belgium, France, Italy, Greece,
and in parts of Germany and Czechoslovakia. There is no organized
Masonry in Portugal, Spain or Russia.
Not the least important of matters claiming attention by Grand
Lodges in English-speaking countries is the problem arising out of
requests for recognition by organizations claiming to be Masonic; especially requests coming from both Europe and Latin America. The
Grand Lodge of England and the Grand Lodge of Canada have deferred consideration of such requests in order that the present general
confused conditions may he clarified.

Correspandence
Your Committee recommends that the request of the Grand Orient
of Italy be granted; that it be accorded fraternal recognition by this
Grand Lodge, with exchange of representatives. (Adopted).
Your Committee is of the opinion that the requests of the two German
Grand Lodges are premature. Germany is still an enemy country, occu~
pied by troops of our own and other nations. Future conditions, geographically, politically, Masonically, are unknown and unpredictable.
No other American Grand Lodge has recognized either of these bodies,
nor is either on the list of the Grand Lodge of England. Your Com~
mfttee feels that hasty, initial recognition by this Grand Lodge, at the
seat of our Nation's Government, would be most inappropriate.
The request of the Grand Lodge of Berlin was forwarded by Major
Harvey N. Brown, a New York Mason who served as Acting Master
of the American "Berlin Lodge U.D." existing by dispensation of the
Grand Lodge of Rhode Island. Major Brown has close personal contact
with the officials of the Berlin Grand Lodge, having assisted consid~
erably in their re~establishment. and by letter and in personal conferences with the Chairman of your Committee he strongly urged the
recognition of this group to the exclusion of any other in Germany.
Your Committee does not at this time express any opinion as to the
merits of the two German bodies. It feels that the conditions above
set forth are controlling, and recommends that both requests be denied
solely upon those grounds. without prejudice to the renewal of the
applications when stable peace and government have been re~established
in Germany.

Repart of Motion by The Board of General Purpases
"To Amend the First Schedule by inserting in the second paragraph
after the words 'British Empire' the following:
'On the recommendation of the Board of General Purposes, the
Grand Master may grant Dispensation in exceptional circumstances to
permit the admission of an unnaturalised applicant.' "
At the present time, an applicant who is not naturalised cannot sign
an application form for admission into a Lodge by reason of the fact
that he cannot take the Oath of Allegiance to the Sovereign of the
British Empire, which is incorporated in the second paragraph of the
First Schedule.
This amendment is for the purpose of giving authority to the Grand
Master to grant a dispensation in exceptional circumstances. Such
circumstances have come before the Board and a dispensation would be
recommended if the Constitution so provided. It is to enable that to be
done that this amendment is sought.

The annual returns for the year ended June 30. 1948, disclose the
highest membership yet attained in this Jurisdiction, namely, 19,430,
as compared with 18,436 as a 30/6/'47-an increase of 994 members

members of Port Darwin Lodge.
( Board of General Purposes)
Committee of Inquiry
In view of the edict of Grand Lodge requiring the establishment in
each Lodge of a Committee of Inquiry for the purpose of ensuring the
most searching inquiry into the character and qualifications of candidates, the Board recommends that each Lodge shall take steps to incorporate in its by-laws a new clause under the heading, "Committee of
Inquiry," reading"There shall be a Committee of Inquiry consisting of the Master
for the time being and three Past Masters who shall be elected at the
annual election of officers. When so directed by the Executive Committee, the Committee of Inquiry shall be responsible for inquiries into
the character and qualifications of candidates for initiation, joining or
affiliation, and shall communicate the result of such inquiries to the
Master.
"For the purpose of any such inquiry, the Committee of Inquiry
shall have power to co-opt the services of any Brother of the Lodge
and to require the intended proposer and seconder or any other member
of the Lodge to attend before it."

Grand Master's Address (Extracts From)
We live in a progressive and enlightened age. Our fixed ideas
receive rude shocks. Men are disappointing-even our faith in the
Eternal is assailed. Press reports reveal that the Craft is used by contending parties in the political world to bring about distraction to the
advantage of their cause. Unfortunately we have Brethren in our Lodges
who have forgotten their solemn promise-Belief in God, Loyalty to
their Country and its Laws. This must be upheld. I strongly appeal
to you with all the earnestness and power at my command. I counsel
you to introduce members who are above suspicion and who definitely
subscribe to the genuine tenets and principles of our Order.

ALBERTA, CANADA
June 8, 1949
After Grand Lodge had been opened in due and ample form by
M." .W." .Dr. Wm. A. Henry, Grand Master, the distinguished guests
and visitors were properly introduced and accommodated. The Grand
Master then proceeded to report his activities for the year and it was
interesting to note that Alberta, like California, is well aware. of the
great number of visitors to her lodges and also that they contmue to
visit but make no effort to affiliate; they are also cognizant of the fact
that many of their own brethren move from the jurisdiction of their
mother Lodge but for some reason do not visit or attempt to affiliate
in their new communities, these Masons, the Grand Master reports
are soon lost to Masonry, for they are no longer personally interested
in its activities.
The reports of the various Deputy District Grand Masters show
that while this Grand Lodge may be small in numbers they are certainly
very active. which of course is the real measuring stick of any fraternal
order.
One new Lodge. Ancient Landmark No. 163, was Constituted and
Consecrated during the year. There were 19 courtesy degrees con£erred by the lodges of this Jurisdiction for their sister jurisdictions.
The reports of the Grand Secretary and the Grand Treasurer show
that there are sufficient funds available to this Grand Lodge. however
the Grand Master in his address found it necessary to admonish the
brethren of the constituent lodges and remind them that several of
them found it necessary to raise their dues and in some cases, the initiation fee was also raised in order to make ends meet. He sounded a
word of warning against continued spending, reminding the brethren
of the lean 30's when it was necessary for certain lodges to curtail
many of their activities because of the lack of finances. The Committee
on Foreign Relations and Correspondence had several requests for
recognition from European and South American Grand Lodges, but all
requests except those of the Grand East of the Netherlands and the
National Grand Lodge of Sweden, were tabled until further information could be obtained. Their treatment of the Grand Lodge of California's report was of a most generous nature and gave clearly the
entire picture of California's activities for 1948.
The 45th Annual Communication was held in Edmonton, Alberta,
beginning June 1i, 1950.

78th Annual Communication
Victoria, July 16, 17, 1949
M." .W.".G. M. Ellis, Grand Master, in his address welcomed those
who might be attending for the first time and then proceeded to summarize his work for the year. It was a very busy and full year as is
evident by his report; some 42 official calls as well as special visits to
other jurisdictions among which were the State of Washington and the
Providence of Ontario. Seven new Lodges were Constituted and three
dispensations were issued to form new Lodges in this jurisdiction.
This Grand Master visited -every district in the Jurisdiction except
the Yukon District. He recommended that his successor in office make
such a visit, as it has been some time since they have had an official
call from Grand Lodge. After giving his general report he proceeded
to thank the brethren, saying in part, "Finally, my brethren, I wish to
thank you for the opportunity I have had to serve Freemasonry in this .
Grand Jurisdiction. It has been a short year, but the most outstanding
one in my life. I have tried to give my best to the Craft this year and I
hope that I have accomplished in some small way, what I set out to do,
which was wherever possible to help our membership to be better Freemasons.
"The memories which will remain, the friendships which. I have
made and the inspiration which I have received, will be all the thanks
I require, for whatever effort I may have expended during a very happy
year."
The detailed reports of the Grand Secretary and the Grand Treasurer indicate that there are funds of sufficient amounts on hand to take
care of the needs of this Grand Lodge for quite some time.
The reports of the District Deputy Grand Masters show that all
20 of the districts were extremely active and were in good, strong.
capable hands as is evident by the report of the committee and the
District Deputy Grand Master's address.
The Grand Historian gave a very complete and interesting report
on the history of Trapanier Lodge No. 83, which was written in a
style that holds the reader's interest.
The review of the Grand Lodge of California was a comprehensive
report of our activities and indicates that California is indeed highly
regarded by the Brethren of British Columbia.

B. C., commencing on the 22nd day of June, 1950.

Grand Lodge convened on July 20, 1949, a~d after the Grand Lodge
officers and distinguished guests had been seated the Grand Master,
M:.W:.T. H. Simpson, invited all Master Masons to seats in the
balcony: There were numerous distinguished guests and visitors who
were presented to the Grand Master ana through him to the Grand
Lodge of Ontario.
In his address the Grand Master thanked the brethren for the honor
they had bestowed upon him by allowing him to serve them as their
Grand Master; he spoke of the Food Parcels that were being sent to
Britain, of the service and assistance that was being derived from these
worthy projects. In complimenting his Grand Chaplain for his again
appointing as District Deputy Grand Chaplains, members of the cloth,
he said, "That through efforts like this there will be a better understanding and a closer co-operation between the Churches and the Craft."
Grand Master Simpson strongly cautioned the brethren on their procedure of investigation of candidates and recommended that all Lodges
review their methods regarding this matter and make sure that all who
are admitted are good men and true. It was very apparent that Toronto
has taken a page from the proceedings of California, for only recently
they have instituted a blood cloning service and although this service
is less than six months old, already there are some four hundred brethren
who have signified their intentions of being regular d,onors. The Grand
Master in referring to this service remarked: "The gift of one's blood
is greater than the gift of one's money. And from the reception the
service is receiving it is very apparent that this is a program that is being
welcomed with open arms by the brethren of this great city of Toronto."
152 brethren received 50 year buttons and there were 17 who received Long Service Medals ( 50 years a Past Master).

Grand Master's Address
Funeral' Ritual
In all our Masonic life I doubt if there is any place where we come
under closer scrutiny than at funerals. Aside from the relatives and

556

557

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

friends of the deceased brother there are often present some who do
not look upon us witli favor and many who are non Masons.
We have a very beautiful service, dignified. reverent and full of
comfort to the bereaved. I have heard it beautifully rendered and I
have heard it literally massacred in dignity, pronounciation and reverence. Thank goodness our lodges are not often called upon for this
service, but we should be ready.
I strongly recommend that in every lodge a team should be chosen
from the very best available material for all the spoken parts, and also
for the office of Director of Ceremonies.
In the Funeral Ritual Masonry reaches out the hand of comfort
and hope to those left behind and I have known many young men whose
thoughts have been turned to the Fraternity by the beauty of this service.

in common with all other jurisdictions. In spite of that fact our lodges

good. The personal element becomes lost; the attendance falls away
and interest lags. In the smaller lodges the personal contact is easier
and there is a stronger bond of fraternity.

Institution of Devonshire Lodge
January 18, 1949
An event unique in the history of our Jurisdiction and which could
only take place at present in two Provinces in Canada, was the institution of Devonshire Lodge, sponsored by St. George, No. 440 ( E.R.).
It is the first time that a lodge under another Jurisdiction has sponsored a lodge in our own. This was a splendid manifestation of good
will and true fraternal spirit. At the banquet the Worshipful Master
was presented with an autographed photograph of the Duke of Devonshire, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of England. The Grand Secretary was also presented with a photograph of the Grand Secretary
of the Grand Lodge of England. Started under these happy auspices
this lodge should have a bright future.

When completed this will be the fulfillment of a dream of those

public building, in every village, town and city. we have our memorials
and it is equally fitting that a room should be set aside in a Temple
that is called a Memorial.

Grand Master's Address
I think the Deputy Grand Master will agree with me that he and I
have had some very interesting experiences during the past year. In
July we went to Edinburgh as the guests of the Lodge of St. Mary's
Chapel, Edinburgh, No. 1. The occasion was the celebration of the

559

Aims and Regulations of the Craft
Declaration
1. From tim~ to time the Grand Lodge of Ireland has deemed it
desirable to set forth in precise form the aims of Freemasonry as consistently practiced under its Jurisdiction since it came into being as an
organized body in 1725 and also to define the principles governing its
relations with those other Grand Lodges with which it is in fraternal
accord.
2. In view of representations which have been received, and of
statements recently issued which have distorted or obscured the true
objects of Freemasonry, it is once again considered necessary to emphasise certain fundamental principles of the Order.
3. The first condition of admission into, and membership of, the
Order is a belief in the Supreme Being. This is essential and admits
of no compromise.
4. The Bible, referred to by Freemasons as the Volume of the Sacred
Law, is always open in the Lodges. Every candidate is required to take
his Obligation on that Book or on the Volume which is held by his

560

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

particular creed to impart sancity to an oath or promise taken upon it.
5. Everyone who enters Freemasonry is at the outset strictly forbidden to countenance any act which may have a tendency to subvert
the peace and good order of the society; he must pay due obedience
to the law of any State in which he resides or which may afford him
protection, and he must never be remiss in the allegiance due to the
Sovereign of his native land.
6. While Irish Freemasonry thus inculcates in each of its members
the duties of loyalty and citizenship, it reserves to the individual the
right to hold his own opinion with regard to public affairs. But neither
in any Lodge, nor at any time in his capacity as a Freemason, is hd
permitted to discuss or to advance his views on theological or political
questions.
7. The Grand Lodge has always consistently refused to express
any opinion on questions of foreign or domestic state policy either
at home or abroad, and it will not allow its name to be associated with
any action, however humanitarian it may appear to be, which infringes
its unalterable policy of standing aloof from every question affecting
the relations between one government and another, or between political
parties. or questions as to rival theories of government.
8. The Grand Lodge is aware that there do exist Bodies, styling
themselves Freemasons. which do not adhere to these principles, and
while that attitude exists the Grand Lodge of Ireland refuses absolutely
to have any relations with such Bodies. or to regard them as Freemasons.
9. This Grand Lodge is a Sovereign and independent Body practising Freemasonry only within the three Degrees and only within
the limits defined in its Constitution as " pure Ancient Masonry." It
does not recognize or admit the existence of any superior Masonic
authority, however styled.
10. On more than one occasion the Grand Lodge has refused, and
will continue to refuse, to participate in Conferences with so-called
International Associations claiming to represent Freemasonry, which
admit to membership Bodies failing to conform strictly to the principles
upon which the Grand Lodge of Ireland is founded. The Grand Lodge
does not admit any such claim nor can its views be represented by any
such Association.
11 . There is no secret with regard to any of the basic principles
of Freemasonry. some of which have been stated above. The Grand
Lodge will always consider the recognition of those Grand Lodges
which profess, and practise. and can show that they have consistently
professed and practised those established and unaltered principles, but
in no circumstances will it enter into discussion with a view to any new
or varied interpretation of them. They must be accepted and practised
wholeheartedly and in their entirety by those who desire to be recognized as Freemasons by the Grand Lodge of Ireland.

The first eleven paragraphs. so numbered, are an exact reprint of
the declaration that was passed at the meeting of Grand Lodge held
in Belfast on the 6th October, 1938, and which has been printed ever
since at the beginning of the book of the Laws and Constitutions. It
was decided to reprint this declaration with the three new paragraphs.
and to pu·blish the whole document, because as you will see in the first
new paragraph, the attitude of the Grand Lodge of England had been
called in question, particularly with reference to paragraph seven, which
refers to politics. The Grand Lodge of England having stated that it
stood by every word of the original declaration, suggested a conference
on the subject. After very full discussion, the Grand Master Mason
of Scotland and I assured our Brethren of the Grand Lodge of England
that we could promise the support of our respective Grand Lodges to
the new declaration which had been drafted at the conference, and
undertook to bring it forward at the next Grand Lodge meetings. the
Grand Master of the United Grand Lodge of England undertaking
to do the same.

Master Brother John Randle Moore's Address to the Grand Communication of the Grand Lodge of California in 1947, where he said:

Masonic Clubs
In the past several years Masonic clubs have been in numerous
instances irksome and a source of trouble to the Constituent Lodges
and to Grand Lodge. In my travels and visitations this year I have
heard and received much criticism of them, some of which is as follows:
1.-They draw the attention of Masons from their Lodges and
interfere with the attendance of Masons upon their Lodges or other
Lodges in the vicinity.
2.-ln their meetings a sense of freedom from Lodge-room decorum
sometimes prevails, and liberties are indulged which are not consonant
with the dignity of Masonry and which sometimes cast umbrage upon
the great institution of Masonry.
3.-Some charge and collect fees and dues and expend part thereof
for purposes not authorized by the laws or rules of this Grand Lodge.
4.-Some of these cltibs are beholden by charter and by-laws to a
national organization with headquarters outside this Jurisdiction, to
which a part of the funds of the club is sent: that the national or parent
organization, by its governing rules and regulations, by its bulletins
and its publications, is influencing or endeavoring to influence the members of the club masonically.
5.-Some of these clubs, by their solicitations and drives for membership, enlist numbers of what we call sojourning Masons: that these
brethren then consider that they belong to a Masonic organization and
probably partly for this reason do not concern themselves about dimitting to a regular Lodge: that this is a definite interference with the
processes of Masonry".
April 2, 1948. I instructed the Grand Secretary to communicate
to the Chairman of the Committee on Work and Ritual that it had come
to my attention that several of our Lodges did not display the three
movable Jewels when at work. As these Jewels are an essential part
of the furniture of a Lodge according to our ritual. they should always
be in evidence and I requested that the Committee so instruct where
necessary.
At the same time I expressed the wish (and specified that it was to
be regarded as a request and not as an order) that during my term of
Office and as a demonstration of respect and gratitude for the liberal
laws of Mexico which favor Masons and Masonry, that a Mexican flag
of the finest quality be displayed in every Lodge to the right of the
Worshipful Master's Chair when at work, the flag , if desired, to be the
gift of the D. D. G. M. in each District.

The colors unfurled before you make the national banner of our
country-the Philippines. It stands for a people united, with every
element forming an integral whole: a geographical territory without
dismemberment: a republic, democratic, free and independent.

of perpetual light that guides the destiny of our race: its eight rays are
the eight first constituent provinces.

nature and by design of the Almighty.

well as the sincerity and purity of our actions, the Masonic trinity of
Peace, Hope and Charity.

we hold on to our tropic skies.

our Flag are Masonic Symbols-the Brotherhood of men and the
Fatherhood of God. As our forefathers have dreamed of it, so may it
forever float over the land of a happy people.

Masonry In The Philippines
By Wor. Bro. Gregorio Velasco
I believe that the reason Masonry in our country does not progress,
as it should, is because of our failure or refusal to acknowledge the
loftiness of its aims. We undervalue our work: we belittle our responsibilities. On the whole, our conception of Masonic duty lacks the idealism
and high moral tone that characterize it. We seem to be satisfied just
to be called Masons for social reasons or business advantages. Hence,
the prevailing belief that our Masonic career ends with the attainment of
a master mason's degree. and that the work of the Lodge should be left
in the hands of only a few brethren. It is high time that we correct these
impressions. Everyone of us owes a tremendous duty: first, to ourselves
to make our life a worthy part of that "spiritual house not made with
hands;" and secondly, to go ou.t of the four walls of our Lodge and
endeavor to build temples of goodness and love in the hearts of others.
There is a common saying which admonishes us to hitch our wagon
to a star. In plain words, we must aim high so that even if we do not
succeed in reaching a high objective, failure will not bring us too low.
It is, I believe, a sensible policy to follow in life. Applying it to the Lodge,
if all of us brethren will so work with enthusiasm as if the honor and
prestige to the entire Masonic fraternity depended on us, it is logical to
presume that even if we may not win the acclaim of mankind by remarkable deeds, at least we will succeed in accomplishing many worthwhile
things.
Let us not be caught off-guard. The enemies of Masonry are fast

568

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

gaining ground. Miracles here and miracles there. The petals of Lipa:
the Virgin in Albay: the Crucifix in Bohol, and the image of Christ in
an Acacia tree in Pampanga-all these more or less are a signal for
Masons to be alerted. They are signs of a device of the long skirted
males of an attempt to conglomerate the minds of the Filipinos. the
young and the old, the intelligencia and the masses. We have already
heard of prominent Filipino Masons that have retracted Masonry according to our enemies: Rizal. Quezon, and others. They are even using
the Intellegencia as their instrument to win the masses, and we may
wake up, too late. to find they.have successfully violated the separation
of Church and State, the downfall of our Constitution and the people.
\Ve have already learned their attempt through the Congress of
the Philippines using our own Congressmen to introduce bills conducive
to the Church, they have succeeded already in having an optional
religious instruction in our public schools, and many more similar
concessions ahead of us.
Most Worshipful Grand Master. these are the very problems that
lay directly on the shoulders of every Mason in the Philippines and all
patriotic minded Filipinos. In my opinion, we as Masons, especially
the Grand Lodge of the Philippines, would be derelict in duty if we
fail to assist a handful of Mason-Congressmen fighting in Congress
against our aggressors in their new and scientific devices of worldly
miracles. Therefore, if democracy has to stay in the Philippines, Masons
must not cross their hands on their breasts, but assit, if not lead. those
. who are already in the battlefield championing the cause of spfritual
and intellectual freedom. Then, in this way alone can the influence
and benefits of Masonry gradually develop to spread and gain the
interest of the public, and thus serve humanity.
M. W. Bro. Clifford C. Bennett, Grand Master of Masons of the Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands Elected
for 1950-1951
The "Empire State of the South" comes to the fore page of present
day Masonic scripts in the Philippines. It is the State of Georgia of the
United States of America that has contributed one of her sons to occupy
the highest seat of authority of the Masonic world under the jurisdiction of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands
today.
Grand Master M. W. Bro. Clifford C. Bennett hails from Nichols,
Georgia. He was born on May 5, 1910.
True to his inborn trait for hard work, he immediately reorganized
his Mother Lodge soon after his release from the internment campthe Sto. Tomas University. He . assumed the responsibilities of the
Oriental Chair up to the end of 1946. M. W. Bro. Bennett is an honorary
member of several Sister Lodges. He is a 32° Mason of the Philippine
Bodies. A. & A. S. R.: and of the Rasario Villaruel Chapter No. 2,
Order of the Eastern Star.

MASONS DISSOLVED
BUDAPEST, HUNGARY, June 13, 1950-(UP)-All 19 Masonic
lodges in Hungary have been dissolved on grounds that they were
"meeting places of the enemies of the peoples republic," the Communist
Ministry of Interior said today.
